en: Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O King, having heard that supreme majesty, Mohinī [was filled with wonder].
He spoke again to the domestic priest regarding Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sins.
Mohinī said:
"O Blessed One, I have been favored by you through your compassion, since you have related this meritorious narrative concerning the Gaṅgā, which purifies all sins."
O best of the twice-born, how did Gayātīrtha become famous in the world?
Desiring to hear that, please show me compassion and speak of it now.
Vasu said:
"The sacred ford named Gayā is remembered as the best of all holy places, where the Lord of the gods, the Grandfather himself, resides. (4)
Regarding this, there is a verse sung by ancestors who desired the attainment of yoga:
"One should desire many sons, so that even if just one among them goes to Gayā. (5)
Or one should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull;
O Goddess, the supreme majesty of Gayā is the most essential of all essentials.
I shall explain in brief that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; listen.
In former times, there was a most powerful and supreme Asura named Gaya.
He performed a most terrible penance that caused distress to all living beings;
tormented by that asceticism, the gods went to Hari for the sake of his destruction.
Hari said to them, "You must become auspicious in soul;
[this shall happen] when he has been cast down upon the great body. The gods said "So be it" to Hari.
Once, having brought lotuses from the Ocean of Milk for the purpose of worshipping Śiva, he made a bed for Hari in a nearby place.
Deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, he was slain by Viṣṇu with a mace;
therefore, Viṣṇu, the wielder of the mace, is remembered as the bestower of liberation at Gayā. || 11 ||
In his body resides the pure Grandfather (Brahmā) in the form of a liṅga;
for the sake of Viṣṇu’s vehicle, he shall become a meritorious field established by sacred boundaries.
The man who performs sacrifices, ancestral rites, the offering of funeral cakes, bathing, and other such acts, shall go to heaven or the world of Brahmā; that man shall not go to hell. || 13 ||
Recognizing Gayātīrtha as supreme, the Grandfather (Brahmā) performed a sacrifice and honored the Brāhmaṇas and the sages who had assembled there.
Having created the river Sarasvatī, he stood pervading the quarters of space;
he likewise created edible and consumable fruits, as well as wish-fulfilling cows.
Having accepted wealth and other gifts out of greed during the sacrifice of Dharma, he gave the Gayātīrtha, extending five krośas, to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, having been cursed by Brahmā at Gayā, those Brahmins remained there with this curse: "May there be no learning for three generations; may there be no wealth for three generations. (17)
"Indeed, the river, the rocks, and the mountains would have become tasteless for you";
thus entreated by them, the Lord Brahmā created sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
"Indeed, the worlds are purified by the śrāddha performed at Gayā, and those who go to the world of Brahmā through it;
those who honor you shall always honor me. (19)
Knowledge of Brahman, the performance of śrāddha at Gayā, death in the house of a cow, and residence for men in Kurukṣetra—this is the fourfold liberation. (20)
O Goddess, all the oceans, rivers, as well as tanks, wells, and lakes, go to the sacred site of Gayā desiring to bathe; of this there is no doubt.

The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher's wife—all such sins, as well as those arising from association with them, are destroyed by the Śrāddha performed at Gayā. (22)
Those who died of natural causes, those killed by beasts, and those bitten by snakes—by performing a śrāddha at Gayā, they are liberated and go to heaven. || 23 ||
The fruit that a man obtains by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā cannot be described by me even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
In this very context, O Goddess, an ancient history is heard;
I shall relate it to you, O fortunate one—listen with a one-pointed mind. (25)
In the Tretā age, there was indeed a king named Viśāla; that fortunate and steadfast ruler of Viśālā, being childless, himself [honored] the foremost of the twice-born in his city.

The slayer of enemies asked for the sake of a son; those brahmins of undaunted spirit said to him, "O King, go to Gayā and satisfy the ancestors with funeral cakes according to the rules for the sake of a son."
"O hero, you will certainly become the lord of the entire earth and a giver of thousands,"—
having been addressed thus by the hosts of brahmins, that king, the ruler of Viśālā, was delighted and exerted himself with great effort.

With his mind fixed upon it, the twice-born man, seeking the welfare of his sons, went to Gayā— the most excellent of all sacred fords— and having arrived at that preeminent tirtha, he became intent on performing sacrifices for his ancestors at Gayāśiras.
While offering the funeral cakes according to the prescribed ritual, the king beheld men endowed with supreme forms in the sky—white, red, and black—and said to them: "Sirs, what is this? (30)
"Tell me all this, for a great curiosity has arisen in my mind.
Śveta said: "O King, I am your father Śveta by name, by caste, and by deed."
"And this father of mine is red-colored, a doer of cruelty, a slayer of Brahmins, and an evildoer; hear what follows regarding my great-grandfather, who is black by name, by deed, and by color. (32)
By this Kṛṣṇa, many ancient sages were indeed slain in former births;
both of these, remembered as father and son, have entered the hell named Avīci.

Therefore, he is his progenitor and he is his supreme goal; even Kṛṣṇa and I, through our own pure deeds performed over a long period of time, attained that most difficult-to-reach throne of Indra. || 34 ||

Furthermore, by you, a knower of mantras, these two were liberated through the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā; yet, by the power of that supreme sacred site, they have gone to the hell known as Avīci.
"O subduer of enemies, this water which has been offered by you is intended to gratify my fathers, grandfathers, and likewise my great-grandfathers. (36)
Therefore, O best of men, our simultaneous union with this speech has occurred; by the power of the sacred ford, we shall go to the world of the ancestors, without a doubt. (37)
There, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), these two grandfathers of yours, though transformed by sin, have attained perfection even while remaining intent upon you.
For this reason, my son, having taken these two with me, I have come; indeed, I shall now go to see you. (39)
Through the power of sacred fords (tīrtha), even a son who has killed a Brahmin can effect the liberation of his father by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā with diligent effort.
Having spoken thus, his father Sita, together with those two grandfathers,
immediately departed for his own world after bestowing blessings upon his son Viśāla.
A single visit to Gayā and a single offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) are difficult to attain; how much more so is perpetual residence in this very place? || 42 ||

However, in some cases, for those who have fallen [from their caste], the rite of readmission is performed by their own kinsmen at Gayākūpa after a year has passed, due to the constraints of place and time. (43)
Then the King of the Pretas said to a certain merchant: "For your own liberation, having seen the sacred site of Gayā, you must bathe there while endowed with purity."
"Perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) with my name in mind;
by that gift of the cake, I shall find happiness from the state of a preta. (45)
"Having said to the merchant, 'I shall attain the auspicious worlds of all those who give,' the King of the Dead, together with his followers," (46)
Having correctly and duly announced his own names in private, he departed for the unsurpassed Gayāśīrṣa after having acquired [the merit]. || 47 ||
He performed the scattering of dust for the deceased in due order,
and having placed his ancestors at the forefront, he made a gift of land.
That man of great intelligence performed the offering of funeral cakes for himself according to the prescribed rite, even without sesame seeds, as well as for his other kinsmen.
When the funeral cake had thus been offered by the merchant, they were released from their state as ghosts; having attained the status of twice-born ones, they then went to the world of Brahmā.
Milk-rice, rhinoceros meat, and iron given by sons at the ancestral rite (pitṛkṣaya) as well as goat-meat lead to infinite merit.
At Gayā, the Śrāddha rite, as well as recitations, fire-offerings, and austerities, become inexhaustible; for when performed by sons at the place of the ancestors' dissolution, they attain infinity.
Anxious and afflicted by the fear of hell, the ancestors long for sons, thinking:
"That son who goes to Gayā will deliver us. (53)
What is given at Gayā, on Dharmapṛṣṭha, in the assembly of Brahmā, as well as at Gayāśīrṣa and the Akṣayavaṭa, becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Having visited Brahmāraṇya, Dharmapṛṣṭha, and Dhenukāraṇya, and having honored one's ancestors, one shall deliver twenty generations of one's lineage.
Sin committed over a great eon (mahākalpa) is destroyed upon reaching Gayā;
likewise, a śrāddha offered at Gavi and Gṛdhravaṭa yields great fruit.
There, the footprint of Mataṅga is seen by all human beings; it proclaims the entirety of the Dharma as an example for the world itself. (57)
That meritorious forest of lotuses is frequented by the virtuous; it is there that Pāṇḍu entered the sacred ford which is the model for all.
Likewise, a Śrāddha offered at the third [site] on the Pāda, at Nikṣīrā, in Maṇḍala, at Mahāhrada, and at Kauśikī, yields great fruit. || 59 ||
The wise Mahādeva set his foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha and performed difficult austerities at sacred fords for many hundreds of years.
Even in a short time, a man devoted to dharma here casts off his evil quickly, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin. (61)
Right there, to the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, is the famous sacred site (tīrtha) known by the name Kanakanandā, frequented by hosts of Brahmanical sages.
Having bathed there, human beings go to heaven in their own bodies;
a śrāddha performed there is always declared to be inexhaustible.
Having bathed there for three days at the Niḥkṣīrā lake, O beautiful-eyed one,
and having bathed in the Mānasa lake, one should perform the śrāddha ceremony there.
Having gone to Uttaramānasa, he who performs a śrāddha there according to his capacity and according to his strength attains unsurpassed perfection. || 65 ||
He obtains divine desires and the means to liberation in their entirety;
thereafter, he should go to the Brahma-lake, which is adorned by Brahmā himself.
One attains the world of Brahmā even as the night is turning into dawn;
for there, in that lake, a meritorious sacrificial post was established by Brahmā.
Having circumambulated the sacrificial post (yūpa) from left to right, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
from there, O blessed lady, one should go to Dhenuka, which is world-renowned.
Having stayed there for one night, he who should bestow a sesame-cow will certainly go to the world of Soma, liberated from all sins. || 69 ||
O highly fortunate lady, even today there remains a great wonder as a sign of that place:
a tawny cow is still wandering upon the mountain together with her calf.
O deluder, footprints of a cow with her calf were seen there; when those footprints of the cow with her calf were observed by the best of men, [they followed them]. (71)
Whatever impure karma they possess, that perishes in an instant;
from there, one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the wise deity.
O Goddess, having approached the bull-bannered god there, one should lie down upon ashes; for a Brāhmaṇa, this shall constitute a twelve-year vow.
But for the other castes, every sin is destroyed;
from there, one should go to the mountain resounding with songs.
Wherever the footprint of Sāvitrī, which bestows great merit, is seen, there a Brāhmaṇa of praised vows should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).
By that act, O daughter of Vidhi, the twilight prayer (sandhyā) is considered performed for twelve years;
and right there, O joy of the rite, the gateway to the womb (yonidvāra) is also located.
Having attained that state, O King, a man who dwells at Gayā for both the bright and dark fortnights shall be liberated from the perilous straits of rebirth.
It purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
From there, O fortunate lady, one should go to Dharmapṛṣṭha, which yields great fruit.
Where Dharma himself resides as the protector of the world of the ancestors, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice by going there. (79)
From there, a person should go to the supreme sacred site of Brahmā;
having reached Brahmā there, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And there is the famous Phalgutīrtha, abounding in many roots and fruits;
and where the river Kauśikī flows, a śrāddha performed there is remembered as inexhaustible.
From there, one should go to Mahīdhara, which is protected by the righteous royal sage Gaya, a performer of meritorious deeds, and is enjoyed by him.
There is the lake Gayaśiras, the sacred Mahānadī river, and the highly meritorious holy site Brahma-sarovara frequented by sages.
There the venerable Agastya went toward the son of Vivasvat, where the eternal Dharmarāja always dwells.
It is there that the source of all rivers is seen,
and where Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is eternally present.
There stands the world-renowned, imperishable banyan tree named Akṣaya-vaṭa, where in ancient times a sacrifice was performed by Gaya while he was engaged in his ritual offerings.
That best of rivers remained present at the sacrifices of Gaya,
protecting Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, Gaya, and the divine mountain Raivata.
By beholding the third [form], Krauñcapāda, one is liberated from sin; likewise, by seeing Śivakara at the Śivanadī and Gadādhara at Gayā.
Having perceived the Supreme Self everywhere, one is liberated from the multitude of sins;
likewise, Viśālākṣī is at Vārāṇasī and Lalitā is at Prayāga. (89)
In Gayā, there is one named Maṅgalā, and at Kṛtaśauca, there is Saiṃhikā; whatever one staying in Gayā gives as a gift, all that attains infinity.
His ancestors rejoice because of his most excellent deed;
for by the food he gives while staying at Gayā, his ancestors become truly possessed of a son.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī within the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 44 ||
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
Vasu said:
Listen, O Mohinī, I shall describe the merit arising from Pretaśilā.
Having bestowed the greatness [of this place], one may uplift the ancestors by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Then, his stone foot having been covered by Atri with radiance, Prabhāsa emerged from the thumb of the stone, and was praised by the sages. || 2 ||
Even the Lord who resides upon the big toe is celebrated as Prabhāseśa;
and that portion of the stone which is the big toe is situated there as Pretaśilā.

Therefore, by the offering of funeral cakes and other rites, a man is released from the state of being a *preta*; likewise, a man who performs ablutions at the confluence of the Mahānadī and the Prabhāsā is liberated. (4)
Vāmadeva himself became present there, and thus it is remembered as Vāmatīrtha; then, when Rāma was entreated, he bathed in the great river.
Rāmatīrtha has arisen here, purifying all the worlds; whatever sin has been committed by men over thousands of previous births [is cleansed here].
All that goes to dissolution through bathing at Rāmatīrtha; the man who, having bathed with this mantra, performs a śrāddha ceremony [attains the same]. || 7 ||
One who offers funeral cakes at Rāmatīrtha is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, you who grant fearlessness to the gods! (8)
I bow to you, O Lord of Gods; may my sin be destroyed.
Having paid homage to Prabhāseśa, one should go to the radiant Śiva. || 9 ||
And having paid homage to that Śambhu, one should then perform the southern offering (yāmyabali), [reciting]:
"O Lord of Gods, you are the waters and indeed the lord of lights. (10)
"Quickly destroy my evil born of the actions of mind, speech, and body; [for] this buttock of the stone has been repeatedly trodden upon by Yama. (11)
The King of Dharma told the mountain, "Do not go," and thus it became known as Naga;
Yamarāja and Dharmarāja remained there, established in an immovable state.
Without making an offering to those two, a Śrāddha performed at Gayā would be fruitless;
for there are two dogs, one dark and one brindled, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata. (13)
"I shall offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) to those two; may they both be free from harm at the sacred ford, on the Pretaśila, and so forth, with sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with ghee. (14)
Having invoked the ancestors and performed meditation upon them at Mount Preta, one should, being self-restrained, offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to them with the sacred mantras.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), facing south and recollecting Kavyavāla, Anala, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman, he should proceed. (16)
May the Agniṣvātta Pitṛ-devas, the Barhiṣads, and the Somapas—those highly fortunate ones—come here; may they protect us in this place.
I have come to this Gayā for the purpose of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to my own ancestors and those born in my lineage who are my kinsmen. || 18 ||
"May they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and then performed the five-limbed prostration, he should diligently practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having thus formed the resolve for the sake of attaining the world of Brahmā from which there is no return, one should perform the śrāddha according to the rules and in the proper sequence.

Having invoked and worshipped the ancestors with mantras, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) after first kindling that spot and sprinkling it separately with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having performed the *śrāddha* for those sapindas, he should spread kusha grass on their southern side and offer water with sesame seeds to them once.

Having taken [the flour] from them with joined palms (añjali) through the pitṛ-tīrtha with effort, one should offer an imperishable piṇḍa consisting of a single handful of barley meal (saktu). || 23 ||
One should employ sesame, clarified butter, curd, honey, and so forth among the substances for the funeral cake (piṇḍa);
and having offered sesame and the other items, one should then invoke the ancestors upon the kuśa grass.

One should indeed recite these three mantras in the feminine gender during the śrāddha; having invoked the ancestors as before, one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) as previously described. || 25 ||

Whether within one's own lineage or a different lineage, when the husband and wife offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the Śrāddha rite, the cake offering, and the water libation (udakatarpaṇa) are not separate; they are ineffective if performed apart. || 26 ||
Having placed sesame seeds in the alms-bowl and filled it with auspicious water,
one should circumambulate those morsels clockwise while reciting this mantra.

He should sprinkle water three times around all [the vessels], prostrate, and ask the ancestors for forgiveness; then, having dismissed the ancestors and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should cause the gods to hear [the declaration] as witnesses.
O Mohinī, in all places one should likewise offer the piṇḍa;
however, at Gayā, one need not consider the specific time for offering the piṇḍa. || 29 ||
One should not abandon the Śrāddha at Gayā even during an intercalary month, on one's birthday, when Jupiter and Venus are in retrograde, or while Jupiter is situated in Leo.
A monk who has gone to Gayā should display his staff, even if he does not offer funeral cakes;
by placing his staff at Viṣṇupada, he is liberated along with his ancestors. || 31 ||

At Gayā, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) is prescribed to be performed with milk-rice (pāyasa), or with roasted barley flour (saktu), or with flour-cakes (piṣṭaka), or with sacrificial porridge (caru), or with rice and other such grains. || 32 ||
O fortunate lady, upon seeing Gayā, even a great sinner or an outcaste becomes purified, qualified for sacred rites, and by performing the śrāddha ceremony, attains the world of Brahmā.
One who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices does not obtain that fruit which one obtains at Phalgutīrtha. || 34 ||
Having reached Gayā, one should offer the piṇḍas which are so dear to the ancestors;
no delay should be made, nor should one create any obstacle.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather;
the mother, the grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother. || 36 ||
To the maternal grandfather, his father, the great-grandfather, and the others—may this pinda offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible. || 37 ||
For the sake of uplifting those who have died in my family and for whom no destination is known, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa). || 38 ||
For the sake of uplifting those who have no kin among their circle of relatives and whose destination is unknown, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa). || 39 ||
For the sake of the deliverance of all those who have not yet cut their teeth and those who were aborted in the womb, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa). || 40 ||
To those who have been consumed by fire, as well as others who have not been consumed by fire, and to those killed by lightning or thieves—to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa). || 41 ||
To those who died in forest fires, and those killed by lions or tigers, or by fanged or horned beasts—to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa). || 42 ||
To those who died by hanging, those killed by poison or weapons, and those who committed suicide—to them I offer this rice-ball (piṇḍa). || 43 ||
To those who have perished from hunger or thirst in the wilderness, on the road, or in the forest,
and to those [afflicted] by bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas— to them I offer this pinda.
For the sake of delivering those who dwell in Raurava, in Tāmisra, and in Kālasūtra, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa). || 45 ||
For the sake of delivering those who have gone to the world of pretas and are subject to manifold torments, I offer this ball of rice.
Having fallen into an evil rebirth and being struck down by curses and the like, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance. || 47 ||
To those who have fallen under the power of Yama’s messengers in all the hells, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance. || 48 ||
And those who have entered the womb of animals— birds, insects, and reptiles— or those residing in the womb of trees, to them I give this rice-ball offering.
To those who wander through thousands of different births by virtue of their own karma, and for whom a human birth is difficult to obtain—to them I give this ball of rice. (50)
To the ancestors and kinsmen dwelling in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, and to those who died before receiving the sacraments—to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa). || 51 ||
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas,
may they all attain satisfaction forever through this rice-ball offering.
Whether they be kinsmen or non-kinsmen, or those who were kinsmen in another birth—may this funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible. || 53 ||
Those who have died in the paternal lineage, those who have died in the maternal lineage, and those other kinsmen of the preceptor, the father-in-law, and relatives who have passed away. || 54 ||
Those in my family for whom the ancestral offerings have ceased, those deprived of sons and wives, those whose rites have been neglected, and those who are blind from birth or crippled; || 55 ||
May the funeral cake offered by me reach those in my family who were deformed, those who died in the womb, and those known or unknown; may it remain inexhaustible for them. || 56 ||

To those who are born in my paternal lineage up to Brahmā, as well as those born in my maternal lineage, and to all those connected to me in both families—to them I offer this *svadhā* rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). || 57 ||
"May the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, be my witnesses;
having reached Gayā, I have performed the rite of expiation for my ancestors. (58)
"O Lord Gadādhara, I have come to Gayā for the sake of ancestral rites;
you alone are my witness, O Blessed One, that I am now free from the three debts. (59)
On the following day, having become pure, one should go to Pretaparvata;
then, having bathed in Brahmakuṇḍa, the wise man should offer libations to the gods and others.

Having performed the invocation of the ancestors on Mount Preta while remaining self-restrained, and having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) as before, he should then cause the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be offered. || 61 ||
Then, having worshipped the supreme ancestral deities with their own mantras,
as many sesame seeds as are taken by men for the ancestral rite— || 62 ||
The Asuras flee in fear, just like Garuḍa devours snakes;
there too, O Mohinī, one should perform the entire ritual exactly as before.
Likewise, one should cast flour mixed with sesame seeds upon the Pretaparvata, saying:
"Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas."
May they all attain satisfaction with these barley-meal mixed with sesame seeds—everything that exists, moving or unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. (65)
"May all beings attain complete satisfaction by means of this alms-food offered by me;
first, however, the rite is performed at the five sacred fords (tīrthas) and at Uttaramānasa. (66)
Having sipped water and sprinkled his head with water while holding *kuśa* grass in his hand, he should go to the Northern Mental Lake and perform his bath with the mantra.
I perform my bath in the Northern Mānasa for the purification of the self,
for the attainment of success in reaching the world of the Sun and other realms, and for the liberation of my ancestors.

Having bathed, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the gods and others according to the rules: "May the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied. (69)
"May all the ancestors—the mother, maternal grandfather, and others—be satisfied.
One should perform the *sapiṇḍana* śrāddha according to the procedure prescribed in one's own sūtra. (70)

On the Aṣṭakā days, on occasions of prosperity, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of her death, one should perform the Śrāddha for one's mother separately; on other occasions, it should be performed together with that of the husband.
Oṃ, salutations be to the Sun, the Sustainer, who takes the forms of the Moon, Mars, and Mercury, and who possesses the very nature of Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. || 72 ||
Having bowed to and worshipped the Sun, one leads one's ancestors to the world of the Sun;
for there is indeed the Mānasa lake here, and therefore it is called Uttaramānasa.
From the Northern Mānasa, the silent sage should go to the Southern Mānasa;
that is called the Northern Tīrtha, which bestows liberation in the north.
To the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is the libation for the celestial sages and ancestors;
in the center is the Kanakhala Tīrtha, which bestows a supreme goal upon the ancestors. || 75 ||
A man who has bathed there shines like gold and attains purity;
therefore, that unsurpassed sacred site is renowned in the world as Kanakhala.
Therefore, on the southern side is the Dakṣiṇamānasa Tīrtha;
indeed, three Tīrthas are proclaimed within Dakṣiṇamānasa itself.
Having bathed in them according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the śrāddha ceremony separately for each; [one should say]:
"O Divākara, I am performing my bath here at Dakṣiṇamānasa. (78)

For the destruction of the flood of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and for the sake of liberation, one should perform bathing, worship, and so forth, as well as the Śrāddha rite with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka). || 79 ||
I bow to the Sun for the satisfaction of the ancestors and for their liberation, as well as for the increase of sons, grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, longevity, and health. (80)
Having seen and worshipped Maunārka, one should recite this mantra:
"And those who are the deities of the ancestors, such as Kavyavāḍ and the others... (81)
O partakers of the *svadhā* offering, you have been gratified together with my ancestors;
therefore, one should go to Phalgu-tīrtha, the most excellent among all holy places.
Liberation always comes to the performers and the ancestors through the Śrāddha;
for in ancient times, Viṣṇu, being entreated by Brahmā, became the Phalguka river.
Surely that Bhava is the Phalgutīrtha performed in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire,
wherein even a weak cow bears fruit as the wish-fulfilling Kāmadhenu, and the earth yields water.
Since Phalgutīrtha is included within creation, it is not fruitless;
indeed, so are all the sacred fords (tīrthas) throughout all the worlds.
They come to Phalgutīrtha to bathe, of this there is no doubt;
for the Gaṅgā is the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, and the Phalgu is the primordial Gadādhara himself.
And because Himavat exists in the form of a bull, they know Gaṅgā to be superior to it;
for by bathing in the waters of Phalgu, one obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices.
Today, indeed, I perform my bath in the waters of Viṣṇu at Phalgutīrtha for the sake of the ancestors' attainment of Viṣṇu’s world, and for the accomplishment of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha, a person should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the Śrāddha rite along with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka), as prescribed by his own Sūtra; then he should bow down to his grandfather.
Salutation to the auspicious God, to Īśāna and Puruṣa, to Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, and Śambhu. || 90 ||
Having bowed to the divine Grandfather (Brahmā), a person who has bathed at Phalgutīrtha and beheld the god Gadādhara should worship him with this mantra.
Having bowed down together with his ancestors, he shall lead them to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Om, salutations to Vāsudeva, and salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa. (92)
Having bathed at the five sacred fords (pañcatīrthī) dedicated to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Śrīdhara, and Viṣṇu, a man shall lead his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
The śrāddha of one who does not represent [the deceased] as having bathed with the five nectars (amṛtas) and adorned with flowers, garments, and so forth, holding a mace in hand, is fruitless.
From Nāgakūṭa, Gṛdhrakūṭa, Viṣṇu, and Uttaramānasa—this is declared to be Gayāśiras, and it is called Phalgutīrtha. || 95 ||
Below Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is the unsurpassed Phalgutīrtha;
by performing śrāddha and other rites here, all ancestors shall attain liberation.
One should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras the size of a śamī leaf; by dropping the piṇḍa under the name of anyone, one leads that person to eternal Brahman.
The god who is of unmanifest form, appearing in the shape of Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha and in the form of Phalgutīrtha and other such places, pays homage to Gadādhara.
Abiding unmanifestly in the form of mountains, stones, fruits, and so forth, the Original Sustainer likewise abides manifestly in the form of Gadādhara and others. || 99 ||
One should then go to Dharmāraṇya, where Dharma is established; having bathed in the Mataṅgavāpī, one should perform libations and the Śrāddha ceremony.
Having gone and bowed to Mataṅgeśa, one should utter this mantra:
"The deities are the authority; Śambhu and the world-protectors are the witnesses. (101)
Having come here, I have previously performed the expiation for my ancestors at this Mataṅga; one should likewise perform the Śrāddha and other rites at the Brahma-tīrtha and the well. || 102 ||
One who performs [this rite] between that well and the sacrificial post protects his ancestors;
having bowed to Dharma, the Lord of Dharma, one should pay homage to the Mahābodhi tree.
On the second day, I have described to you the ritual that bestows happiness upon the ancestors through bathing, libations, funeral cakes, worship, prostrations, and so forth. (104)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Offering the Piṇḍas," in the section concerning the Greatness of Gayā within the Dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 45 ||
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Vasu said:
"I shall now fully declare to you that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
On the third day, there is a rite that bestows the fruit of the Gayā-śrāddha.
Having bathed in the Brahma-lake, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony with the offering of the Piṇḍas, saying:
"I perform this bath in this sacred ford for the sake of liberation from the three debts."

By performing [this rite] between that well and the sacrificial post for the sake of ancestral rites, the offering of funeral cakes, libations, and the attainment of one's goals, he causes his ancestors to cross over to liberation.
Having performed his bath, he should raise up a sacrificial post, saying, "This is the sacrificial post of Brahman";
and having performed the Śrāddha at the Brahma-lake, he leads his ancestors to the world of Brahman.
The mango trees situated near the cow-pasture were established by Brahmā;
by merely watering them, the ancestors attain liberation. || 5 ||
I sprinkle this mango tree, which has arisen from the Brahma-lake, which is all-pervading and composed of all the gods, and which is the very form of Viṣṇu, for the liberation of the ancestors.
A certain sage, with a water-pot and *kuśa* grass in his hand, offered water at the root of a mango tree;
the mango trees were watered and the ancestors were satisfied. This single act is renowned for accomplishing two purposes.
Therefore, a man who, having sipped water, offers water at the root [of a tree] should not be disregarded by the wise. (7)
By circumambulating the sacrificial post (yūpa), one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
and by bowing to Brahmā, one leads the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
Oṃ, salutations to Brahmā, the unborn, the cause of the birth and other states of the universe; salutations again and again to the savior of devotees and of the ancestors. || 9 ||
Then, having offered the bali-oblation to Yama with this mantra, the practitioner remains restrained;
thus Yamarāja and Dharmarāja stand firm, their purpose unshakable.
I offer an oblation to those two for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors;
then, O Mohinī, having performed the dog-oblation with the previous mantra.
Then, being self-restrained, one should offer the "crow-oblation" with this mantra:
"Those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and likewise those of Nairṛta."
"May the crows accept the ball of rice offered by me upon the ground;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath at Brahmatīrtha while holding kuśa grass. (13)
Thus, having completed the observance on the third day, the wise man,
having bowed to the god Gadādhara, should remain devoted to celibacy.
Then one should perform the bath and other rites at Phalgutīrtha on the fourth day; thereafter, one should perform the Śrāddha with the Sapiṇḍana rite at Gayāśiras and at the Padas.
There, the actual Gayāśiras was established, taking its support from the Phalgutīrtha;
from Krauñcapāda as far as the Phalgutīrtha is the actual Gayāśiras.
Gayāśiras, the mountains, and others are present there; that very Phalgutīrtha is the mouth of the demon Gayāsura. Having bathed there, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony. || 17 ||
The primordial Lord Gadādhara, abiding for the sake of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
exists in the form of the stations of Viṣṇu and others as the cause of liberation for the ancestors.
Therein lies the divine Viṣṇupada, which destroys sins by its mere sight, and grants liberation to the ancestors through touch as well as worship. || 19 ||

Having performed the Śrāddha ceremony with the offering of the rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka), a man, having uplifted a thousand generations of his own lineage, shall lead them to the world of Viṣṇu and establish them in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having performed a śrāddha at Rudrapada, a man leads a hundred generations of his lineage, along with himself, to the auspicious city of Śiva; likewise, he does so at Brahmapada.
One who performs a śrāddha at the site of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
one who performs a śrāddha at the site of the Gārhapatya fire obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 22 ||
Having performed a śrāddha at Candrapada, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha);
having performed a śrāddha at Satyapada, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. || 23 ||
By performing a śrāddha at the site of Āvasathya, one attains the world of Soma;
by performing a śrāddha at the site of Candra, one leads the ancestors to the world of Śakra.
Furthermore, one who is faithful in the Śrāddha rite shall lead the ancestors to the station of Brahmā;
and he who is faithful in the Śrāddha rite at the station of the Sun shall lead even sinners to the city of Indra.
One who performs a śrāddha at Kārtikeyapada leads his ancestors to the world of Śiva;
having performed a śrāddha at Agastyapada, one leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Among all [deities], Kāśyapa is the most excellent; O Viṣṇu, the station of Rudra and the station of Brahmā are indeed there, and that is declared to be the most excellent of all. || 27 ||
O Mohinī, at both the commencement and the conclusion, the recollection of any one of these is remembered as bringing prosperity to the performer of the śrāddha.
In ancient times, at the sacred site of Kaśyapa, the divine sage Bhāradvāja was indeed intent on offering a śrāddha ceremony and funeral cakes (piṇḍaka) to his ancestors and others.
Then, seeing his two hands— white and black— emerging from the ground after breaking through the earth, he fell into doubt regarding his father.
Then Bhāradvāja questioned his mother Śāntā regarding which of Kaśyapa’s footprints were white and which, again, were black.
"O Mother, I must offer the funeral ball (piṇḍa); tell me of my father.
Having heard these words of the wise Bhāradvāja, she replied: || 32 ||
Śāntā said: "O highly wise Bhāradvāja, with a serene countenance, give a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to Kṛṣṇa, my son who bestows the śrāddha offerings. (33)
Then Bhāradvāja, intent on offering the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to Kṛṣṇa, was addressed by Śveta, who appeared before him: "O son, give it to me; I am your legitimate son. (34)
Kṛṣṇa said, "You are my son born of my wife; therefore, give me the funeral cake.
Śukla replied, "Since she was my wife, you are my legitimate son. (35)
The son of a woman who was self-willed first gave [the offerings] to the husband from the wife's field (kṣetrin), and then to the biological father (bījin);
thereafter, O highly fortunate one, the high-minded man, having given the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with devotion, [proceeded].
Having invited his ancestors to the Śrāddha ceremony at Viṣṇupada, Bhīṣma considered himself to have accomplished his purpose because of their direct speech.
Having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rite, as Śantanu was preparing to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), his two hands emerged at Gayāśiras.
Bhīṣma offered the funeral ball (piṇḍa) upon the ground because he had no authority over his hand;
Śantanu, being satisfied, said, "You are steadfast in the meaning of the scriptures. (39)
"May you become a seer of the three times, and may Viṣṇu be your refuge at the end;
let death come according to your own will. Having said this, he attained liberation.
While Rāma was making efforts to offer funeral cakes at the beautiful site of Rudrapada,
his father Daśaratha arrived, extending his hand from heaven.
Then, placing the Piṇḍa in Rāma's hand at the sacred site of Rudra,
Daśaratha, fearing a transgression of the scriptural injunctions, spoke to Rāma.
"O son, I have been delivered by you; indeed, the world of Rudra has become mine through the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa), for the attainment of heaven is not within my reach. (43)
And you, having ruled for a long time and protected your own subjects,
and having performed sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having said, "Together with all the people of Ayodhyā, including even the worms and insects," that king went to the supreme world of Rudra along with Rāma. || 45 ||
Having worshipped Kanakeśa, Kedāra, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana at Rathamārga, one shall deliver all of one's ancestors.
Whoever offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras by the name of those [ancestors], those residing in hell go to heaven, and those already in heaven attain liberation. || 47 ||
Whoever offers a ball of rice at Gayāśiras, even if it is only the size of a Śamī leaf, or with bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, shall lead his ancestors to heaven. || 48 ||
Wherever the footprints of Viṣṇu and others are seen, having performed a śrāddha ceremony before them, one leads the ancestors to the worlds of those whose footprints they are.
Everywhere, that Muṇḍapṛṣṭha mountain is marked by these footprints;
there the ancestors go, having been honored, to the abode of Brahmā.
Because the head of the demon Gayāsura was split in two by the mace (gadā) and washed at that sacred bathing place (tīrtha), it has since been known as Gadālola. || 51 ||
For the sage performed austerities on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha in the form of a curlew; because it bears the mark of his foot, it is therefore known as Krauñcapāda.
The stations of Viṣṇu and the other deities are situated here in the form of the Liṅga;
having performed the libation for the gods and others, one should perform the Śrāddha rite beginning from the station of Rudra.
Having performed this rite on the fourth day, O Mohinī,
the performer of the śrāddha becomes purified, authorized for ritual action, and shall partake in the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed in the sacred bathing places situated on the stone and having performed the libations and the *śrāddha* ceremony with the *sapiṇḍa* rite, those people go to the world of Brahmā.
Having abandoned their bodies upon the surface of a stone, those born from sweat, eggs, or wombs shall remain and rejoice until the dissolution of all beings.
They attain union with Viṣṇu together with seven hundred generations of their lineage.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Offering Piṇḍas at the Abodes of Viṣṇu and Others," within the Dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī on the Greatness of Gayā, in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 46 ||
Then begins the forty-seventh chapter.
Vasu said:
On the fifth day, having performed the bathing and other rites at Gadālole as before, [one should proceed].
Then a person should perform the Śrāddha rite with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka) at the Akṣaya-vata tree.
Having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other ceremonies there, one should lead the ancestors to the city of Brahmā;
then, one should feed and worship the Brahmins appointed by Brahmā.
Having performed the śrāddha rite at Akṣayavaṭa with this very effort, one should then behold, bow down to, and worship Vaṭeśa with a concentrated mind.
One should lead one's ancestors to this imperishable and eternal city of Brahmā at the great and excellent pilgrimage site Gadālole, known as Gadāprakṣālana.
I perform this bath for ultimate purification, for inexhaustible merit, and for the attainment of my own true nature—
to Him who lies beneath the banyan tree in the solitary place, absorbed in yogic sleep.
Salutations to you who assume the form of a child, who lie in the state of Yoga, who are the weapon against the tree of worldly existence, and who bring about the destruction of all sins. || 6 ||
Salutations to the giver of imperishable Brahman and to the imperishable Vaṭa tree; for by it the worlds belong to Maheśvara in the Kali age, therefore he is Gadādhara.
He became manifest in the form of a *liṅga*, and I bow to you, my great-grandfather;
by bowing to that great-grandfather, Rudra, one leads the ancestors to his supreme abode.
Having struck down the Asura Heti and split his head in two with his mace, the Lord washed that very mace there. || 9 ||
That excellent holy place became known as Gadālola;
there, Heti, the son of Brahmā and a Rākṣasa, performed a great and wonderful penance.
Having gratified Brahmā and the other gods through his ascetic penance, he chose a boon from those givers of boons,
as did the Daityas and others with various weapons and so forth, and even by men.
"May I be invincible against Kṛṣṇa, Īśāna, and the rest, beginning with the Cakra, and may I possess great strength.
Having said, "So be it," they vanished; then Heti conquered the gods.
Then Indra made Heti his weapon; thereupon Brahmā, Hara, and the other gods took refuge in Hari and said to him, "Slay Heti! || 13 ||
Hari said: "O gods, this weapon is indestructible by gods or asuras;
therefore, grant me the Brahmāstra, for with that weapon I shall slay him. (14)
Having been addressed thus, those gods then gave that mace to Viṣṇu;
Brahmā and the others said, "O Upendra, slay [the demon] with this weapon. || 15 ||
At the outset, having been addressed by the gods, Gadādhara took up that mace;
striking Heti with the mace, he gave the triple heaven back to the gods.
Then, having fasted, one should bathe before Gāyatrī at the Gāyatrī-tīrtha situated on the Mahānadī river, and thereafter perform the Sandhyā prayers.

Having performed the Śrāddha rite with the offering of the rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka), a man who bathes at the prepared sacred ford (tīrtha) in front of Sāvitrī leads his lineage to the state of Brahmanhood. || 18 ||
Having performed the midday twilight ritual, he should lead the ancestors to their place of dissolution;
then, having bathed in the Prācīsarasvatī, he should remain before the Sarasvatī.
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (sandhyā), one leads one's lineage to omniscience; one is purified from the sin of omitting the twilight devotion committed over many lifetimes.
At Viśālā, at Lilehāna, at the Tīrtha, at Bharata’s hermitage, at the footprint-marked Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, and in the vicinity of Gadādhara. || 21 ||
One who offers śrāddha and funeral cakes at the holy ford of the Ākāśagaṅgā and at the openings of the mountain ears shall lead a hundred generations of ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed in the Godāvarī and the Vaitaraṇī, one shall uplift twenty-one generations of one's kin;
likewise at the Devanadī, the Gopracāra, and the Mānasaka-pada.
One who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Puṣkariṇī, at Gadālola, at the Āmaraka Tīrtha, as well as at Koṭitīrtha and Rukmakuṇḍa, shall lead his ancestors to heaven.
O fair-eyed one, by bowing to Mārkaṇḍeyeśa and Koṭīśa, as well as to the meritorious Pāṇḍuśilā, one becomes a savior of one's ancestors.
"By a mere glance, he shall lead even those dwelling in hell who have committed grave sins to heaven";
having said this, Pāṇḍu departed for the eternal, imperishable state.
The Ghṛtakulyā, the Madhukulyā, and the great river Devikā converge there upon the rock; that place is celebrated as Madhusravā.
By bathing there and having offered the ancestral Śrāddha with the Sapiṇḍa rite, a man obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices after having gratified the host of his ancestors.
Having uplifted a thousand families, that man shall lead them to the city of Viṣṇu—
whether they be born from sprouts, born from sweat, born from eggs, or born from a womb.
Having reached Madhusravā, those who have died go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
by performing a Śrāddha at Daśāśvamedhika Haṃsatīrtha, one shall go to heaven.
Having bowed to Daśāśvamedha and Haṃsa, one shall go to the city of Śiva;
one who performs a śrāddha at the feet of Mataṅga shall dwell in the city of Brahmā.
Having churned the fires within the womb of the *śamī* tree together with Vidhi, Viṣṇu, and the others,
that churning-pit indeed became a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) that grants liberation to the ancestors.
By performing libations and offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas), the one who bathes shall attain liberation;
by bowing to Rāmeśvara and Karakeśvara, he leads his ancestors to heaven.
By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayākūpa, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
furthermore, by bathing with ashes at Bhasmakūṭa, one delivers one's ancestors.
Then, a man who has washed away his sins, having performed a ritual bath at the confluence of the Niḥkṣīrā and offering Śrāddha at Rāmapuṣkariṇī, shall lead his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
In the great river Suṣumnā, one shall uplift twenty-one generations of one's lineage;
having bathed there and bowed to Vasiṣṭheśa at that holy ford, one partakes in the merit of a horse sacrifice.
One who offers funeral cakes at Dhenukāraṇya and bathes at the sites of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), having bowed to that deity, leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed at Kardamāla, Gayānābhi, and near Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one who performs the Śrāddha rite, after bowing to Caṇḍikā, leads his ancestors to heaven.
Having worshipped the Lord of Saṅgama named Phalgucaṇḍīśa, as well as Gayāgaja, Gayāditya, Gāyatrī, and Gadādhara; || 39 ||
Gayā, Gayāśiras, and the six Gayās are bestowers of liberation;
by performing the rite of releasing a bull at Gayā, one delivers twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
Wherever he may be situated, the brahmin who has conquered his senses,
meditating upon the primordial Gadādhara, should cause the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the śrāddha to be offered.
Having uplifted a hundred lineages, he shall certainly lead them to the world of Brahmā; thereafter, having offered an excellent food offering (naivedya) consisting of curd and boiled rice, || 42 ||
Having worshipped the divine Janārdana according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and live upon that very remnant.
Because that stone rested upon the shaven back (muṇḍapṛṣṭha) of the Daitya, that mountain Muṇḍapṛṣṭha indeed bestows the world of Brahmā upon the ancestors.
When Rāma had gone to the forest, Bharata ascended the mountain and remained there;
having offered the funeral cakes and other rites to his father, he installed Rāmeśa at that very spot.
Having bathed and bowed to Rāmeśa, Rāma, and Sītā with a concentrated mind,
and having performed the śrāddha and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas), one shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
The righteous-souled one, together with his ancestors and hundreds of lineages, was established behind the sacrificial pit, with a stone placed in his right hand. || 47 ||
There, by means of ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other ceremonies, one may lead all the ancestors to the city of Brahmā;
furthermore, penance was performed at Kuṇḍa on the mountain to the south of Sītādri.
At the meritorious site of Mataṅga, one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) leads his ancestors to heaven;
for on the stone slab, Mount Antaka was indeed held in the left hand. || 49 ||
Indeed, this mountain Udayādri was brought here by the high-souled Agastya and established; one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there shall lead the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
There, Brahmā had prepared the Udyantaka pool for his own ascetic penance; and there he remained together with Sāvitrī and the two Kumāras.
Hāhā, Huhū, and others began singing and playing musical instruments; and when Agastya had bathed at midday, he performed the worship of Sāvitrī.
One who has bathed at the site of Agastya becomes a Brahmin for ten million births, wealthy and a master of the Vedas; by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there, he leads his ancestors to heaven.
That man who, having entered the womb of Brahman, then emerges,
goes to the Supreme Brahman here, liberated from the peril of the womb.
By bowing to Gayākumāra, a man attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa;
and through bathing in Somakuṇḍa and other rites, he leads his ancestors to the world of Soma.
At Bali Kākaśilā, he grants momentary liberation from crows;
having bowed to Svargadvāreśvara, he leads one from heaven to the city of Brahmā. || 56 ||
The giver of funeral cakes at the celestial Gaṅgā leads his ancestors to the stainless heaven;
on the right hand of the stone, he held a heap of ashes.
Therefore, Dharma caused that place to be named Hara; where that mountain of heaps of ashes stood, it was called Mohinī after the name of the ash.
There stands the Lord of Varesha, the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā),
and in front of him is the Rukmiṇī-kuṇḍa, while to the west flows the Kapilā river.
On the riverbank is Kapileśa, where Umā and Soma meet;
having bathed in the Kapilā, a man should bow to and worship Kapileśa.
One who offers ancestral rites (śrāddha) at Maheśīkuṇḍa shall partake in heaven;
and Gaurī, as well as Maṅgalā, being worshipped there, bestows all good fortune.
Janārdana, however, offered the funeral ball (piṇḍa) into his hand upon a heap of ashes,
using the mantra for himself and others even with the left hand and without sesame seeds.
And all those who offer a ball of rice mixed with curd go to the world of Viṣṇu;
"O Janārdana, this ball of rice is given by me into your hand. (63)
"At Gayā, you must offer a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) to me when I am dead;
and I shall offer a rice-ball to you, O Janārdana, on whose account it was given by me. (64)
"Grant [the fruit], O Lord, at Gayāśīrṣa for each and every one who has died there.
Janārdana, salutations to you; salutations to you who are the very form of the ancestors. || 65 ||
O vessel of the ancestors, salutations to you; salutations to you, the cause of liberation.
At Gayā, Janārdana himself exists in the form of the ancestors.
Upon seeing that lotus-eyed one, one is liberated from the three debts;
salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, the liberator from the three debts!
Obeisance to you, O beloved of Lakṣmī; obeisance to you, O giver of liberation to the ancestors.
By worshipping Janārdana, the lotus-eyed one, one shall go to heaven.

Having prostrated himself by touching the ground with his left knee and having performed the Śrāddha ceremony along with the offering of the Piṇḍas, he becomes an inhabitant of the world of Viṣṇu together with his brothers.
On the left foot of Śilā, however, is held the mountain Pretakūṭa;
by Dharmarāja is held the mountain consisting of the Preta-śilā, which is rich in sin.
Thrown far away by the foot of a stone through the weight of that foot, the pretas take the form of archers and seize [the victim] by the hand. || 71 ||
And many such obstacles stand apart, acting as impediments for men performing ancestral rites and other ceremonies at sacred pilgrimage sites for the sake of the liberation of their ancestors.
Through contact with the mountain of stone, Pretakūṭa has attained sanctity;
there lies Pretakuṇḍa, where the gods stand by their very footsteps.
Having performed the entire rites of the ancestral offerings and the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one may liberate the ancestors from the state of being a preta;
Gayā is meritorious among the Kīkaṭas, and the forest of Rājagṛha is sacred.
The hermitage of Cyavana is meritorious, as is the meritorious river Punarpunā; also Vaikuṇṭha, Lohadaṇḍa, Girikūṭa, and Śoṇaga.
One who performs the ancestral rites, such as offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa), there leads the ancestors to the city of Brahmā;
moreover, on the southern foot of the Śilā mountain, Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is supported.
In order to quickly restore stability for Dharmarāja, the great sages, having perfected themselves through asceticism, assumed the form of vultures as purifiers. || 77 ||
Therefore, on that mountain Gṛdhrakūṭa, Śiva resides as Gṛdhreśvara;
having seen Gṛdhreśvara and bathed there, a man goes to the city of Śambhu.

Having gone there to Gṛdhrapura, when the time has come, one should ascend to heaven; having seen Śiva, who grants liberation from debt and liberation from sin, one shall go to the auspicious state. || 79 ||
There, the Śilodaka spring is stepped upon by the mountain with its foremost foot;
there dwells Vighneśa, the destroyer of obstacles, in the form of an elephant. || 80 ||
Having seen him, one is liberated from obstacles; one should lead the ancestors to the city of Śiva.
Having bathed and seen the Gāyatrī and Gayāditya, one shall go to heaven.
Seeing a Brahmin standing at the threshold of the doorway, one becomes a savior of one's ancestors;
and he who offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at the navel shall lead his ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
For the sake of beauty, there was a supreme lotus on the back of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha; by seeing that lotus on the back of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one is liberated from sins. || 83 ||
One who dies while engaged in play must be avoided from afar by those with horns, fangs, or serpents, as well as by poison, fire, women, and water. (84)
Having acted unfavorably toward the Nāgas, he was struck by lightning; or else, he was arrested by the king himself on account of the crime of theft. || 85 ||

Delighting in the wives of others, they were slain out of hatred by their husbands; and they engaged in conflict with those of unequal status, with those of mixed castes, and with Caṇḍālas and the like. (86)

Having done so, they were slain by them; and those heretics of cruel intellect, who had taken refuge with outcasts and the like, and who gave [dead] cattle, fire, and poison, [were also destroyed]. (87)
Out of anger, those lowest of men generally resort to poison, fire, weapons, hanging, water, or falling from mountains and trees. (88)
Those who live by ignoble crafts, those who are in charge of the five slaughter-houses, those who are like eunuchs, and any others who are weaklings in sacrifices or assemblies; || 89 ||
Those who have been struck down by the Brahma-staff, those who have been slain by Brahmins, and those who are great sinners—these are proclaimed to be the fallen (patita). || 90 ||
"O Goddess, it has been told to you that purity is attained by bathing in the Gayā-kūpa with ashes; thus, the supreme majesty of Gayā has been described."
The man who listens with devotion to this [text], which pacifies all sins and bestows liberation upon the ancestors, whether during a śrāddha ceremony, on a festival day, or daily; || 92 ||
Or, O lady of excellent limbs, he who causes it to be heard shall also attain the world of Brahmā;
for this is a meritorious rite of benediction that bestows wealth and grants heaven to men. (93)
It brings fame and long life, and increases one's sons and grandsons. || 94 ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the dialogue between Mohinī and Vasu within the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Then the forty-eighth chapter begins.
Māndhātṛ said:
"O Blessed One, everything has been correctly explained by you, the compassionate Omniscient One."
The meritorious account of Mohinī’s deeds, which destroys even the greatest of sins. || 1 ||
She who, by her own power and at the command of her father, rescued her husband, son, and co-wife from the ocean of worldly existence for the sake of preserving righteousness. || 2 ||
That daughter of Brahmā, omniscient and devoted to the welfare of all the worlds, approached the domestic priest and sought refuge with her own lord.
Having heard the supreme majesty of Gayā, which grants the highest destination to the ancestors,
he again questioned the brahmin Vasu, the best among the knowers of the Vedas.
Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O King, I shall relate that which Mohinī asked Punarvasu when she had fallen into delusion, desiring to visit sacred fords.
Mohinī said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born! You are intent upon the upliftment of the world;
for I have now been graced by you, whose soul is compassionate. (6)
O Brahmin, I have heard this supreme and meritorious majesty of Gayā—a secret narrative of dharma that grants liberation to the ancestors and brings happiness. (7)
Now, O best of Brahmins, tell me the supreme majesty of Kāśī;
O Brahmin, I have previously heard something of it from the mouth of Sandhyāvalī.
"Therefore, relate to me now in detail that which has come to my memory.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Having heard those deluding words, Vasu, her domestic priest," || 9 ||
The knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences said to her, "Listen," and Vasu spoke:
"Auspicious is the city of Kāśī; blessed is the Lord Maheśvara. (10)
He who constantly serves Kāśī, the city of Viṣṇu that bestows liberation—having requested this field of Hari, the eternal Lord remains established there. || 11 ||
He worshipped that Hṛṣīkeśa, while being worshipped in turn by the gods and others.
Vārāṇasī, indeed the very essence of the three worlds,
is delightful and bestows a happy rebirth upon those who dwell there;
it is said that even those who have committed various misdeeds come here [to find liberation].
With their evil destroyed, they are free from passion and as radiant as blossoming flowers.
This is the most secret field, which brings happiness to all living beings; it bestows liberation upon all creatures, being sacred to both Viṣṇu and Śiva.

One who has killed a Brahmin, a cow, or violated the bed of his guru; one who betrays a friend, misappropriates a deposit, or follows forbidden livelihoods such as usury— one whose body is liberated from the firm fetters of worldly existence.
A mortal reaches Vārāṇasī, the city of Śiva. || 15 ||
Likewise, having reached this field frequented by gods and siddhas, a mortal through the power of his meritorious deeds shall become renowned among all the gods and asuras.
And when dead, he shall go to the supreme state. || 16 ||
Those virtuous devotees of Hari or Hara who dwell in this sacred field,
seeing [the deity] daily with reverence, being pure, saintly, and equanimous like Śambhu— they are mortals freed from fear, suffering, and sin, their ritual actions being perfectly purified.
Having shattered the dense thicket of the net of worldly existence, they attain supreme liberation. || 17 ||
It is situated two and a half yojanas from east to west, and is recorded as being half a yojana in width from south to north. || 18 ||
O auspicious lady, from the Varaṇā river as far as the Asi river, which is a dry riverbed—this extent of the sacred field has been proclaimed by Lord Śambhu. (19)
The northern journey (ayana) is to be known as Timicaṇḍeśvara; thereafter, the southern [journey] is Śaṅkukarṇa, and immediately after that is Oṃkāra.
The sacred ford named Piṅgalā is proclaimed as belonging to Agni; it should be known as a dried-up river where Lolārka resides. || 21 ||
The channel named Iḍā is proclaimed to be lunar (saumyā);
it should be known as Varaṇā, where Keśava is established. || 22 ||
Between these two, the channel which is proclaimed as Suṣumṇā is to be known as Matsyodarī; that is declared to be the discordant sound (visvara). || 23 ||
Because it was never not liberated and will never at any time cease to be liberated, this great field is therefore known as Avimukta (the Unreleased). || 24 ||
O auspicious lady, even more than Prayāga and other holy places, liberation is attained there without effort, even from that which is otherwise difficult to cross. || 25 ||
There were Cāṇḍālas of various complexions with disfigured ears, who were loathsome and whose bodies were filled with sins and the most heinous crimes. || 26 ||
The wise know that for those who are wicked, blind, wretched, miserable, sinful, and doers of evil deeds, the "Unreleased" (Avimukta) is the supreme medicine. || 27 ||
Out of compassion, Hara swiftly leads all beings to the supreme goal when the Gaṅgā, emerging from the midst of the Kṣetra, joins the lord of rivers. || 28 ||
From that time forth, O lady of auspicious countenance, that city became holy; and the Gaṅgā flowed toward the north, while the Sarasvatī flowed toward the east.
There, indeed, the skull was released by the great-souled Śiva; and those who go to that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to their ancestors, [attain success].
In the ancestral rites (śrāddha), they will be gratified, and their worlds shall be radiant;
even a slayer of a Brahmin who should ever go to Avimukta [shall attain the same].
By the majesty of that sacred field, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is averted for those men who have gone to Avimukta and performed great meritorious deeds.
For they become indeed imperishable, ageless, and bodiless, whether by ignorance or by knowledge, and whether by a woman or by a man. || 33 ||
Whatever unwholesome karma has been committed by one of evil intellect, all of that shall be reduced to ashes upon entering Avimukta. || 34 ||
A man who remains established in Avimukta always performs sacrifice with the sacrificial rite, always bestows gifts, and is indeed always an ascetic. || 35 ||
That destination which is ordained for men dwelling in Avimukta is not attained at Kurukṣetra, nor at Gaṅgādvāra, nor at Puṣkara. (36)
For all living beings, austerity and truth are the essence of everything; of this there is no doubt.
But he who dwells in Avimukta is Maheśvara himself. (37)
Those deluded men of tamasic nature who do not resort to Avimukta dwell again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and menstrual blood.
Those of evil deeds who are touched by the dust raised by the wind while staying eternally in Avimukta indeed attain the supreme goal. || 39 ||
Whatever mortal dwells there with self-restraint and a concentrated mind,
even while enjoying the three worlds, he is considered equal to one who subsists only on air.
He who dwells there for a month, subsisting on whatever food is obtained and with his senses subdued, has truly performed the great Pāśupata vow. || 41 ||
Having conquered the fear of birth and death, he goes to the supreme goal; thus he shall attain the meritorious state of ultimate liberation as well as the state of yoga. || 42 ||
Indeed, the path of yoga cannot be attained even in hundreds of other births;
yet it is obtained through the greatness of the sacred field and the power of Śaṅkara.
O lady of auspicious countenance, for one who remains there for a month eating but a single meal a day,
the sin committed throughout an entire lifetime is destroyed in that single month.
The mortal who, until the fall of his body, never leaves Avimukta and remains endowed with celibacy, shall become Śaṅkara himself.
Even if struck by obstacles, he who does not abandon Avimukta liberates himself from old age, death, and this perishable birth. (46)
But those who worship Avimuktaka until the fall of their bodies, indeed go to the divine worlds upon the vehicle of swans after they have died. || 47 ||
Even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects, if he dies in this sacred field with his devotion surrendered, shall not enter into saṃsāra again.
This excellent sacred ford on earth is the cause of both heaven and liberation;
whoever meets their death there attains emancipation, without a doubt.
The state which a yogi might attain after a thousand previous births, he attains here itself as supreme liberation immediately upon death.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, those of mixed castes, worms, Mlecchas, and those of mixed and sinful births—[all these were there]. || 51 ||
Even insects, ants, and whatever other beasts and birds there may be,
when they meet their end through time, they too are remembered as lords of the gods.
O auspicious lady, all those beings who truly cast off their lives there possess crescent moons upon their exalted crowns, have eyes on their foreheads, and have the bull as their emblem.
O Rudra, having attained you, they rejoice in the presence of Śiva—whether they are free from desire or possessed of desire, or even if they have entered the womb of an animal. || 54 ||
Those men who are constantly devoted to Śiva and do not worship others will attain liberation if they give up their lives at Avimukta; of this there is no doubt. (55)
With their minds fixed on that and their life-breaths absorbed in it, they are undoubtedly liberated while living, even those who enter the fire at Avimukta after due reflection. (56)
O Mohinī, those devotees of Śiva who are firmly resolved and practice fasting unto death attain union with Kālāgnirudra. (57)
There is no returning for them even in hundreds of millions of eons;
at the time of death, the Lord himself is present among living beings in Avimukta.
To those being impelled by their past actions, he himself grants the mantra to be whispered into the ear; and it was also spoken by Rāma for the sake of Śiva, the performer of auspicious deeds.
With a mind of extreme clarity, one should personally whisper it into the right ear of anyone who is about to die and who has not yet attained liberation.
O Śiva, at the time of death, when the karmas of men are being severed, you shall teach my mantra to him, and he shall become liberated.
For those Rudras who reside in Avimukta and bestow affection upon their devotees, no memory arises when they are driven by the wind.
Ḍimi, Caṇḍeśvara, and others bestow the Karṇajāpya mantra;
indeed, no sinner who dies in Avimukta goes to hell.
For all those who are favored by the Lord attain the supreme goal;
thus have the virtues of Avimukta been described to you merely by way of outline.
This is the detailed exposition of the ocean of jewels belonging to the Unreleased One,
for those established in knowledge and discernment who desire supreme bliss.
The resolve that was surely formed for the one led to heaven after death—that man, having abandoned his vital breaths here, is never born again anywhere. (66)
Infinite is that goal which is declared for yogins alone;
it is the seat of yoga known as the cremation ground, the sacred ford called Maṇikarṇikā.
Liberation is declared for those who have fallen due to their own karma when they are in those [holy places];
even among them, Maṇikarṇikā is the most excellent of all sacred sites.
O lady of excellent hips, it is remembered that the presence of Dhūrjaṭi is eternally established there;
and whatever fruit is traditionally ascribed to ten horse-sacrifices, [that is obtained there].
O fair-faced one, that righteous soul obtains all that by bathing there; furthermore, whoever gives even his own property to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, he likewise attains it.
That man who, having observed a fast, gratifies the Brahmins, attains an auspicious state and shines like a blazing fire. || 71 ||
He certainly attains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice by offering a lamp there; his sensory faculties flash forth with wisdom.
By the offering of incense, O Rudra, one attains the abode frequented by you—
a place characterized by a young, gentle bull accompanied by four heifers.
He who, having branded [the animal], releases it, goes to the supreme goal;
accompanied by his ancestors, he surely attains liberation—of this there is no doubt. (74)
What is the use of saying more in this regard? For one who performs acts such as dharma with Śiva as the intended goal, that shall yield infinite fruit. (75)
The merit of performing ten horse-sacrifices is proclaimed for the offering of flowers; the fruit of the agnihotra sacrifice for incense; and the fruit of gifting land for fragrant substances. (76)
In this context, the fruit of gifting a cow is proclaimed for sweeping; it is remembered that for anointing the fruit is tenfold, and for offering garlands, it is likewise tenfold.
It is remembered that [the merit] is a thousandfold for singing and a hundred-thousandfold for instrumental music;
indeed, they worship and praise Mahādeva in Avimukta.
Having reached Avimukta and worshipping the Linga, those men remain free from all sins, established in well-being, and ageless and immortal. (79)
Even after hundreds of millions of eons, there is no further rebirth for him; indeed, being ageless and immortal, he shall sport in the presence of existence.
But those who, having attained meditative absorption, being liberated in soul and composed, restrain the entire collection of their senses and chant the Śatarudriya; || 81 ||
O illustrious lady, those best of the twice-born who dwell eternally in Avimukta have already accomplished their purpose; so too shall he who observes a fast for a single day.
One obtains here the fruit of a hundred years; of this there is no doubt.
Beyond that, however, is union (sāyujya) with Gaṅgāvaruṇasaṅgama.
When the conjunction of Śravaṇa and the twelfth lunar day (Śravaṇadvādaśī) falls on a Wednesday, a man who bathes at that time shall obtain the fruit of bathing at Sannihatī. || 84 ||
O lady of auspicious countenance, he who performs a śrāddha ceremony there at that time,
having delivered all his ancestors, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
By giving a horse according to the prescribed rite at the world-renowned confluence of the Varaṇā and the Jāhnavī, one is not born again. (86)
The man who, full of devotion, worships Saṅgameśāna there, becomes the Lord of the God of Gods in person, capable of both restraint and grace. || 87 ||
To the east of Deveśvara, Keśava himself resides; and to the east of Keśava is the renowned Saṅgameśvara. || 88 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Kāśī," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī within the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 48 ||
Then the forty-ninth chapter.
Vasu said:
"O beautiful one, in the northwestern direction of that sacred seat (pīṭha)..."
There, Sagara installed a four-faced Liṅga.
To the northwest of the ocean, O Bhadra, the lake known as Bhadradēha is said to exist;
it was produced from the milk of cows and destroys all sins. || 2 ||
O Mohinī, by merely bathing there, a mortal obtains that same fruit which results from the perfect gift of a thousand tawny cows.
When the full moon occurs in conjunction with the constellation Pūrvābhādrapadā, that is indeed the most meritorious time, bestowing the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 4 ||
Where that goddess, the renowned Bhīṣmacaṇḍikā, is seen—in a cremation ground—by worshipping her there, a man shall not go to an evil state. || 5 ||
To the east of Antakeśvara and to the south of Sarveśvara, Kṛttivāseśvara is remembered as being to the north of Mātalīśvara. || 6 ||
O Goddess, by beholding Kṛttivāseśvara and worshipping him, the supreme goal is attained in a single birth;
yet the sin committed in previous lives is not purified even by austerity. || 7 ||
At that very moment, sin is destroyed by the sight of that Liṅga;
formerly it was called Tryambaka, and in the Tretā age, Kṛttivāsas. || 8 ||
In the Dvāpara age, the name of the god is sung as Maheśvara, while in the Kali age, it is sung by the Siddhas as Hastipāleśvara.
If one desires that liberating knowledge which is eternal and bestows immortality, the god Kṛttivāseśvara should be beheld again and again.
By the sight of the God of gods, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated;
by touching and worshipping him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. || 11 ||
Those who, with supreme faith and concentrated minds, worship the eternal God on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna; || 12 ||
With flowers, fruits, and likewise leaves, with various kinds of edible foods, as well as with milk, honey, water, and clarified butter. || 13 ||
They gratify the supreme Liṅga and worship the auspicious Śiva with shouts of "Ḍuṇḍuka," prostrations, as well as with dances and songs. || 14 ||
Having fasted for one night with supreme devotion to Hara, [one should worship] with many musical instruments, as well as hymns and mantras.
Having worshipped Mohinī, those who worship the Supreme Lord on the Bhūtā day in the month of Caitra go to the supreme abode. || 16 ||
Having attained the status of the Lord of Wealth, he indeed sports like the king of the Yakṣas—
he who, being self-restrained, worships Śiva on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha.
Having reached the world of Vaiśākha, he shall become an attendant of that very deity;
and whoever worships Hara with faith on the fourteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, [attains the same].
He who, being pure and self-restrained, worships Śiva on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, O auspicious lady, attains the heavenly world until the dissolution of all beings.
Having reached the world of the Sun, he sports there for as long as he desires;
on the fourteenth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the Liṅga of Kāma arose.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara during the month of Bhādrapada, one bestows the world of Varuṇa and sports accompanied by Apsarases.

By worshipping with various flowers and fruits on the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors (the dark half of Bhādrapada), one goes to the same world as Indra, having worshipped him like a lord.
Having worshipped Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, during the month of Prabhava, one attains the world of the ancestors and sports there, honored by them. (23)
Having reached the world of Candra and worshipped the wielder of the Pināka bow during the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one sports there for as long as one desires.
Having worshipped Sthāṇu with a joyful heart in the month of Pauṣa, one attains the world of Piṣṇu and sports there for imperishable time.
Having worshipped [him] in the month of Māgha with auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits, he attains the abode of Nairṛta and rejoices there together with him.
Having abandoned the ocean of worldly existence, he attains the world of Śiva;
one should worship the god Kṛttivāseśvara with great effort. || 27 ||
One should dwell in Avimukta if one desires the state of Śaṅkara;
there, to the west of Vyāseśa, is the Ghaṇṭākarṇa lake.
Having bathed in that lake and beheld Vyāseśa,
O Goddess, wherever one may die, one becomes as if dead in Vārāṇasī.
O Goddess, by bathing in Daṇḍakhāta and offering libations to one's own ancestors, those who reside in hell go instead to the world of the Pitṛs.

O Goddess, for those men who have become Piśācas due to their sinful deeds, it is traditionally taught that their bodies are delivered [from that state] by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa). || 31 ||
By the mere sight of that pit, one becomes fulfilled;
right there resides Goddess Lalitā, the bestower of happiness upon the world.
And those who, remaining in that very place, shall personally worship her, she, the giver of honor, will bestow upon them various enjoyments.
But those who keep a vigil before her with lamps,
O Mohinī, she will indeed bestow upon them imperishable worlds.
For those who prepare the dwelling and sweep the ground, there shall be the fruit of eight thousand pieces of gold. || 35 ||
O Goddess, listen to the fruit of merit for him who, with that [image] in mind, shall feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas with sweet foods. || 36 ||
