Whatever fruit is found in all the Vedas and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, that fruit a man attains by bowing down to Kṛṣṇa. (54)
Whatever fruit is obtained from all forms of giving, from religious observances, and from restrictive vows—
that same fruit a man attains by beholding Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for celibacy (brahmacarya) when it is perfectly practiced,
a man attains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him.
Whatever fruit has been declared as resulting from the householder's life as previously described,
a man attains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for a forest-dweller through the life of a vānaprastha, a man attains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him. || 58 ||
By beholding Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him, a man attains that fruit which has been declared as the result of renunciation performed according to the prescribed rules. || 59 ||
Moreover, O beautiful lady, what is the use of saying more regarding his majesty?
Having seen Kṛṣṇa with devotion, a person attains liberation, which is difficult to obtain. (60)
Freed from sins arising over ten million eons, his soul purified, endowed with supreme splendor, and possessed of all excellent qualities. || 61 ||
By means of a radiant celestial chariot (vimāna) that fulfills all desires, a person, having uplifted twenty-one generations of their family, shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Then, for as long as a hundred kalpas, he shall enjoy delightful pleasures together with Gandharvas and Apsarases, like the four-armed Viṣṇu.
Having passed away from there and come here, he is born into a family preeminent among Brahmins as one who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, and free from envy.
Devoted to his own duty, peaceful, charitable, and intent on the welfare of all beings, he shall attain Vaiṣṇava knowledge and thereby obtain liberation. || 65 ||
Then, having worshipped Subhadrā, who is affectionate toward her devotees, with the mantra according to the prescribed rite, one should propitiate her by prostrating with palms joined in reverence.
Salutations to you, O omnipresent Goddess; salutations to you, the bestower of auspiciousness and happiness.
Protect me, O lotus-petal-eyed Kātyāyanī; let there be homage to you.
In this manner, let the Goddess be propitiated— the sustainer of the world, the benefactress of the world,
the sister of Balarāma, Subhadrā, the bestower of boons, and the auspicious one.
By means of a celestial chariot that moves at his will, the man shall go to the city of Viṣṇu and sport there like a god until the dissolution of all beings.
Having attained human birth here, a Brāhmaṇa may become a knower of the Vedas;
having obtained the yoga of Hari therein, he certainly attains liberation.
Having emerged from the temple of the deity, a man who has fulfilled his duty should then bow down at the sanctuary and proceed there with a concentrated mind.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, who is made of sapphire and lies there covered by sand even while remaining invisible, one should then proceed to the city of Viṣṇu.
O Goddess, there dwells eternally that god who embodies all the gods, the uprooter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, whose form is composed of half a lion.
O auspicious lady, by beholding that god Nṛhari with devotion and bowing down to him, a mortal is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter. || 74 ||
Those men on earth who are devotees of Narasiṃha shall have no evil deed whatsoever, and whatever they desire shall come to fruition. || 75 ||
Therefore, with every effort one should take refuge in Narasiṃha, since he bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (76)
Therefore, one should always worship that lion of great prowess with devotion in the abode of Brahmā, for he bestows the fruits of all desires. (77)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, and even those born of the lowest castes,
being devoted, worshipped the best of gods who had assumed the form of a lion.
And by worshipping that best of gods, they are liberated from inauspicious suffering arising from ten million births and attain their heart's desire. (79)
O beautiful lady, it bestows the state of a god, the lordship of the immortals, the status of the Lord of Wealth, as well as that of a Yakṣa or Vidyādhara, and likewise other [attainments]. (80)
Listen, O daughter of Vidhi, to the power of Narasiṃha—
the unconquered, the immeasurable, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O lady of virtuous vows, who is able to describe all his qualities?
I shall speak of him, whose body is formed as half a lion, only in brief.
Whatever supernatural or human perfections (siddhis) are heard of here, all of them are accomplished through his grace; there is no doubt in this matter. || 83 ||
By the grace of that Lord, one’s movement becomes unimpeded in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, in the sky, in the waters, among the gods, and upon the mountains. (84)
O fortunate lady, there is nothing impossible for that god Narasiṃha, who is ever compassionate toward his devotees, within this world of the moving and the unmoving. (85)
I shall describe the ritual procedure for his worship, which brings benefit to devotees,
by means of which he who has assumed the form of a half-lion becomes propitious.
That true nature of the God remained unknown to the gods and asuras,
even as they subsisted on vegetables, barley-gruel, roots, fruits, oil-cakes, and parched grain flour.
Or else, O blessed lady, the lord of practitioners subsists on milk alone;
wearing a loincloth and a garment of bark, he is absorbed in meditation with his senses conquered. (88)
In a lonely forest region, at the confluence of rivers or on a mountain, in a field of the perfected ones (siddhakṣetra), on saline soil, and likewise at the hermitage of Narasiṃha; || 89 ||

Having installed it oneself and performed worship according to the prescribed rite, O Goddess, one who has committed minor offenses as well as even those who have committed great sins [is purified]. 90.
The practitioner shall be liberated from sins; there is no doubt about this.
Having performed a circumambulation there, one should worship Narasiṃha. || 91 ||
Having prostrated with his head before the Lord with perfumes, flowers, and incense,
he placed jasmine flowers smeared with camphor and sandalwood upon his own head.
One should offer [this] to Narasiṃha; from that, success arises, and the Blessed One is never thwarted in any of his undertakings.
Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, are not able to overcome him; how much less so the Dānavas in this world, along with the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and humans? (94)
The Vidyādharas, the hosts of Yakṣas, along with the Kinnaras and Mahoragas—
all these go to their destruction by the divine splendor of the celestial fire.
By reciting it once with the Agniśikhā mantra, one may destroy all calamities;
by reciting the divine Kavaca three times, one shall be protected from Daityas and Dānavas.
One must be protected from spirits, piśācas, and other adversaries; this divine armor, when recited three times, is impenetrable even by gods and asuras.
Within twelve yojanas, O highly fortunate lady, the god Narasiṃha, possessed of great strength and prowess, protects forever.
Then, having gone to the entrance of the cave and fasted for three nights,
he kindled the blessed Jātavedas with wood from the Palāśa tree.
There, one should offer oblations of palāśa wood fuel drenched in the three sweets;
O lotus-eyed one, twenty thousand [oblations] shall bring about both a cart and the practitioner's success.
Then, in an instant, the opening of the *kavallī* becomes manifest; thereupon, the wise man, free from hesitation, should enter the opening of the *kavallī*. (101)
As he proceeded, O Mohinī, the darkness and delusion vanished; moreover, a wide royal highway was seen there.
Then, remembering Narasiṃha, he enters Pātāla;
having gone there, being purified, he should mutter the name of that imperishable Narasiṃha.
Then thousands of women, skilled in playing the lute and waving the fly-whisk, emerged from the city and said, "Welcome! to them.
Taking hold of that lord of practitioners by the hand, they lead him inside;
then, O fair-eyed one, they cause him to drink the divine elixir.
Upon merely drinking it, one becomes possessed of a divine body and great strength;
one sports with celestial maidens until the dissolution of all beings.
When his body is severed, he is led to Vāsudeva; of this there is no doubt.
When these [visions] do not please him, he then departs once more.
A silk cloth, a trident, a sword, yellow pigment, a jewel, as well as an elixir, an alchemical potion, sandals, and collyrium. || 108 ||
And [he gave] Kṛṣṇāñjali, Subhagā, Guṭikā, Manaḥśilā, Muṇḍalā, Akṣasūtra, Ṣaṣṭhī, and likewise Sañjīvanī. || 109 ||
Having mastered the vidyā and the scriptures, the best of practitioners [visualizes] the thirty [gods] within his heart, surrounded by waves of blazing sparks from a fire.
Once placed [upon it], it burns away all sin born of ten million lifetimes;
just as poison applied to poison destroys it, so too does it destroy leprosy situated in the body. (111)
Having committed the murder of a fetus in a beautiful body or similar sins, one is purified by means of the divine rite;
for those seized by great malevolent spirits, one should visualize [the deity] blazing. 112.
Then indeed the terrible grahas will quickly weep and perish;
by tying this around the necks of children, it becomes a constant protection. || 113 ||

It certainly effects the destruction of swellings, tumors, and malevolent spells; for the eradication of disease, one should perform a fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and milk. || 114 ||
By practicing this for one month at the three junctions of the day, one shall destroy all diseases;
I see nothing, whether among the moving or the unmoving, that is incurable for this reality.
Whatever success he desires, that he certainly attains, having worshipped the Lord of Beasts one hundred and eight times. (116)
One should smear with cow's milk earth taken from seven anthills, a cremation ground, and a crossroads, mixed with red sandalwood. || 117 ||
Having fashioned an image of a lion measuring six finger-breadths, one should especially inscribe it upon birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā). || 118 ||
Having tied it around the neck of the Narasiṃha image with the accompaniment of mantras, one should worship it at a body of water and recite [the mantra] without a fixed number of repetitions.
As long as one recites the mantra for seven days with the senses restrained,
[the earth] becomes pierced by all [means] in a mere moment, even when covered by water.
Alternatively, one should worship Narasiṃha at the top of a pure tree;
by reciting the mantra eight hundred times, that [obstructing] element will be warded off for a year.
Having tied that very [substance] in a tuft of wool, the supreme practitioner should whirl it around;
in a mere moment, a great wind will arrive—of this there is no doubt. || 122 ||

Furthermore, having sprinkled it with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, the practitioner should then bury that image at the door of the person [against whom he practices]. 123.
The lineage of that person would perish; however, when it is extracted, it bestows peace.
Therefore, one should always worship the son of Brahmā with devotion.

O auspicious lady, having seen, praised, bowed to, and fully worshipped Nṛhari— the king of beasts, possessed of great heroism, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires— [one attains liberation].
Having beheld Narasiṃha, men obtain their desired fruit: kingship, heaven, and even liberation, which is difficult to attain. (126)
Liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by merely beholding that god, who bears the form of a lion, with devotion. (127)
One is liberated from all transgressions arising from body, speech, and mind, even in battle, in times of distress, in difficult terrain, or when afflicted by thieves, tigers, and the like. || 128 ||
In the wilderness, when life is in peril, amidst poisons, fires, and waters, in fear of kings and the like, in battle, or when afflicted by planetary influences and diseases; || 129 ||
Indeed, that man who remembers him is liberated from all perils, just as the great darkness goes to its destruction at the rising of the sun. || 130 ||
Likewise, upon seeing it, all afflictions go to their destruction;
this pill is a rasāyana for the feet that causes one to traverse the underworld (pātāla). 131.
When Narasiṃha is pleased, a person obtains other desired things as well; whatever desires a man contemplates while worshipping Nṛhari, he attains them.
A man attains those various desires; there is no doubt in this matter. || 133 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Majesty of Puruṣottama," within the dialogue between Vasu and Mohini in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 55 ||
Now begins the fifty-sixth chapter.
Vasu said:
Listen to something else, O highly fortunate lady, regarding that Śrī Puruṣottama.
A great multitude of sacred fords, highly meritorious and destructive of sins through the mere sight of them. || 1 ||
Having beheld Vāsudeva named Ananta and having bowed down with devotion, a person, liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme state. || 2 ||
The man who, having bathed in the Śvetagaṅgā, beholds Śvetamādhava and Mādhava known as Matsya, goes to Śvetadvīpa. || 3 ||
Resembling snow in purity, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, endowed with all the auspicious marks, and possessing long eyes like white lotuses. || 4 ||
He was endowed with the Śrīvatsa on his chest, exceedingly serene, four-armed,
with a forest garland covering his breast, and wearing a crown and armlets.
Wearing yellow garments, with well-filled shoulders and adorned with two earrings,
he was like the white son of Gaṅgā, O Indra among kings, even when touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Having touched it, the devoted followers of Viṣṇu, being composed in mind, shall go to heaven;
so too shall he who beholds this image named Mādhava, which possesses the luster of the moon.
Having bowed even once with devotion to her whose eyes resemble lotuses, who is like the color of a conch shell or cow’s milk, and who destroys all sins without exception; || 8 ||
Having indeed abandoned all desires, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
there, surrounded by celestial maidens, one remains for many Manvantaras.
Being sung of by the Gandharvas and honored by the Siddhas and Vidyādharas,
he enjoys vast pleasures at his will together with the deities.
Having passed away from there and come here, he shall become a wise Brāhmaṇa in the human world, learned in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, possessed of enjoyments, and long-lived. || 11 ||
Rich in elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles, surrounded by wealth and grain, pure, handsome, highly fortunate, and endowed with sons and grandsons. || 12 ||
Furthermore, having reached Puruṣottama at the foot of the banyan tree by the ocean, and having abandoned the body while remembering Hari, one shall then proceed to the state of peace. || 13 ||
Having beheld Śvetamādhava nearby, [he saw] Matsyamādhava, who formerly assumed the form of a Rohita fish in the waters of the single ocean.
For the purpose of seizing the Vedas, he who was stationed in the depths of the netherworld (rasātala) meditated upon the earth as a fish and established himself in that place.
Having assumed a youthful form, Mādhava, the Fish-Mādhava, liberates one from all miseries by bowing down to him with a disciplined mind. || 16 ||
He goes to the supreme abode where Lord Hari himself resides;
returning here again in due time, he shall become a king upon the surface of the earth.
Having approached Matsyamādhava, a man becomes invincible;
he becomes a donor, an enjoyer, and a warrior—a Vaiṣṇava true to his promise. || 18 ||
Having attained union with Hari, one shall thereafter obtain liberation;
thus has the majesty of Matsya-Mādhava been proclaimed by me to you. (19)
O son of Brahmā, having seen which one may obtain all desires;
I shall now describe the ritual purification at that auspicious Mārkaṇḍeya lake.
But by means of devotion, having become single-minded, bathing at all times in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake is praised as meritorious and bestowing liberation. (21)
Especially on the fourteenth day, it destroys all sins;
likewise, bathing in the ocean is praised at all times.
On the full moon day, one especially obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice, provided that the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha coincides with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism. || 23 ||

Then, with a pure disposition and a mind focused on nothing else, one should especially go to the supreme and most auspicious king of holy places (tīrtharāja), purified in body, speech, and mind. (24)
Completely liberated from all dualities, free from passion and devoid of envy,
he went to the beautiful banyan tree, the wish-fulfilling kalpa-vṛkṣa, where Janārdana himself is present.
One should perform circumambulation three times with a well-concentrated mind;
whatever sin has arisen from seven births perishes upon seeing [it]. (26)
O Mohinī, he attains vast merit and a desirable destination;
I shall declare its names along with their authoritative basis for each respective age (yuga).
They know Vaṭa as Vaṭeśvara, the peaceful, the Ancient Puruṣa;
these names of Vaṭa have been proclaimed throughout the Kṛta age and the others.
The dimensions of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree are, respectively, one yojana, three-quarters of a yojana, half a yojana, and a quarter of a yojana in the Kṛta and subsequent ages.
Having paid homage to that banyan tree with the previously mentioned mantra,
one should proceed facing south for three hundred dhanvantaras.
Where that sign is seen— the delightful gateway to heaven— a piece of wood endowed with every excellence, drawn from within the ocean.
Having prostrated and then performed worship once more, one is liberated from the flood of all sins as well as from malefic planets and the like. || 32 ||
In ancient times, Ugrasena, having gone to the ocean through the gateway of heaven,
performed ritual sipping of water (ācamana) there and, being pure, meditated upon the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Thereafter, one should assign the eight-syllable mantra—“Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya,” which the wise declare—to both the hands and the body. (34)
What need is there for many mantras that merely produce mental exertion?
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" alone accomplishes all goals. || 35 ||
Because they are the offspring (sūnu) of Nara, the waters are indeed celebrated as "Nārāḥ";
since those waters were formerly the abode of Viṣṇu, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. || 36 ||
The Vedas have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal; the twice-born have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal;
knowledge has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal; and ritual action has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal. || 37 ||
Dharma is centered on Nārāyaṇa; austerity is centered on Nārāyaṇa; charity is centered on Nārāyaṇa; and religious observance is centered on Nārāyaṇa. || 38 ||
The worlds are devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the gods are devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the eternal is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the supreme state is devoted to Nārāyaṇa. || 39 ||
The earth is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the water is devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
the fire is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; and the sky is devoted to Nārāyaṇa. (40)
Vāyu is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the mind is devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
both the ego-sense and the intellect have Nārāyaṇa as their very essence. (41)
Whatever exists— past, present, and future— that which is designated as a living being,
whether gross, subtle, or supreme, all has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
O deluder, I see nothing here superior to Nārāyaṇa;
by him all this—visible and invisible, moving and unmoving—is pervaded. (43)
For water is indeed the abode of Viṣṇu, and he is the lord of the waters;
therefore, one should thus meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of sins, as being "in the waters. (44)

Especially at the time of bathing, having approached the water and become pure, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, meditate upon him, and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands and the body. || 45 ||
One should place the syllable Oṃ on the left hip, likewise the syllable Nā on the right; the syllable Rā at the region of the navel, and the syllable Ya on the left arm.
Having placed the syllable ṆA on the right, one should place the syllable YA upon the head;
[one should likewise place them] below and above, in the heart, on the sides, at the back, and in front. || 47 ||
Having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, the wise man should thereafter begin the armor-rite:
"May Govinda protect me in the east; may Madhusūdana protect me in the south. (48)
May the god Śrīdhara protect [him] in the west, and likewise Keśava in the north; may Viṣṇu protect [him] in the southeast, and the imperishable Mādhava in the southwest.
May Hṛṣīkeśa protect [me] in the northwest, and likewise Vāmana in the northeast; may Varāha protect me upon the earth, and Trivikrama above. || 50 ||
Having thus performed the armor-rite (kavaca), one should thereafter contemplate oneself as follows:
"I am the Lord Nārāyaṇa, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. (51)
Having meditated thus, one should then recite this mantra, identifying oneself with that [deity]:
"You are Agni, O Lord of bipeds, the depositor of semen, the inflamer of desire. (52)
O Lord of Waters, you are the foremost of all beings, the imperishable master of living creatures, the source of immortality, and indeed the womb of the gods.
"O King of Tīrthas, take away all my sin; salutations be unto you!
Having uttered this according to the prescribed rite, one should then perform the ritual bath.
Otherwise, bathing at Brahmatanaya is not recommended; however, having performed the ritual sprinkling and purification with mantras dedicated to the deities of the waters, [one may bathe]. || 55 ||
O Goddess, just as the horse-sacrifice is a rite that removes all sins, so too does the recitation of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged within the water [accomplish the same].
Likewise, having recited here the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn which wipes away all sins, and having emerged [from the water], he should put on two clean and stainless garments.
Having restrained the breaths, sipped water, and performed the twilight worship, he should then stand worshipping the Sun after casting a handful of flowers and water upwards.
Then, having performed the service with arms raised and with those [prescribed] signs, one should recite the purifying goddess Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times while facing the Sun.
Having recited other solar mantras while remaining composed, and having performed circumambulation of the Sun, offered salutation, and sat down; || 60 ||
Having performed his private recitation while facing the east, he should duly offer libations to the gods, humans, sages, and his own ancestors, knowing their names and lineages.

With water mixed with sesame seeds, being well-composed and acting according to the rules, one should offer the oblation with a single hand during a śrāddha ceremony and at the time of the fire-sacrifice.
In the libation (tarpaṇa), however, one should perform both; this indeed is always the rule:
with the left hand holding [the vessel] and with the right hand [pouring].

If one, restrained in speech and with a steady body, performs the libation for the ancestors with sesame seeds out of delusion, without clearly pronouncing the name and lineage while saying "May they be satisfied," [it is ineffective].
By him the ancestors were gratified with skin, flesh, blood, and bones;
what was given while standing in water reached those on land, and what was given while standing on land reached those in water.
That water does not reach [the ancestors] which is not offered upon the earth;
for the earth was given by Virañci as an inexhaustible abode for the ancestors.
Therefore, one who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors should give right there;
for the earth was produced by him, and it is indeed established upon the earth. (67)
They dissolve into the earth itself; therefore, one should offer water upon the ground.

Having spread out *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing forward, one should invoke the deities with their respective mantras upon the grass whose tips point eastward, and likewise the ancestors upon that whose tips point southward.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Puruṣottama," within the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 56 ||
Now begins the fifty-seventh chapter.
Vasu said:
Having gratified the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others, and having sipped water while restraining one's speech—
One cubit in measure, four-cornered, with four doors, and most beautiful. || 1 ||
Having drawn a city on the shore of that great ocean, O knower of rites,
one should draw there in its center a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having thus drawn the mandala, O Mohinī, one should worship there the unborn, all-pervading Nārāyaṇa according to the ritual of the eight-syllable mantra.
Now I shall fully explain to you the supreme purification of the body:
one should contemplate the syllable *kṣa*, red in color and joined with the letter *ra*, within the heart. (4)
One should contemplate the syllable E, blazing with three points and burning away the accumulation of sins, situated in the center of the lunar disc upon the crown of the head.
Showering white-colored nectar and flooding the earth,
one whose sins have thus been shaken off shall thereafter possess a divine body.
Then the wise one should perform the placement of the eight-syllable mantra upon the body and the self;
beginning from the left foot, he should place it in successive order.
The practitioner should perform the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi) with the root mantra, as well as the five-limbed Vaiṣṇava rite and likewise the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
One should place each syllable individually upon the fingers; one should place the syllable Oṃ, the Earth, and the color white upon the left foot.
The syllable *na*, which is dark blue, is situated on the right side of the earth; one should place the syllable *mo*, which they call Time (*kāla*), upon the left hip.
The letter *nā* is the seed-syllable of the east, while the letter *rā* is established in the south;
they say *rā* is fire, and it is established in the region of the navel. || 11 ||
This letter *ya*, belonging to Vāyu, is situated on the left shoulder; the letter *ṇa* should always be known as established on the right shoulder. (12)
This letter *ya* is situated at the head, wherein the worlds are established;
having placed the syllable *oṃ* in the heart, or else the letter *vi* at the head. (13)
One should indeed place the syllable *ṣṇa* on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the syllable *ve* on the armor (*kavaca*),
the syllable *na* on the two eyes, and the syllable *ma* is declared to be the weapon (*astra*).
Vāsudeva, white in color, is established on the forehead;
and Saṅkarṣaṇa, red like fire and the sun, is on the face. || 15 ||

Pradyumna is yellow and resides in the heart; Aniruddha is situated in the genitals; and Hari, who possesses all powers, is worshipped as the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) throughout the entire body.
Viṣṇu stands before me, and Keśava behind; Govinda is on my right side, while Madhusūdana is on my left.
Above is Vaikuṇṭha, and on the surface of the earth is Vārāha; as for all the intermediate directions, Mādhava resides in them all.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
I am indeed composed of Vāsudeva, protected by Narasiṃha.
Having thus become one with Viṣṇu, one should then commence the ritual action;
just as in the body, so too in the deity, one should unite all the principles (tattvas).
The auspicious syllable ending in the letter *pha* has been taught as the remover of all obstacles;
therein, one should contemplate the mandalas of the Sun, the Moon, and Fire. (21)
One should place Viṣṇu in the center of the lotus of the intermediate world, and then, having meditated upon the supreme light of the Praṇava within one's heart.
Seated upon the pericarp is the eternal one in the form of light;
then, one should assign the eight-syllable mantra in its proper sequence.
By that [mantra], both individually and collectively, worship is considered supreme;
one should worship the eternal God with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Then, having fixed him in one's heart, one should place that four-armed Great Being, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, upon the pericarp outside.
Having meditated upon Mahāyoga, one should then invoke [the deities] in sequence:
Mīnarūpāvaha, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana.
May the boon-granting gods come before me, O Nārāyaṇa;
Sumeru shall be your footstool and a lotus-seat prepared for you. || 27 ||
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, remain here, O Madhusūdana; O God, O eternal Padmanābha, this water for the feet is for your feet.
O Viṣṇu, lotus-petal-eyed one, O Madhusūdana, O Mahādeva, accept this madhuparka prepared by me and offered by Brahmā and the other gods.
O Puruṣottama, accept this arghya offered with devotion;
then [accept] the auspicious water of the Mandākinī, which removes all sins.
Please accept this water for sipping, which has been offered by me with devotion;
you are indeed the waters and the earth, and you are likewise light and the wind. (31)
I bathe [thee] with water that merely sustains the world, which is joined with the thread of the deities and endowed with the colors of sacrifice.
"O Lord, please accept these two garments of golden hue;
O Keśava, I am no longer aware of my own body or my movements. (33)
"Accepting the fragrance offered by me, let it be anointed with the threefold [mantras] of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as recited by the Lotus-born One."
An upper garment joined with the Sāvitrī-knot is offered to you, together with divine jewels possessing a luster equal to fire and the sun. (35)
O Mādhava, ornaments shall indeed beautify the limbs, as well as the light of the sun and moon, lightning, and fire. (36)
O Lord, you alone are the lamp among all lights; may this divine essence of the forest, rich in fragrance and sweet-smelling, be accepted by you. (37)
"May this incense offered by me with devotion be accepted; and may this fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors, be accepted. (38)
"O Keśava, this food offering has been presented by me with devotion;
one should place Vāsudeva on the eastern petal and Saṅkarṣaṇa on the southern petal. (39)
One should place Pradyumna in the west and Aniruddha likewise in the north; Vārāha in the southeast and Narasiṃha in the southwest.
One should place Mādhava in the northwest, Trivikrama in the northeast, and likewise Garuḍa around the eight-syllabled deity.
Likewise, one should place the discus on the left side and the conch on the right;
similarly, one should place the great mace on the right side of the deity.
Then, the knower of the Śārṅga bow should place [the bow] to the left of the deity; he should place two divine quivers to the right and a sword on the left.
Having placed Śrī to the right, one should place Puṣṭi to the left; then, in front, one should place the forest garland, as well as the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem.
One should then assign the heart and the other [limbs] in the four directions starting from the east, and likewise assign the weapon (astra) of the God of gods in the corner.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, as well as Vāyu, Dhanada, Īśāna, Ananta, and Brahmā; || 46 ||
One should worship them with their respective mantras, both below and above;
having thus worshipped Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, as he resides within the maṇḍala.
By this very procedure, a man shall obtain his desired objects; there is no doubt in this matter regarding Janārdana residing within the mandala.
Whoever should behold [Viṣṇu] thus worshipped shall enter the imperishable Viṣṇu, by whom Keśava has been honored even once according to this rite.
Having crossed over birth, death, and old age, he who remembers Nārāyaṇa constantly with devotion and without sloth shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
Śvetadvīpa is proclaimed as his dwelling place for every day;
his salutation is joined with the syllable Oṃ and other [mantras]. (51)
The mantra of all principles (tattvas) that share the same name is thus designated;
by this very procedure, one should offer fragrant flowers.
One should perform [the rites] for each one individually in the prescribed order;
thereafter, one should bind the mudrās as they are known according to the stated sequence.
And the knower of reality should perform the recitation with the root mantra twenty-eight times, or eight times, or likewise one hundred and eight times.
And regarding rites for specific desires, one who is composed should perform them according to his capacity as prescribed;
[he should draw] a lotus, a conch, the Śrīvatsa, a mace, and Garuḍa.
The discus, the sword, and the Śārṅga bow—these eight are proclaimed as the mudrās.
Go, go to the supreme abode, O Purāṇa-Puruṣottama! (56)
That supreme state which even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not find, and which they do not know how to worship with the mantras of Hari as prescribed; // 57 //
But they, O auspicious lady, worship Acyuta here with the root mantra.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Puruṣottama," within the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī in the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 57 ||
Now begins the fifty-eighth chapter.
Vasu said:
Having thus worshipped that Puruṣottama according to the rules with devotion, [he...]
Having bowed his head, he should afterwards propitiate the ocean.
You are the vital breath of all beings in the universe, O Lord of Rivers;
O King of Tīrthas, beloved of Acyuta, salutations be unto you, protect me! || 2 ||
Having thus properly bathed in that ocean within that auspicious and excellent sacred field, he duly worshipped the flawless Nārāyaṇa on the shore.
By bowing down to Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā, as well as to the ocean, a human being obtains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices. || 4 ||
Freed from all sins and devoid of all suffering, he was a glorious lord of gods, Hari, proud of his beauty and youth.
Having sustained twenty-one generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and resounding with divine gandharvas. || 6 ||
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there and sported with the gods, he fell from that state and came here as a Brahmin, the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman.
Famous, wise, illustrious, truthful, and having conquered his senses,
such a Brahmin who knows the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras shall indeed later become a Vaishnava.
And having attained Vaiṣṇava yoga, one shall thereafter obtain liberation during an eclipse of a planet, at the transit of the sun, at the solstices, and likewise at the equinoxes.
On the beginnings of the Yugas and Manvantaras, during Vyatīpāta, on the day of the sun’s turning point,
on the full moon days of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Māgha, or on any other auspicious lunar day.
Those wise ones who bestow gifts here upon the Brahmins obtain a fruit a thousand times greater than that of other sacred fords.
Those who offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the ancestors there according to the prescribed rule,
their ancestors indeed attain imperishable satisfaction.
Thus, O Goddess, I have correctly described to you the fruit of bathing in the ocean, as well as the fruit of giving gifts and indeed of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
It bestows the fruits of dharma, wealth, and liberation; it grants longevity, fame, and renown; it provides enjoyment and liberation to men; it is auspicious and destroys evil dreams. || 14 ||
This merit, which removes all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires,
must not be told to an atheist, nor to a rogue, nor to a miser.
The sacred fords roar with their respective greatnesses individually only so long as the greatness of the King of Tīrthas is not described by the twice-born. (16)
The sacred fords, such as Puṣkara and others, bestow their own respective fruits;
but the ocean, the king of sacred fords, bestows the fruit of all sacred fords.
Whatever sacred fords, rivers, and lakes on the earth enter the ocean, by that very fact he has attained preeminence.
The ocean, the lord of rivers, is the king of all sacred fords; therefore, it is superior to all other holy places and bestows all desires.
Just as darkness comes to an end when the sun has risen,
so it is at that place where ninety-nine million sacred fords (tīrthas) truly exist.
Therefore, whatever is performed there— whether bathing, giving gifts, fire-offerings, recitation, or worship of the gods— it is declared to be inexhaustible.
Mohinī said:
"O Preceptor, tell me how this lord of rivers became salty among all the oceans; for you, O twice-born one, are omniscient. (22)
Vasu said:
"Listen, O fortunate one, I shall tell you how this ocean attained its saltiness and how it was formerly the mother of all the worlds."
O Mohinī, in the ancient order of creation, seven oceans were born;
they arose from the womb of Rādhikā, possessing divine bodies of various kinds. || 24 ||
Once, the Lord of Rādhikā, the manifest master of the cowherds, cowherdesses, and cows, was dwelling in Vṛndāvana together with his beloved.
In the midst of the circle of the rāsa dance, within a brilliantly shining pavilion of jewels,
he was united with that beloved in a most tender embrace of amorous passion.
Those seven young sons, their moment of need satisfied by drinking her breast milk,
then looked everywhere for their mother, the progenitor of the world.
Afflicted by hunger and weeping, they all approached the jeweled pavilion; there they went, their eyes fixed upon the drinking of breast milk. || 28 ||
Although all were forbidden by the groups of cowherd women stationed at the gate,
those boys, intensely enraged and desiring milk, forced their way inside.
Neglected by the cowherd girls while they remained on their mother's lap,
they went to the jeweled pavilion weeping bitterly.
O Goddess, when the mother did not call those children who were crying for milk, they cried out loudly, saying, "O Mother! Where are you? (31)
Then the youngest of them all entered that place of delight; seeing her son there, charming and capable of shattering even the heights of passion, Rādhā—
Agitated, she cursed them: "O blessed ones, go to the world of mortals without delay, since you have set yourselves to destroy my amorous passion. (33)
"Therefore, my sons, having gone to the earth, you shall remain all alone.
Having heard these words of their mother, the progenitor of the world, the sons of Viriñci [departed].
They all wept most bitterly, distressed by the fear of separation;
then the blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the remover of the suffering of those who bow before him, became gracious.
"Do not fear; I shall remain near you, my sons. You, however, shall always move about in various forms, assuming different appearances. (36)
"Stay here; let the youngest one who stands inside become salty.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the World dismissed the boys.

To provide them with consolation, he who had entered the chamber of delight remained always nearby, and he became the salt-ocean (Kṣāroda). But the others, indeed in the form of oceans such as the Ocean of Milk (Kṣīroda) and so forth, remained situated separately.
Mohinī said:
"O Guru, who is this Rādhā whom you have mentioned, the virtuous mother of the world?
Explain her true nature to me; I am eager to hear it. (39)
O observer of noble vows, since you know everything according to its true nature, the secret within the Purāṇas— the description of Rādhā and Mādhava— is yours to know.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, having heard those words of Mohinī, that great Vasu became exceedingly devoted to Govinda, his heart being deeply immersed in Him. || 41 ||
With all his limbs marked by horripilation and his heart overflowing with joy,
that best of the twice-born, overcome by infatuation, spoke to Mohinī.
Vasu said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most secret of secrets, the highly guarded account of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, which establishes the oneness with Brahman. (43)
I bow down to the Blessed One, the controller of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the ordainer of destiny, and the destroyer even of the Destroyer. 44.
O Goddess, all incarnations indeed belong to Brahmā in the form of Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa himself is the original incarnator, being both possessed of attributes (saguṇa) and devoid of attributes (nirguṇa). || 45 ||
That very Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are, in reality and by their essential nature, distinct from all material worlds; Goloka itself is beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa).
O auspicious lady, cows are determined by the knowers of the Vedas to be portions of the splendor of Oṃ;
whereas Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others are composed of material nature and fashioned from the [three] guṇas. || 47 ||
O Goddess, that fire is always considered to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) yet the producer of qualities;
O auspicious lady, all qualities are its rays, possessing manifested forms.
Those designated as arising from passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas) should be known as the indicators of the auspicious qualities of the indeterminate person. 49.
Those who have become his bodies are known as his power, which is considered to be primordial nature (prakṛti);
they call this the primary nature, which takes the form of both cause and effect.
They call the Puruṣa the witness, devoid of qualities and eternal; the Puruṣa then deposited his seed into Prakṛti, and from that, the qualities (guṇas) arose.
For from those [elements] beginning with *sattva*, the principle of *mahat* emerged;
by the will of the Puruṣa, that indeed became the manifest "I" (*ahaṃkāra*).
In that regard, O blessed lady, it became threefold, consisting of substance, knowledge, and action;
thus I am threefold: as Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa.
From the Vaikārika [ego] the mind was born, and from it the ten Vaikārika deities.
They say that the sense organs, consisting of both knowledge and action, are composed of the elements of space, wind, sun, Varuṇa, the Aśvins, Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Mitra.

O fortunate one, the ear, skin, nose, eye, and tongue are the forms of the sense-faculties (vijñānendriya); the organs of action (karmendriya) are speech, hands, the generative organ, feet, and the anus. || 56 ||
Sound was born from the tamasic [element], and from that, space itself;
from space, touch arose, and from that, wind came into being.
From that, the form of wind arose; from that, fire was born; from fire, taste emerged; and from that, water came into being. || 58 ||
From the waters fragrance was produced, and from fragrance the earth was born; indeed, the foundation of all that is moving and unmoving is seen to rest in the earth alone. || 59 ||
In the principles beginning with space, one, two, three, and four qualities are found respectively;
on earth, five qualities are proclaimed, and from that [earth] arises the "particular" (viśeṣa).
From these—Time, Illusion, and the Portion (Aṃśa)—the insentient egg was produced; it became sentient when the Conscious Being entered it through its cavity.
From that egg, Virāj was born; he lay within the waters, and from his mouth and other parts, the limbs of Virāj were produced.
And for the sake of accomplishing his word, O beautiful lady, as he stood in the water, a lotus with the brilliance of a thousand suns arose from his navel.
In that [lotus] arose the Self-Existent One, the great-grandfather of the worlds; having performed intense austerity and having obtained the permission of the Supreme Person (Puṃs), he [proceeded].
When [the body] exists, the worlds and the world-protectors were fashioned by Brahmā from the hips and other parts for the seven below, and from the loins and other parts for the seven above. (65)
By these fourteen worlds, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is said to be described;
within it, he created all beings, both stationary and moving. || 66 ||
O Goddess, from the mind of Brahmā were born the four [sages] beginning with Sanaka, and from his body were born Bhava and the others, by whom this world was caused to flourish.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Cosmic Egg," within the Puruṣottama-māhātmya of the Vasumohinī-saṃvāda in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 58 ||
Now begins the fifty-ninth chapter.
Vasu said:
"That Lord Janārdana, who is stainless and whose nature is consciousness,"
O illustrious lady, Kṛṣṇa is the embodiment of light; hear now its characteristics. || 1 ||
In Goloka, that all-pervading Lord, the Supreme Brahman alone, eternally resides within the light, assuming both visible and invisible forms.
In that world, O Mohinī, there are indeed cows, cowherds, and cowherd-maidens;
and to the east of Vṛndāvana are Śataśṛṅga and a river.
O daughter of Vidhi, as long as Prakṛti remains awake, there shall be trees named Virajas and various kinds of birds.
For that duration, the omnipresent Lord remained visible indeed in Goloka;
however, during the dissolution, the cows and other beings, being asleep, did not perceive the Supreme Lord.
Within a mass of light, he bears a lovely form; a youth, dark as a rain-cloud, clothed in yellow silken garments.
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand and adorned with a crown and other ornaments,
the Lord of Liberation sits there, radiant upon the breast of Rādhā.
She by whom Rādhā—the goddess of golden complexion, whose nature is consciousness, who is beyond primordial matter (prakṛti), and who is dearer than life itself—was worshipped. (8)
There is no difference between those two residing in the body, as they are both eternal by nature, just as there is none between whiteness and milk, or between the earth and its fragrance.
That cause of causes cannot indeed be pointed out;
that which is indefinable according to the Vedas cannot be described at all. || 10 ||
That form which is described as being within the light, beautiful and dark-complexioned, was seen by Śiva; that form is sometimes beyond the range of meditation.
From that time forward, Nārada and the others, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the yogis such as Sanaka and his brothers, came to know the desired narrative of Goloka.
They all meditate upon him as heard [in scripture], yet they have never seen him directly; even today, the eternal Śiva continues to perform penance in order to be seen face-to-face.
He does not see that form, but meditates upon the object of meditation; sometimes, O Goddess, he beholds the bodies of Rādhā and Mādhava as they play.
There, he became twofold; his left side was four-armed, with limbs of identical form and identical garments and ornaments.
In that same way, the nature of the Sun became twofold;
when that true nature was perceived by those two, they themselves became equal to it.
That four-armed form, the beloved of Lakṣmī and captivating to the mind, was indeed seen many times by Śiva and others, as well as by multitudes of devotees. (17)
O Goddess, once that four-armed form was seen by Brahmā, who was utterly bewildered regarding the task of creation; it was revealed to him directly out of compassion.
O daughter of Brahmā, Lakṣmī described this to Sanatkumāra,
while she pointed out her own essential form to Viṣvaksena, whose very body is the Absolute Truth.
O Goddess of gods, it was then taught by Nārāyaṇa to Vidhi, and from him it was meditated upon in every way; O Queen of gods, it was subsequently proclaimed by the son of Dharma to Nārada.
The entire description of Goloka is likewise permeated by Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa; she who is Rādhā, the daughter of Brahmā, the goddess worshipped by the best of gods. (21)
Out of curiosity, O fair-faced one, she herself became the form of Śiva; seeing that sudden wonder, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Lords of Yoga, [was amazed].
But Vāmadeva, filled with joy, assumed a form contrary to his own, taking on a shape suited to that occasion which was of the nature of primordial matter (mūlaprakṛti).
One should meditate day and night upon the Lord Hari, who assumes the form of Durgā; she who is Rādhā is indeed Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī.
O daughter of Brahmā, there is no difference in reality between Gaṅgā and Vidyā; she exists in five forms, having the nature of the wish-fulfilling cow. || 25 ||
He who is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhikā, is proclaimed as the Lord of Lakṣmī; he alone is Brahman, Dharma, and likewise Nārāyaṇa.
Thus the unborn Lord, established in fivefold form as both cause and effect, is meditated upon by those on the surface of the earth.
Indeed, that Śiva who is the subject bound by love is himself Rādhā’s Lord, whose form is Rādhikā, and whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
O highly fortunate lady, the Sovereign Root-Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), born from the splendor of the gods, takes the form of Kṛṣṇa and is the destroyer of the Daityas.
Satī, having become the daughter of Dakṣa, took refuge in Śiva, the Lord of the senses;
but upon hearing the censure of her husband, Satī abandoned her body.
And she was born once again in the domain of Himavat from Menā; then, having performed penance, O auspicious lady, she attained Śiva, the bestower of welfare.
In reality, Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā are intent upon deluding Śiva and are the very embodiment of the Mother of the World, for Māyā herself is all-pervading.
For this very reason, in the Brahmasūtra, Skanda and Gaṇapati likewise became Śiva himself;
Kṛṣṇa himself became Gaṇapati, and Śiva himself became Skanda. || 33 ||
Some say that Śiva himself has thus taken recourse to the form of Rādhā; since she resides upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa, no distinction between the two is perceived. (34)
Whether Kṛṣṇa is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) or Śiva is Rādhikā herself, or whether they are a single entity or a couple— it is certain that this cannot be determined by anyone.
But that reality which is inexpressible cannot be described;
for this description of the Lord's sovereignty is merely an indicative mark.
O fortunate one, know that everything which the scriptures and the Vedas describe as the Lord is merely composed of primordial nature (prakṛti) and is indeed capable of being defined. || 37 ||
But that which is inexpressible, O Goddess, is negated by the words "not this, not this";
that which remains as the residue of negation is proclaimed as the all-pervading Lord by those who have sought refuge. (38)
O blessed lady, the scripture shall be the regulator of all actions;
the agent, however, is said to be the individual soul (jīva), who is himself an omnipresent portion of the Lord.
But he who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), eternal, deluded by Māyā, O auspicious one, who is the witness himself, full, and remains associated with latent impressions (anuśaya). || 40 ||

And he does not perceive that one who dwells within him as his latent desire; yet he, whose two arms are adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, perceives the one who possesses that latent desire. || 41 ||

O Vidhinandini, those who have sought refuge should be known to be of two kinds, distinguished as the distressed (ārta) and the haughty (dṛpta); among them, the distressed are considered to be helpless. || 42 ||
Those people, whether good or bad, who have taken refuge in Mahālakṣmī and embraced her as their friend, are arrogant, endure through many births, and are fearless. || 43 ||
I shall proclaim their mantra, which proceeds according to the prescribed rule: one should utter the word "vallabha" at the end of the syllables "gopījana. (44)
One should utter the word "caraṇam" followed by "śaraṇam" and then "prapadye";
this sixteen-syllable king of mantras was revealed directly by Lakṣmī herself. || 45 ||
First to Sanatkumāra, and immediately after that to Śambhu;
then, assuming the state of a friend, [he appeared] in the midst of the multitude of gopīs.
O auspicious lady, one should contemplate oneself as being designated as Rādhā and Mādhava; one should always remain bowed before the gurus, regarding them with the disposition of a lord.

One should show honor to the Vaiṣṇavas and likewise treat others with equanimity; day and night, through the bonds of love for the two Lords, one should practice constant contemplation, and always, even on festival days, celebrate the great festivals of the sacred processions.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Puruṣottama," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī within the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 59 ||
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Vasu said:
From there, O daughter of Vidhi, one should go to the Tīrtha born from the constituent parts of the sacrifice.
There stands the auspicious and purifying lake named Indradyumna-saras. || 1 ||

Having gone there, being pure and learned, having sipped water for purification (ācamana), and having meditated upon Hari in his mind and worshipped the All-pervading Lord, he should recite this mantra: || 2 ||
O Tīrtha born from the constituent parts of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, destroyer of all sins, I perform my ablution in you today; remove my evil, salutations be unto you! || 3 ||

Having recited thus and bathed according to the rules, he should satisfy the gods, sages, ancestors, and others with water mixed with sesame seeds, and then, having sipped water, remain restrained in speech.
Having offered rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the ancestors and having worshipped Puruṣottama, a human being obtains the full fruit of ten horse-sacrifices. || 5 ||
Having uplifted seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu like a god, by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there for as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist,
he falls from that place and comes here, where he certainly attains liberation.

Having thus performed the pilgrimage to the five sacred sites (pañcatīrthī) and fasted on the eleventh day, he who beholds Puruṣottama on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha [attains the supreme goal].
Having obtained the previously mentioned fruit and having sported in the abode of Acyuta,
he goes to the supreme station from which he does not return again.
Whatever sacred fords, rivers, lakes, lotus ponds, tanks, oblong ponds, wells, and pools there are upon the earth; || 10 ||
Various rivers and oceans always visibly flow into Puruṣottama for seven days, beginning from the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Because when the deity is beheld, whatever bathing, giving of gifts, and so forth is performed by men, all of that shall become inexhaustible.
O Mohinī, the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha removes the ten sins; therefore, it is remembered as Daśaharā.
The man of firm vows who beholds Halin and Kṛṣṇa, as well as Bhadrā, at that place shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having seen Govinda, the Supreme Person, mounted upon the swing on the full moon day of Phālguna, a man who has become self-restrained shall go to the city of Govinda. || 15 ||
When the day of the equinox arrives, O fair-eyed one, having beheld Saṅkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā according to the ritual of the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha), [one attains the fruit].
A person obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, which is difficult to attain;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 17 ||
He who beholds Kṛṣṇa anointed with sandalwood paste on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha goes to the abode of Acyuta.
When the Mahājyaiṣṭhī occurs through the conjunction of the lunar mansion and the zodiacal sign, mortals should then go to Puruṣottama with great effort. (19)
Having beheld Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Bhadrā on the Mahājyeṣṭhī day, a person attains the fruit of twelve pilgrimages and even more. || 20 ||
At Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gayā, Gaṅgādvāra, Kubjāmra, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. || 21 ||
At Kokāmukha, at Śūkara, in Mathurā, in Marusthala, at Śālagrāma, at Vāyutīrtha, on Mandara, and at the ocean of the Indus. || 22 ||
At Piṇḍāraka, Citrakūṭa, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Kanakhala, Śaṅkhoddhāra, Dvārakā, and Badarikāśrama; || 23 ||
At Lohakūṭa, at Aśvatīrtha which liberates one from all sins, at Kardamāla, at Koṭitīrtha, and likewise at Amarakaṇṭaka; || 24 ||
At Lolārka, at Jambumārga, at Somatīrtha, at Pṛthūdaka, at Utpalāvartaka, at Pṛthutuṅga, and at Kubjaka; || 25 ||
And at Ekāmra, Kedāra, Kāśī, or Viraja, as well as at Kālañjara, Gokarṇa, Śrīśaila, and Gandhamādana; || 26 ||
On Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, Pāriyātra, Himavat, Sahya, Śuktimat, Gomanta, and likewise Arbuda; || 27 ||
And whatever merit is found in the Gaṅgā, O illustrious one, and in the Yamunā, in the Sarasvatī, in the Gomatī, and in the seven [rivers] that are the sons of Brahmā; || 28 ||
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Narmadā, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Kāverī, Śiprā, and likewise the Carmaṇvatī. || 29 ||
The Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Śatadrū, the Bāhudā, as well as the Ṛṣikulyā, the Marudvṛdhā, the Vipāśā, and the Dṛṣadvatī. || 30 ||
The Sarayū, the Nākagaṅgā, the great river Gaṇḍakī, the Kauśikī, the Karatoyā, the Trisrotā, and the Madhuvāhinī. || 31 ||
The great river Vaitaraṇī and those others which have not been mentioned— all of them are said to be no equal to the sight of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa on the great Jyeṣṭhī day.
Therefore, with every effort, those who desire the fruit of all their wishes should go to Puruṣottama on the day of Mahājyaiṣṭhī, O daughter of Vidhi.
Having seen Rāma on the full moon of Jyeṣṭha and Kṛṣṇa on the auspicious day of Subhadrā,
a man goes to the world of Viṣṇu, having uplifted a hundred generations of his lineage.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings,
he returns here upon the exhaustion of his merit and becomes a twice-born master of the four Vedas.
One who is devoted to his own duty, peaceful, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and has conquered his senses,
having resorted to Vaiṣṇava yoga, shall thereby attain liberation.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, under the lunar mansion presided over by Indra (Jyeṣṭhā),
a bath in the waters of the ocean on the full moon day is then highly recommended.
Then there stands a pure, water-filled well embodying all sacred fords;
likewise, Bhogavatī is certainly manifest there in person.
Therefore, O Mohinī, having drawn water with golden and other jars during the month of Jyeṣṭha for the sake of the consecration of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā; || 40 ||
Having constructed a very beautiful couch, adorned with banners, firm and easy to traverse, and decorated with cloths and flowers; || 41 ||
It was spacious, perfumed with incense for the bathing of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, draped with yellow garments, and hung with strings of pearl necklaces. || 42 ||
There, having placed Kṛṣṇa, who was dressed in blue garments, upon a couch along with Bhadrā amidst various kinds of musical instruments and the sounds of auspicious victory hymns; || 43 ||
O Mohinī, she was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others, as well as by men and women.
Then householders, bath-graduates (snātakas), ascetics, and celibate students bathe Kṛṣṇa, who is on the bier along with Balarāma.
Likewise, O beautiful one, all the holy fords previously mentioned bathe [the deity] individually with sweetmeats mixed with flowers. || 46 ||
Afterwards, with the sounds of kettledrums and conchs, the resonance of bherīs and murajas, the calls of kāhalas, the clapping of cymbals, as well as mṛdaṅgas and jharjharas; || 47 ||
And with various other musical instruments mingled with the sound of bells, along with the auspicious voices of women and delightful sounds of praise. || 48 ||
With shouts of victory, hymns of praise, and the sounding of lutes and flutes,
a very great noise was heard, like the roaring of the ocean.
With the Vedic recitations of the sages, with other sounds of mantras, and with various meritorious sounds of hymns augmented by the chanting of the Sāmaveda; || 50 ||
Rāma and Keśava were fanned with yak-tail whisks having jeweled handles by dark-complexioned courtesans dressed in yellow and red garments. || 51 ||
By the yakṣas, vidyādharas, siddhas, gods, gandharvas, and cāraṇas; by the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts. || 52 ||
The world-protectors and others likewise praise the Supreme Person:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Ancient Supreme Person! (53)
O God who effects creation, preservation, and destruction; O Lord of the worlds, Master of the universe;
the God who is the refuge of the three worlds, devoted to Brahman, and the cause of liberation.
Having thus praised Kṛṣṇa and the exceedingly powerful Rāma, the gods bowed with devotion to Him who bestows the fruits of all desires. (55)
And at that time, O twice-born one, the gods and Gandharvas stationed in the sky sang to Subhadrā, while the Apsarases danced.
Divine musical instruments were sounded, cool breezes blew, and then clouds moving through the sky rained down a shower mixed with flowers. || 57 ||
And the sages, the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, all the gods beginning with Śakra, as well as the Ṛṣis and the Pitṛs, raised shouts of victory.
The lords of creatures, the Nāgas, and others who dwell in heaven, [honored him] with auspicious materials, preceded by ritual and mantras. (59)
Taking the materials for the consecration, the hosts of deities—
Indra and Viṣṇu of great prowess, as well as Sūrya and Candramas— [approached].
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, as well as Anila and Anala, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aryaman, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvat, and Aṃśumat; || 61 ||
The wise one was accompanied by Rudra and Śibi, as well as by Mitra and Varuṇa, along with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Vālakhilyas, and the sons of Marīci.
The Grandfather (Brahmā), Pulastya, and Pulaha of great asceticism were there, along with the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, all of whom were firmly established in every branch of knowledge.
Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Atri, Marīci, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Hara, Pracetas, Manu, and Dakṣa likewise. (64)
O best of the twice-born, the seasons, the planets, the luminaries, the personified rivers, and the eternal gods were also present. || 65 ||
O best of the twice-born, Subhadrā, the lakes, various sacred fords (tīrthas), the earth, the sky, the cardinal directions, and the trees [all came there]. (66)
Aditi the mother of the gods, Hrī, Śrī, Svāhā, Sarasvatī, Umā, Śacī, Sinīvālī, as well as Anumati and Kuhū. || 67 ||
Rākā and Dhiṣaṇā were the wives, as were the other wives of the inhabitants of heaven;
Himavat was the best of mountains, Vāmana the king of serpents,
and there were Pāriyātra, Vindhya, and Meru with its many peaks.
Erāvata with his followers, as well as the Kalās, the Kāṣṭhās, the months, the fortnights, the seasons, the nights and days, and the years. || 69 ||
Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses; Vāmana, the king of elephants;
Aruṇa and Garuḍa; and the creepers together with medicinal herbs.
The Blessed Lord Dharma, Kāla, Yama, Mṛtyu, and those who are the followers of Yama, all arrive from every direction.
And because of their great number, those various hosts of deities who come from here and there for the sake of the god's consecration have not been mentioned.
With golden jars endowed with divine materials, as well as with the meritorious waters of the Sarasvatī that are truly celestial; || 73 ||
Standing in the sky, they bathed Kṛṣṇa, who was united with Rāma, with excellent flowers and water from jars drawn from the celestial Gaṅgā.
Likewise, the celestial palaces of the gods move about in the sky—divine, of various heights, moving at will, and stable. || 75 ||
Variegated with divine jewels, they were frequented by throngs of apsarases and adorned on all sides with songs, musical instruments, and banners. || 76 ||

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Consecration," in the section concerning the Greatness of Puruṣottama within the Dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 60 ||
Now begins the sixty-first chapter.
Vasu said:
Thus, at that time, Kṛṣṇa was united with Rāma, the son of Vidhi.
And the highly fortunate ones, filled with joy, offered praises to Subhadrā. || 1 ||
The gods said:
Victory, victory to you, O Guardian of the World! Victory, O Padmanābha, Supporter of the Earth!
Victory, victory to you, O Primordial God, Cause of all causes! || 2 ||
Victory, victory to Vāsudeva! Victory to the one who possesses true conduct and performs good deeds!
Victory, victory to the divine Fish! Victory to the best among the gods! || 3 ||
Victory, victory to You who recline upon the ocean! Victory, victory to Lord of Yoga! Victory, O upholder of the Vedas!
Victory, victory to You whose form is the universe! Victory, O wielder of the discus! || 4 ||
Victory, victory to you, O Lord of Beings! Victory, O Abode of Śrī! Victory, victory to you, O Best of Yogis!
Victory, victory to you, O Sun-eyed One! Victory to you, O Divine Varāha! 5.
Victory, victory to you, O enemy of Kaiṭabha! Victory, victory to you, O best of the Vedas!
Victory, victory to you in the form of the Tortoise! Victory to you, O best of sacrifices! 6.
Victory, victory to you, O lotus-navelled one! Victory to you, O upholder of the mountain!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord of Yoga! Victory to you, O possessor of speed! || 7 ||
Victory, victory to you, O Universal Form! Victory, O Wielder of the Discus!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord of Beings! Victory, O Supporter of the Earth! || 8 ||
Victory, victory to You who recline upon Śeṣa! Victory to You, O wearer of yellow garments! Victory to You, O beloved of the Moon! Victory to You, O dweller in Yoga! Victory, victory! 9.
Victory to you, O abode of Dharma, who burn away the cycle of existence! Victory, victory to you, O treasure-house of virtues! Victory to you, O Śrīnivāsa! Victory, victory! 10.
Victory to you, O Garuḍa-throned one! Victory, O abode of bliss! Victory, victory, victory, victory, O beloved of Dharma! Victory, victory, O abode of wisdom! 11.
Victory, victory to you who dwell in the depths of the forest;
victory, victory to you who are accessible to yogis; victory to you who dwell in the sacrifice! 12.
Victory, victory to you, O one known through the Vedas! Victory, O bringer of peace! Victory, victory to you, O one contemplated by yogis! Victory, O bringer of nourishment! || 13 ||
Victory, victory to you, O embodiment of knowledge! Victory, O source of the lotus!
Victory, victory to you, who are to be known through devotion! Victory, O bestower of liberation! 14.
Victory to you of pure body! Victory, victory to you, the abode of courage! Victory, victory to you, the collection of virtues! Victory, victory to you, the performer of sacrifice! 15.
Victory, victory to you who are devoid of qualities! Victory, victory to you, the bestower of liberation!
Victory, victory to you, the treasure of the earth! Victory, victory to you, endowed with splendor! 16.
Victory, O refuge of the world! Victory, victory, O Lord of Lakṣmī! Victory, O lotus-eyed one! Victory, victory, O Creator! || 17 ||
Victory to You, endowed with yoga; victory to You whose body is dark like the atasi flower!
Victory, victory to You who have taken up the form of Subhadrā; victory to You whose body is the enjoyment of Lakṣmī’s lotus! || 18 ||
Victory, victory to you, O embodiment of devotion, whose praises are sung by the world!
Victory, O beloved of the world! Victory, O supremely peaceful one! 19.
Victory, victory to you, O supreme essence! Victory, O wielder of the discus!
Victory, O one endowed with enjoyments! Victory, O blue-robed one! || 20 ||
Victory to you, O one praised by the Sāṅkhyas; victory to you, O remover of impurity;
victory, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World; victory to you, younger brother of Saṅkarṣaṇa! || 21 ||
Victory, victory to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one! Victory, O bestower of desired fruits!
Victory to you, whose chest is adorned with a garland! Victory to you, the wielder of the discus and the mace!
"Victory to you, O beloved of Padmālayā! Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! Salutations be unto you!
Having thus praised him, the gods, headed by Śakra, were then delighted in their minds. (23)
The Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and others who dwell in heaven, having seen him, praised him, and bowed down with their inner selves absorbed in him. || 24 ||
They went each to their own residence,
having obtained that fruit which is traditionally said to result from the gift of a hundred tawny cows at Puṣkara.
Having beheld that dark-complexioned one on the couch along with Halāyudha, one obtains the fruit which is proclaimed to result from the gift of a hundred maidens. || 26 ||
Beholding that image of Kṛṣṇa situated upon the platform, a man obtains that fruit which results from the gift of land made with gold weighing a hundred niṣkas. || 27 ||

And that fruit is equal to the fruit obtained by the gift of food, by hospitality toward all guests, by the ritual release of a bull, and by the giving of water during the summer season according to the rules. (28)
By the gift of sesame seeds and a milch-cow, by the giving of elephants, horses, and chariots, by the performance of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, and likewise by fasting for a month; || 29 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained at all sacred fords through vows and gifts, that same fruit Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, together with Subhadrā, shall obtain by beholding them upon the dais.
Therefore, O Mohinī, if a man or a woman should behold that Puruṣottama with the water remaining from Kṛṣṇa’s bath, [they shall attain the goal]. (31)
Whether they be barren, or those whose children have died, the unfortunate, those afflicted by planetary influences, those seized by Rākṣasas and the like, or those overwhelmed by diseases; || 32 ||
When consecrated according to the prescribed rite, O lady of radiant luster, they immediately attain purification and obtain their desired objects, whatever else they may long for.
Whatever other meritorious waters exist upon the surface of the earth, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the water remaining after one has bathed here.
Therefore, one should sprinkle all the limbs of the Lord who reclines upon the waters with the water remaining from His bath, which grants all desires.
Those who behold Kṛṣṇa after he has bathed and as he proceeds facing the south are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. (36)
O Kṛṣṇa, by beholding you facing south, a man obtains that fruit which is declared in the scriptures to result from circumambulating the earth three times.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed on earth for the pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā), one obtains that same fruit by seeing Kṛṣṇa going toward the south.
Whatever fruit is traditionally declared to come from bathing at Gaṅgādvāra, Kubjāmra, Kurukṣetra, Akaparvaṇi, Puṣkara, and other such places; || 39 ||
And having beheld that fruit, which was black and facing south as it departed, what more need be said? Such is the fruit of meritorious action. (40)
Having observed that fruit in the Vedas, Shastras, Puranas, the Mahabharata, the Samhitas, and other texts, the skillful-faced Subhadra, Bala, and Keshava [acted].
Those who behold Kṛṣṇa, together with Bhadra and Balarāma, seated upon the chariot as He proceeds to the Guṇḍicā pavilion, go to the abode of Hari.
By performing the pilgrimage even once at the time of the Guṇḍicā procession, on the full moon of Phālguna, or likewise at the equinox, a person goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 43 ||
For as many journeys as a person intoxicated with pride makes to Śrī Puruṣottama, for that many kalpas shall he dwell in the world of Viṣṇu; this is the settled conclusion.
O daughter of Vidhi, O destroyer of sins, when twelve complete circumambulations have been performed according to the rite, then one should perform the consecration according to the prescribed rule.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the eleventh day, being composed,
having gone to a holy body of water, and having sipped water, he should remain restrained and pure.
Having invoked all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and likewise meditated upon Nārāyaṇa,
one should then perform the bath according to the path prescribed by the rules.
Having bathed properly, he should then satisfy the gods, the sages, his own ancestors, and others as well, preceded by the recitation of their names and lineages.
Having crossed over and put on two clean, stainless washed garments,
and having sipped water according to the rule, he likewise performed the ritual worship of the Sun.
Having recited the meritorious Mother of the Vedas one hundred and eight times, as well as the solar mantras and other [mantras], and having circumambulated three times, O Sage, one should bow down.
The bath and the recitation of prayers prescribed in the Vedas have been declared for the three castes.
O beautiful lady, for women and Śūdras, [the worship] is devoid of the rites prescribed in the Vedas;
therefore, they should go with devotion to Śrī Puruṣottama residing in the temple. 52.
Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water according to the prescribed rule,
he should bathe the deity with ghee, and immediately thereafter with milk.
Then, with water scented with honey and with water from sacred bathing places mixed with sandalwood paste, one should devoutly clothe him in an excellent pair of garments.
One should smear Puruṣottama with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, and worship Him with lotuses and supreme devotion. || 55 ||
Having thus worshipped Hari, the Lord of the Universe, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should offer incense mixed with agallochum before the body of the God.
One should burn well-purified guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter,
and one should indeed light a lamp with clarified butter according to one's ability and with devotion.
O Goddess of the Gods, one who is composed should also offer twelve other lamps, either with cow's ghee or again with sesame oil.
One should offer as an oblation milk-rice, cakes, *śaṣkulī* pastries, *veṣṭaka* sweets, *modaka* sweets, molasses, and other fruits.
Having thus worshipped Puruṣottama with the fivefold offerings,
one should mutter the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ puruṣottamāya" one hundred and eight times.
Then, having prostrated like a staff, one should propitiate the Lord;
thereafter, one should worship the Guru with devotion using flowers, garments, and unguents.
O daughter of Vidhi, since there is no difference between these two,
one should construct a pavilion above the deity with a well-concentrated mind.
Having first prepared a very bright and variegated mandala with various flowers, one should subsequently perform the vigil at night.
The wise man, meditating upon, reciting, and praising the Lord, should cause the narrative of Vāsudeva and his songs to be performed, and thus pass the night.
Then, on the twelfth day at the clear dawn, he should invite twelve Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and have bathed for the vow.

Having bathed according to the proper ritual procedure and wearing clean garments, one who has conquered his senses should [approach] those learned in the Vedas who know the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and whose senses are restrained. (66)
One should devoutly bathe Puruṣottama, who resides there, as before, with perfumes, flowers, offerings, food oblations, and likewise with lamps.
With various kinds of services, prostrations, circumambulations, recitations, praises, salutations, and enchanting songs and instrumental music; || 68 ||
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the World, one should then worship the Brāhmaṇas;
having given twelve cows and gold to them, [one attains the fruit]. || 69 ||
Having respectfully offered an umbrella, a pair of sandals, and a bronze vessel,
he should then feed those Brahmins with food beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then, having eaten cooked food— both solid and soft— with molasses and sugar, the Brāhmaṇas were well-satisfied and composed in mind.
One should cause twelve water-pots, filled with equal amounts of water, to be taken up, and offer a sacrificial fee according to one's ability to Viriñci, who is equal to Viṣṇu.
Having honored them with gold, garments, cows, grain, and other excellent articles, the wise man, having bowed down to them, should recite this mantra: || 73 ||
May the all-pervading Lord of the World, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, the beginningless and endless God, Puruṣottama, be pleased. 74.
Having uttered this, and then having respectfully circumambulated the Brahmins three times and bowed his head with devotion, he should dismiss them along with the preceptor.
Then, one should follow those Brahmins with devotion as far as the boundary of the village; having followed them, paid homage to those Brahmins, and turned back.
Then, joined by his kinsmen and relatives, he should eat while remaining restrained in speech; by performing this correctly, a man or a woman obtains the fruit. || 77 ||
That best of men, having extracted a hundred past [lives] from a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred rājasūya sacrifices, [attained this state]. (78)
And in the future, O Goddess, he shall become one who possesses a divine form, imperishable, endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament. (79)
His every desire fulfilled, endowed with virtue, beauty, and youth, he was then being praised on all sides by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
By means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored, moving at will, stable, adorned with banners and flags, and possessing the radiance of a hundred suns. || 81 ||
Illuminating all directions in the sky, free from fatigue,
that youth— possessed of great strength and wisdom— goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
There, O Goddess, praised by the best of sages, he shall enjoy his desired pleasures for as long as a hundred kalpas and remain free from all affliction.
O Goddess, just as the Lord of the World is divine, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, so too did he appear joyful, assuming a four-armed form.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there and having sported for a very long time, O virtuous lady, at the end of that he goes to the abode of Brahmā, which grants all desires.
Adorned by accomplished Vidyādharas as well as gods and Kinnaras, a person who has enjoyed happiness there for a period of nine kalpas [is reborn]. (86)
One goes to the world of Rudra, which bestows happiness, is frequented by the gods, and is adorned by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Daityas, and Dānavas. || 87 ||
Having enjoyed happiness there for a period of eighty kalpas, that man at its conclusion goes to Goloka, which is endowed with every enjoyment.
Adorned by gods, siddhas, and apsarases, it was exceedingly beautiful; there, having enjoyed desired pleasures for seventy kalpas, [he dwelt]. || 89 ||
Thereafter, he indeed comes to the unsurpassed world of Prajāpati;
