"O child, become my vehicle; I am pleased with you.
This stone shall attain fame on the surface of the earth by your name. (17)
"O you who bestow merit upon men by the mere sight of her, it was here that you performed your austerities; here, at this most preeminent tirtha on the Gaṅgā, out of a desire for my pleasure. (18)
O illustrious one, may the merit-bestowing Pañcagaṅgā manifest for those who perform their ablutions there; for whoever bathes in it shall offer libations to the gods and other beings. (19)
There is no returning for him from the eternal world of Brahmā;
having thus granted the boon, Viṣṇu then vanished.
By the command of Viṣṇu, Garuḍa also attained the status of his vehicle;
from that time forward, that sacred site became a destroyer of sins.
One should indeed remember it as the bestower of merit and the grantor of the state of Vainateya;
furthermore, there is another stone there called Vārāhī, which brings auspiciousness.
There, the Lord, the destroyer of sins, having lifted up the earth and struck down Hiraṇyākṣa, remains standing, treading upon him in the form of a stone. || 23 ||
In that regard, whatever person goes there and, having bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā, worships that stone with devotion, shall not encounter an evil destiny. || 24 ||
Then there is another stone there, called Nārasiṃha, the sovereign goddess,
where she remained after having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Then all the celestial sages restrained his anger and requested that he should indeed always remain there in Viśālā.
Likewise, there he exists in the form of a stone with four arms,
constantly engaged in water-sports while remaining in the midst of the waters.
There, the person who bathes and worships the stone of Nṛhari shall indeed attain the abode of Viṣṇu, from which return is difficult to find.
O Goddess, I shall now describe the fifth stone, known as Nara-Nārāyaṇa, situated on the bank of the fire-pit; listen. (29)
In the Kṛta Yuga, Hari, who is both Nara and Nārāyaṇa, dwells there visibly, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all.
In the auspicious Tretā age, he is perceived by sages, gods, and yogis who are established in yoga; he is not seen by others, for he ordains the maintenance of the world.
When the Dvāpara age has arrived, he is perceived through the yoga of knowledge and by no other means whatsoever; in the Tiṣya age, he has become visible.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, and the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
having praised the Lord Hari with various words, propitiated him.
Then an incorporeal voice spoke to those who had performed the rites according to the rules:
"In the Kali age, which is devoid of all righteousness, I do not manifest my vision."
O lords of the gods, if you have faith in my vision, then take hold of my form at Śailadya, located at Nārada-kuṇḍa, within the pavilion.
Then, having heard those words, Brahmā and the others, with delighted minds,
brought forth that divine form from the mountain peak and led it to Nārada-kuṇḍa.
Having worshipped him, they established [the image] and then departed for their respective abodes;
in the month of Vaiśākha, those gods go to their own mansions.
Having arrived in the month of Kārttika, human beings perform worship again; then, starting from the month of Vaiśākha until the end of the cold season, they continue their practice.
Those who are meritorious and free from evil deeds obtain a vision [of him];
for six months they are to be worshipped by the gods, and likewise for six months by human beings. (39)
Thus, by that very arrangement, the image appeared from that time forward; whoever worships an image of Viṣṇu made of stone with a spirit of devotion, [attains the fruit]. (40)
One who partakes of the food offering (naivedya) also certainly attains liberation;
these five meritorious stones are situated in Viśālā. || 41 ||
Among these, the food offering (naivedya) of the gods is difficult even for Hari to obtain; how much more so for humans and others? Yet, when consumed, it is a means to liberation.
Even a single grain of the food offered to Viṣṇu at Badarī purifies the sin residing in the body, just as blazing fire purifies gold. (43)
For this is the Kapālamocana tīrtha, which purifies sins;
in its midst there are five stones that liberate one from sin.
Now hear of another great sacred site right here, O Mohinī, where a man who bathes with devotion becomes one who has mastered the Vedas. (45)
While Brahmā was asleep, a demon named Hayagrīva, who struck fear into the gods and others, carried away the Vedas that had issued from his mouth. || 46 ||
Then, requested by Brahmā, Viṣṇu became manifest in the form of a fish; having slain him, he restored the Vedas to the Creator.
And that great holy site, O highly fortunate lady, which illuminates all branches of knowledge, is known as Taimiṅgila; it destroys sins merely by being seen. (48)
Furthermore, the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, in the form of Hayagrīva,
slew the two intoxicated asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
The two who had stolen the Vedas returned them to Brahmā;
that sacred ford (tīrtha) destroys all sins merely by bathing there at the place of the Creator.
O auspicious lady, those Vedas exist eternally in their embodied forms within the Matsya and Hayagrīva [tīrthas]; that water is the destroyer of sins.
There, in the south-eastern direction, is the famous sacred site (tīrtha) called Indrapada;
by bathing there, O Goddess, a person shall attain the station of Indra.
And there is another beautiful sacred site there called Mānasodbhedaka;
it pierces the knot of the heart and cuts away all doubt. || 53 ||
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, there is another holy site there called Kāmākāma, which removes all sins and pierces through the fetters of the mind.
O auspicious lady, to the west of that is the sacred ford named Vasudhārā, which grants desires to those who possess them, but bestows liberation upon those who are free from desire.
Having bathed there with devotion, a person obtains their desired fruit;
here, the merit of the virtuous proceeds, and it is seen situated within the water.
Having seen which, a living being never again enters a womb;
from that point, five streams fall downwards toward the direction of the Nairṛtas (the southwest). || 57 ||
By bathing in those [streams] known as Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Gayā, and the Araṇya of Naimiṣa, a mortal shall individually obtain the fruit of each respective sacred site (tīrtha). || 58 ||
Beyond that is another pure sacred site known by the other name Somakuṇḍa,
where Soma, the lord of Kheṭaka and others, performed intense penance.
O auspicious lady, having bathed there, a person becomes free from all defects;
there is another supreme holy site there, the Dvādaśāditya, which removes all sins.
Having bathed there, a man becomes like the sun in brilliance; there is another sacred ford there called Catuḥsrotas, where a man who has immersed himself [is purified].
One obtains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, whatever one desires;
there, moreover, is the enchanting holy ford named Saptapada.
By the mere sight of this sacred ford, even great sins are certainly destroyed; how much more so, then, by bathing in it when it exists?
In the three worlds, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara reside at that Kuṇḍa;
by dying there, a man shall attain the state of truth.
O auspicious lady, there is another sacred bathing place here in the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa named Urvaśīkuṇḍa; one who bathes here becomes enchanting in form.
He shall become exceedingly dear to Nārāyaṇa and a subduer of the entire universe;
thereafter, in the southern quarter, there is a supreme holy site named Astra.
There, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, having laid aside their weapons and remaining engaged in ascetic penance,
[deposited] their divine armaments, such as the conch, the discus, and so forth.
O highly fortunate lady, since these [deities] are seen by the wise in embodied form, a man who bathes there with devotion shall not experience fear of his enemy. (68)
And Meru-tīrtha is also located there; having seen Dhanurdhara and bathed there, O auspicious lady, one obtains all of one's heart's desires. (69)
There is another excellent sacred site there named Lokapālāhvaya, where the world-protectors performed austerities; a man who bathes there [is purified].
O Goddess, by striking with his staff, Hari created this holy place (tīrtha); therefore, a human being obtains the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 71 ||
From there flows the Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī, which bestows happiness upon the world, where indeed the Bhāgīrathī has united with the Alakanandā. || 72 ||
That sacred ford is the most excellent of all in the meritorious hermitage of Badarikāśrama;
having bathed there and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, one should worship them with devotion.
O fair-faced one, by visiting the Field of Dharma (Dharmakṣetra) on the southern side of the confluence, one who is saluted by all the gods attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
I consider that field to be purifying, the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
having bathed there, O auspicious lady, a man shall attain proximity to Sādhya.
The Urvaśīsaṅgama Tīrtha removes all sins of men, and there is another called Karmoddhāra, which is the sole means for attaining devotion to Hari.
The sacred site named Brahmāvarta is the sole cause for attaining the world of Brahmā;
these sacred sites situated along the Gaṅgā have thus been described to you.
Even Brahmā is not capable of describing those things situated therein in their entirety;
whoever should constantly hear this, or cause it to be heard, with a concentrated mind. || 78 ||
Even he who remains here for just one month with devotion, firm in his vow, shall be liberated from all sins and attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
O Goddess, wherever this majesty arising from Badarī is written down, there one shall behold Hari himself as Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
There, there shall be no premature death, nor fear of mental anguish, physical disease, or serpents;
indeed, by the grace of Hari, auspicious things always prevail there.
All prosperities increase likewise through the grace of Viṣṇu. || 82 ||

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Badarikāśrama," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the latter portion of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Thus ends the Greatness of Badarikāśrama. Now begins the Greatness of Kāmodā;
this is the sixty-eighth chapter.
Mohinī said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me of the greatness of Kāmodā, hearing which from your mouth I shall become delighted as if my purpose were fulfilled. || 1 ||
Vasu said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate the auspicious narrative known as Kāmada;
having heard it, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt. (2)
O Goddess, there is a city named Kāmoda situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
where the beloveds of Hari dwell together with the gods.
When the ocean of milk was churned by the gods and demons, Kāmodā then arose among the four jewels of maidens.
The first maiden is named Ramā; the second is known as Vāruṇī;
the third is called Kāmodyā; and the fourth is designated as Varā. || 5 ||
In that matter, three maidens were obtained by the powerful Viṣṇu; however, Vāruṇī was taken away by the Asuras, O virtuous lady, at the command of Lord Viṣṇu.
From that time forward, O auspicious one, Lakṣmī remained upon the chest of Viṣṇu; as the wife of Viṣṇu, she became free from any rival wives.
Having understood the future task, the gods, by the command of Viṣṇu, indeed worship the goddess Kāmodā in the city named Kāmodā.
There she dwells eternally, desiring union with Viṣṇu; having attained the state of being his wife through her devotion, she is solely intent on meditating upon Viṣṇu.
There, the great Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent and accessible through meditative realization,
dwells eternally in close proximity to her as well.
O Goddess, that Soul of the Universe, whose body is invisible, exists as the object of meditation for gods, asuras, sages, and likewise for human beings. (11)
Through meditation alone, the gods and sages behold the All-pervading Lord;
for when that illustrious enchantress Kāmodā laughs, [the world is moved]. 12.
Commanded by Harṣa, her tears then fell;
those tears of joy fell into the Gaṅgā, O Goddess of the Gods. (13)
And there are lotuses called Kāmodya, which are yellow, fragrant, and bestow great delight. || 14 ||
But he who, by the power of fortune, having obtained them, worships Śiva with them, shall obtain his desired objects; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
For tears born of suffering sometimes fall from them, and from those tears, those lotuses arise devoid of fragrance. || 16 ||
But he who worships the god Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, with those [materials], shall be joined with all miseries, being deluded by his former sins. || 17 ||
Ten yojanas upstream from Gaṅgādvāra is situated Kāmoda; there, he who should recite the twelve-syllable mantra for one year [attains success].
O daughter of Vidhi, at the end of the rainy season, on the twelfth day of the month of Caitra,
having seen the spring goddess Śrī, she shall always laugh with joy.
Only that person who bathes there, a human being devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, shall obtain those lotuses; no one else at any other time or place shall ever obtain them.
Having meditated upon the city of Kāmoda, he shall become beloved by Viṣṇu; he will be dear to the gods and the ancestors—of this there is no doubt. || 21 ||
O fair-faced one, he who remains there for twelve years, devoted to the recitation of mantras, shall obtain the direct vision of Kāmadā.
O lady, whatever desire a pure man contemplates at that sacred ford, he obtains it all simply by bathing there in this world.

For this is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), which can only be attained through the power of good fortune; O auspicious lady, it is difficult to reach and consists of rugged terrain during the winter season.
Thus has this entire auspicious narrative of Kāmodā been told;
the man who hears it with devotion is also liberated from his sins. (25)

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmodā," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the latter section of the Great Narrative (Bṛhad-upākhyāna) of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 68 ||
Thus ends the *Kāmodāmāhātmya*.
Now begins the *Kāmākṣāmāhātmya*, together with the account of Siddhanātha;
herein begins the sixty-ninth chapter.
Mohinī said:
"O twice-born one, I have heard the narrative of Kāmodaka, which destroys the sins of men and bestows merit; now I desire to hear the fruit of Kāmākṣā. (1)
Vasu said:
The supreme goddess Kāmākṣā is situated in the eastern direction; dwelling on the coastal marshlands of the ocean, she bestows spiritual perfection upon men in the Kali age. || 2 ||
O auspicious lady, he who goes there, restrains his diet, worships Kāmākṣā, and remains for one night with a firm posture, shall behold her.
That goddess moves about in a terrifying form to appear before men;
indeed, he who beholds her and does not waver shall obtain his desired perfection (siddhi). || 4 ||
But whoever, upon seeing Kāmākṣā, the queen of the gods who possesses a formidable form, should immediately move from his seat, he will certainly become distracted. || 5 ||
There dwells Siddhanātha, the son of Pārvatī, O fair-faced one;
he is engaged in fierce austerity and is never seen by worldly people.
In the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, [the Lord] is perceived directly by all; however, He remains hidden during the Kali age until its very end.
When one quarter of the terrible Kali age has passed upon the surface of the earth,
he will indeed become manifest and bring all people to spiritual perfection.
O illustrious lady, by means of such methods as delusion and the like, he shall then bring the people, who are mostly barbarians, under his control and lead them to the three steps of Kali.
He who, having gone there, endowed with a spirit of devotion, should meditate upon Siddheśa for the duration of one year while constantly worshipping Kāmākṣā; || 10 ||
Concentrated in mind, he shall obtain a vision in a dream; at the conclusion of that vision, having attained the success indicated by it, he shall become an accomplished master on earth.
O auspicious one, while fulfilling the desires of all the worlds, he would reflect upon them;
by his boon, he could summon whatever objects exist within the three worlds.

O blessed lady, that Matsyanātha, established there and having reached the further shore of higher knowledge, performed most formidable austerities favored by the world, yet he did not come within the range of sight.

Having wandered through all the worlds for many ages in the past with his unimpeded movement, that great-souled one now stands engaged in ascetic penance; O auspicious lady, he has not been overcome by the force of time.
O Subhadrā, he who was born during a *gaṇḍānta* period in a previous birth was the son of a certain twice-born man;
as soon as he was born, it is said, he was cast by his father into the ocean on the island named Puṣkara.

As soon as the boy was thrown there, it is said that some fish swallowed him by the decree of fate; remaining there for many eons, he indeed became one whose body was free from old age and death through the passage of time.
Then once, O auspicious lady, Maheśvara, the immeasurable one, being requested by his beloved wife Pārvatī, went together with her to Lokāloka mountain to impart instruction in the ultimate reality.
Standing for half a moment on that beautiful peak, which was radiant with jewels, his mind absorbed in Hari,
he awakened the goddess Umā by means of his power and overcame the beings with three claps of his hands.

She spoke that truth which is a supreme secret—the very nature of the meaning of the twelve syllables—and then, having bowed down to Maheśa, the destroyer of Māra, that daughter of the mountain [continued]. (19)

While she remained established in that state, having realized the truth, that fish dwelling in the great ocean suddenly leaped up and went to the mountain peak; for that young Brahmin who was situated within its belly had attained the perfection of reality and was liberated from all bonds.
Having emerged from the belly of the fish, O fair-faced one, Maheśvara paid homage before you both; and although he already knew the truth, he asked him the cause of his passage through her womb.
He described everything exactly as it had occurred before them;
having heard that account, Somā became pleased and, with the permission of Maheśa, [acted accordingly]. || 22 ||
Placing him on her lap, she kissed his face and conceived him as her son, O lady of auspicious limbs;
for this lord of the fish was indeed my son, one who had realized the ultimate truth and was the master of all perfected beings.
"Let him now go to the worlds at his own will, spreading our fame; from that time forth, this son of Ambikā shall sport at pleasure through all the worlds."

Having reached that seat of accomplishment (siddhapīṭha), a person who remains there as if instructed in asceticism and meditates upon that Siddhanātha with the mind shall have all his desires fulfilled. || 25 ||

Having acquired this knowledge, one should immerse the entire assembly of the learned in the flow of one's own words—that sacred narrative which purifies the world, for whoever hears it as it enters the path of their ears. (26)
Having attained his desire upon the earth, he whose feet are worshipped by the gods indeed goes to heaven.
O fair-eyed one, I have thus related to you this account endowed with the life-story of Śrī Siddhanātha;
this is the primordial majesty of Kāmākṣā, which destroys all sins. What more shall I tell you, O blessed lady?

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Kāmākṣā," accompanied by the life-story of Siddhanātha, within the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, in the latter part of the *Bṛhadupākhyāna* of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīyapurāṇa*. 69.
Thus ends the *Māhātmya* of Kāmākṣā, together with the *Carita* of Siddhanātha.
Now begins the *Māhātmya* of Prabhāsa;
this is the seventieth chapter.
Mohinī said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me the greatness of Prabhāsa, hearing which I may become gracious in soul and blessed through your favor. (1)
Vasu said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the most meritorious sacred site named Prabhāsa, which removes the sins of men and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 2 ||
In which there exist countless holy fords, O delighter of the ritual,
where resides Someśa, the Lord of the Universe, the Blessed One, the husband of Girijā.
Having bathed at the Prabhāsa tīrtha and having worshipped Somanātha, a person attains liberation; this which I have spoken is the truth. || 4 ||
The circumference of its radiant halo is twelve yojanas, and its central pedestal is said to be five yojanas in width. || 5 ||
In its center is a sacred ford (tīrtha) the size of a cow's hide, superior even to Kailāsa;
there is the meritorious Arkasthala and another very beautiful sacred ford.
Where there are thousands of lingas, such as Siddheśvara and others,
where a person, having bathed with devotion and having satiated the ancestors and the deities, [attains merit].
And having worshipped the Liṅgas, one goes to the same world as Rudra;
likewise, there is another Agnitīrtha situated on the shore of the ocean.
O Goddess, having bathed there, a person shall attain the world of Fire;
and having worshipped the god Kapardīśa there while observing a fast, he shall likewise attain that state.
Having enjoyed his desired pleasures here, he attains the world of Śiva;
then, having gone to Kedāreśa and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, [he attains liberation].
He attains the heavenly realm, honored by the gods, traveling in a celestial chariot;
[he visits] Bhīmeśa, Bhairaveśa, Caṇḍīśa, and Bhāskareśvara.
One should visit, in sequence, the fourteen lords: Aṅgāreśa, Gurvīśa, Someśa, Bhṛgujeśvara, and the lords Śani, Rāhu, and Śikhī.

Having performed their worship individually with devotion according to the prescribed rules, one who knows the ritual procedure attains residence in the same world as Śiva and becomes capable of both punishment and grace.
O daughter of Vidhi, by worshipping the five other lingas, beginning with Siddheśvara, a man attains success in this world and the next. || 14 ||
By worshipping these in due order—Varārohā, Ajāpālā, Maṅgalā, and Laliteśvarī—a man becomes free from sin. || 15 ||
Having worshipped Lakṣmīśvara, Bāḍaveśa, Arghyeśa, and Kāmakeśvara with devotion, a person shall attain the status of a world-protector (lokeśa) in person. || 16 ||
Having reached Gaurī-tapovana and having fully worshipped Gaurīśa, Varuṇeśvara, and Uṣeśvara, a person shall attain the state of heaven. || 17 ||
Gaṇeśa, Kumāreśa, Svākakeśa, Kuleśvara, Uttaṅkeśa, Vahnīśa, Gautama, and Daityasūdana. || 18 ||
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, a man shall not go to an evil state;
then, having reached Cakratīrtha and bathed there according to the rite, he attains the highest goal. (19)
Having worshipped Goddess Gaurī at the sacred ford named Sannihatya, O lady of beautiful countenance, a man shall obtain his heart's desire.
Having bathed and offered libations to the gods and others, one obtains the fruit of having performed a *sannihati* sacrifice;
furthermore, whoever worships the eleven *liṅgas*, beginning with Bhūteśa, [attains the same].
Having obtained excellent enjoyments here in this world, that best of men, having fully worshipped the Lord Ādinārāyaṇa, shall go to the state of Rudra in the end.
O Goddess, he shall become a partaker of liberation; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Then, having reached the Holder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), he who worships according to the prescribed rite [shall attain the same]. || 23 ||
Having conquered his enemy, he shall obtain various kinds of enjoyments;
then, having reached Sāmbāditya and bathed according to the prescribed rules, [he attains his goal].
Then, having reached the goddess Kaṇṭakaśodhinī, that man becomes free from disease and enriched with wealth and grain on this earth. (25)
Having worshipped Mahiṣaghnī, a man becomes fearless;
and having duly honored Kapālīśa and Koṭīśa, he becomes the best among men. (26)
Thus becoming truly fortunate, one should conclude the mid-journey;
thereafter, O Queen, having reached the place named Bālabrahma, the mortal [attains his goal]. (27)
He becomes a lord of enjoyment and liberation, worshipped by all the gods; then, having reached Narakīśa, Saṃvartīśa, and Nidhīśvara.
By worshipping Balabhadreśvara, one becomes possessed of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, by reaching Gaṅgāgaṇapati and worshipping him according to the prescribed rite. || 29 ||
Having reached the river Jāmbavatī with devotion and a concentrated mind, one obtains one's desired objects both in this world and in the next. (30)
Having bathed and worshipped the gods and others, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his duty;
then, having bathed at Pāṇḍukūpa, he should worship Pāṇḍaveśvara.
That man goes to heaven and sports in the Nandana groves and other celestial realms,
[reaping the fruits] of a hundred sacrifices, a hundred thousand sacrifices, and ten million sacrifices in succession.
Having worshipped the three Liṅgas and having beheld and duly honored Durvāsādityaka, one rejoices in heaven like a god.
Having reached Yādavasthala and having worshipped Varṣeśa, a human being undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 34 ||
Honored by the king of the gods, he attains his desired success;
having bathed at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā, he should give a golden chariot to a Brahmin.
He who, with devotion, dedicates [a gift] to Śiva shall obtain imperishable worlds;
thereafter, having worshipped Nagārka, he shall attain the world of the Sun.
But by seeing and worshipping Subhadrā along with Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa at the side of Nagarāditya according to the prescribed rite, one attains union (sāyujya) with Kṛṣṇa. || 37 ||
Then, having obtained a maiden and worshipped her according to the prescribed rite, one obtains all desired objects and conquers even Śakra; of this there is no doubt. || 38 ||
Then, having worshipped Kṣetrapāla, one shall obtain all desires;
and having fully honored Brahmeśvara, who is situated on the bank of the Sarasvatī. (39)
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
having reached the river named Piṅgalā and bathed there, [he honors] the gods and others.
A mortal who performs a śrāddha ceremony after having offered libations is not born again in this world;
and a man who worships Saṅgameśa shall not go to an evil state.
Having worshipped Śaṅkarāditya, Ghaṭeśa, and Maheśvara, a person shall obtain all desires; there is no doubt in this matter. || 42 ||
Then, having reached Ṛṣitīrtha and bathed with a restrained mind, one who worships the sages there shall obtain the fruit of all holy fords (tīrthas). || 43 ||
Then, having worshipped Nandāditya, one is liberated from all diseases;
thereafter, reaching Tritakūpa and bathing there, a man goes to heaven.
O Mohinī, having bathed at Śaśopāna, a man beholds the gods and shall obtain his desired objects; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth. (45)
Having seen Parṇāditya, a man shall become free from disease and possessed of enjoyments;
then, having reached the Nyaṅkumatī river and bathed there according to the prescribed rite, || 46 ||
Having worshipped Siddheśvara here, one becomes a possessor of the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*;
and by beholding Vārāhasvāmin, one is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
By worshipping the Chāyā-liṅga, one is liberated from all sins;
by seeing and worshipping the Gulpha, a man obtains the fruit of a Cāndrāyaṇa fast.
By worshipping the goddess Kanakanandā, a person attains all desires while living and, at the end of the body, shall obtain the state of heaven. || 49 ||
By worshipping Kuntīśvara, one is liberated from all sins;
and by worshipping Gaṅgeśvara, a person who has bathed in the Gaṅgā [attains the same].
He who bathes at Camasodbheda and performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) is liberated from all three kinds of sins; of this there is no doubt.
He shall obtain merit equal to ten million Gayās; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having gone from there to Vidhija, he reaches the excellent hermitage of Vidura.
By worshipping Triga, the Lord of the Three Worlds, one shall become happy here;
by honoring Maṅkaṇeśvara, a person attains the supreme goal.
Having worshipped Traipura and Triliṅga, one is liberated from sins;
then, having reached Ṣaṇḍatīrtha and bathed there, a man becomes a giver of gold.
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall attain the state of Śiva;
having bathed in Sūryaprācī, a man becomes free from evil and a possessor of enjoyments.
Having bathed at Trilocana, a man shall attain the world of Rudra;
and having worshipped the Lord of Umā at Devikā, the best of men [attains the same].
One obtains one's desired objects and, at the end of the body, shall attain heaven;
by duly worshipping Bhūdvāra, one obtains the fruit of one's desire.
Having paid homage to Vālmīki at the site of the stake, one shall become a poet;
then, by worshipping Cyavanārka, one shall possess the fulfillment of all desires.
By worshipping Cyavaneśa, a mortal shall become an attendant of Śiva;
by worshipping Pajāpāleśa, one shall be endowed with wealth and grain. || 59 ||
A mortal who worships Bālārka shall become learned and wealthy;
by bathing at the abode of Kubera, he will certainly obtain a treasure. (60)
Having reached the river Ṛṣitoyā and bathed there, a pure man who gives gold to a brāhmaṇa is liberated from all sins.
By worshipping Saṅgāleśvara, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
by worshipping Nāradāditya, one becomes possessed of knowledge of the three periods of time.
Then, by worshipping Nārāyaṇa, a person shall become a partaker of liberation;
having bathed in the water of the Taptakuṇḍa, one should worship Mūla-caṇḍīśa.
Freed from all sins, a man shall obtain his desired object;
by worshipping the four-faced Vināyaka, he attains his heart's desire. (64)
Having worshipped Kālambeśvara, one becomes possessed of an abundance of wealth and grain;
through the worship of Gopālasvāmin, one indeed becomes a possessor of cattle, wealthy, and a poet.
The worship of Bakulasvāmin bestows the attainment of heaven upon men;
by fully honoring the goddess Mārutā, one obtains the fruit of all desires.
By worshipping Kṣemāditya, a mortal becomes secure, attains his goals, and possesses truth;
and by propitiating the Lord of Obstacles known as Unnata, one is not struck down by impediments. (67)
Jalasvāmī and Kālamegha, when worshipped, grant all perfections; the goddess Rukmiṇī, when worshipped, bestows the desired objects upon men.
By worshipping Durvāseśa and Piṅgeśa, one is liberated from sins;
and by bathing at the confluence of the Bhadrā rivers, a man beholds auspicious things.
Having bathed at Śaṅkhāvarta, a man shall become a lord of all supernatural powers;
having bathed at Mokṣatīrtha, a man shall be liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
By merely bathing at Goṣpada, one attains all happiness;
having gone to the abode of Nārāyaṇa, a person does not grieve again.
Through the worship of Jāleśvara, men shall attain their desired perfections;
moreover, one who has bathed in the Huṅkāra-kūpa shall never again undergo residence in a womb.
Likewise, by worshipping Caṇḍīśa, one obtains the fruit of all holy places; and by worshipping Vighneśa residing in Āśāpura, one shall encounter no obstacles. || 73 ||
A mortal who has bathed in Kalākuṇḍa becomes a partaker of liberation, without a doubt;
by worshipping Kapileśa, one shall obtain a herd of tawny cows (kapilā).
By worshipping Jaradgaveśvara, one is not overcome by old age;
the worshipper of Naleśvara becomes an enjoyer of pleasures, and the worshipper of Karkkoṭeśa becomes wealthy. (75)
Through the worship of Hāṭakeśvara, all desires are fulfilled;
one who worships Nāradeśa shall obtain devotion toward both Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara.
By worshipping the Goddess adorned with mantras, one becomes worthy of heaven;
by honoring Gaṇapati, the peak of Durga, one shall become happy. || 77 ||
By worshipping the Sovereign of the Kauravas, one shall become possessed of wealth and grain;
and by worshipping Suparṇelā and Bhairavī, one shall become happy. || 78 ||
Having bathed at Mallatīrtha, a man is liberated from all sins;
having bathed at Kardamāla, a man is freed from transgressions.
Having seen Guptasomeśvara, one does not have to grieve ever again;
having seen Bahusvarṇeśvara, one attains the path to heaven.
A mortal who worships Śṛṅgeśvara is not overcome by miseries;
having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa tīrtha, a human being attains liberation. || 81 ||
By worshipping Mārkaṇḍeśvara, a man becomes long-lived;
likewise, by bathing in the Koṭīhrada lake and worshipping Koṭīśvara, one becomes happy.
Furthermore, having bathed again at the site of accomplishment (siddhasthāna), that mortal who worships the innumerable lingas there becomes an accomplished one (siddha) on earth. || 83 ||
Having seen the abode of Dāmodara, one attains unsurpassed happiness; O auspicious lady, Vastrapatha is situated at the very center of Prabhāsa. || 84 ||
Having worshipped Bhava there in person, one becomes equal to Bhava himself;
likewise, at Dāmodara, Svarṇarekhā, and Brahmakuṇḍa on Mount Raivata.
Kuntīśa, Bhīmeśa of great splendor, and Mṛgīkuṇḍa are known as the entire essence of the sacred field at Vastrāpatha. || 86 ||
Having bathed in these in succession and having diligently worshipped the gods and gratified the ancestors with water, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords.
Having bathed at Dunnābila, a man who has enjoyed his desires shall go to heaven;
then, by worshipping Gaṅgeśvara, he shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. || 88 ||
O Goddess, there are numerous sacred fords (tīrthas) on Mount Raivataka;
by bathing in them with devotion, a person [worships] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
By worshipping Indra and the guardians of the worlds, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
these sacred sites have been described to you in brief, O beautiful lady. (90)
Those intermediate [sites] are infinite and cannot be fully described; for even each single sacred ford (tīrtha) has extensive accounts. || 91 ||
Therefore, O enchantress, I have described to you in brief the merit born of Prabhāsa; there is no sacred ford equal to Prabhāsa in the three worlds.
Even a man who has merely bathed there vies with the inhabitants of heaven in auspiciousness; and the greatness of Prabhāsa remains inscribed in his home. (93)
Wherever he may be, there shall be no fear arising from spirits, thieves, snakes, or enemies for that man who listens with devotion or causes others to hear it with a concentrated mind. (94)
Even he who hears the greatness of Prabhāsa Tīrtha shall attain a virtuous state. || 95 ||

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prabhāsa Tīrtha," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the latter section of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*. || 70 ||
Thus ends the majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra. Now begins the majesty of Puṣkara;
this is the seventy-first chapter.
Mohinī said:
"O best of the twice-born, the greatness of Prabhāsa, which bestows great merit, has been heard;
now I desire to hear the greatness arising from Puṣkara."
Tell me in detail about that sacrificial ground of my father, which is the foremost of all sacred sites, purifying and destructive of sins.
Vasu said:
"Listen, O blessed lady, I shall proclaim the meritorious majesty of Puṣkara, which always grants the desires of men and is endowed with many sacred fords."
Where the gods, together with Viṣṇu, and Indra and the others are established,
as well as Gajavaktra, Kumāra, Raivata, and Divākara.

Likewise, the goddess Śivadūtī, who always brings security and well-being to the sacred field, resides in the Puṣkara forest during the month of Jyeṣṭha; he who stays there becomes free from worldly exertion.
He shall obtain the merit born of the eightfold yoga; of this there is no doubt.
There is no sacred field on this earth superior to this.
Therefore, this should be practiced with every effort by the best of men—
whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras— who dwell within the sacred field.
Those who are devoted to Brahman with their whole being and who act for the benefit of all living creatures go to the world of Brahman, where the yogis go.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing in all the holy fords (tīrthas), a mortal shall obtain all of that by bathing but once in the Jyeṣṭha-kuṇḍa.
Having reached the Puṣkara forest, where the Sarasvatī flows toward the east,
she is known by the names Mati, Smṛti, Dayā, Prajñā, Medhā, and Buddhi.
Even those standing on the bank who behold that water situated there attain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) and go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
There are three white peaks and three springs,
as well as three lakes there, namely the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Therein is another very great sacred ford named Nandā Sarasvatī, where it flows toward the western direction at a distance of one yojana from the lake.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and having given a milch cow to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, a man shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Likewise, Koṭitīrtha exists there, where ten million sages arrived;
having bathed there and honored the twice-born, one is liberated from all sins. || 15 ||
Having reached the hermitage of Agastya, bathed, and worshipped the Pot-born Sage, one becomes long-lived and enjoys prosperity; at the end of the body, one attains the heavenly state. || 16 ||
Likewise, having reached the hermitage of the Seven Sages there with undistracted mind,
one who bathes and worships them with devotion attains the same world as they.
Having bathed at Manūnāmāśrama, one obtains worship from all sides;
having bathed at Gaṅgāvinirgama, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. || 18 ||
Having bathed at Puṣkara during the month of Jyeṣṭha and having given a cow to a twice-born man,
one enjoys all pleasures here and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed in the Madhyama Puṣkara and giving land to a Brāhmaṇa,
one attains the world of Viṣṇu, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
But a man who bathes at Kaniṣṭha and gives gold to a Brahmin attains all his desires and, in the end, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Then, having bathed at Viṣṇupada and given something to a twice-born man, one obtains all desires through the very grace of Viṣṇu. || 22 ||
Then, having bathed at Nāgatīrtha and worshipped the Nāgas,
men who give gifts to the twice-born rejoice in the third heaven for a yuga.
Having bathed at Piśācatīrtha and given food to a Brahmin, one never again attains the state of a Piśāca; he shall go to heaven.
Having bathed in the Śivadūtī lake, having worshipped Śambhu there, and having fed the Brahmins with sweet food, one is glorified in the heavenly world. || 25 ||
Having bathed in the Ākāśapuṣkara, a person who bestows the fruit of mantra-yoga attains liberation; this which has been spoken to you is the truth, the absolute truth. (26)
He who bathes in the Puṣkara forest while meditating upon that [water] situated in the sky with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" shall attain the eternal state. || 27 ||
When the constellation Āgneya (Kṛttikā) occurs on the full moon day of Kārttika, that lunar day is considered great; one should perform an ablution there at Ākāśapuṣkara.

A man who performs his bath on the full moon day of Kārttika during the conjunction with the lunar mansion of Yāmya (Bharaṇī) obtains that same fruit which arises from bathing in the Puṣkara of the Sky.
On the day of Kārttikī when it is joined with the constellation Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī), one who bathes at Kaniṣṭhaka obtains that fruit which arises from the Puṣkara in the sky.
When the Puṣkara-born [wind] occurs in the sky in sequence during the days of Nandā, Arka, Guru, Soma, Yāmya, Vahni, and Vidhu, then the full fruit shall be attained. || 31 ||
When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, then, having bathed during the conjunction known as Nabhaḥpuṣkara, one shall go to heaven.
Those men who perform their ablutions in this auspicious, ancestral tirtha that has descended from the intermediate space, attain worlds of great prosperity.
In the Puṣkara forest, within the Sarasvatī river of five streams,
holy fords and sanctuaries were established by sages and perfected beings.
Among all of them, Sarasvatī should be known as the source of Dharma;
the gift of gold, land, and Gaurīs yields great fruit in those [tirthas]. (35)
That man who gives grains and sesame seeds here to an excellent brahmin obtains enjoyments in this world and the supreme goal in the next.
He who bathes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī and honors the twice-born attains the foremost state after having enjoyed his desired pleasures here.
But having bathed in the pond named Aviyogā and offered a funeral cake (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rite, O virtuous one, a man indeed leads his ancestors to heaven. || 38 ||
Likewise, by bathing in the Saubhāgyakūpa and offering libations to one's ancestors, a mortal attains a good state and incomparable good fortune on earth. (39)
Having bathed at the two boundary mountains (maryādā-parvatau), touched them, and worshipped them,
one obtains the desired worlds as well as the fruit of a complete pilgrimage.
Having reached Ajagandha, which is auspicious, and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one obtains one's desired objects both in this world and in the next.
He who worships Sāvitrī, who is situated upon a mountain on the southern side of the lake, is also a knower of the true essence of the Veda.
Of Vārāha, Nṛsiṃha, Brahmā, and likewise Hari;
and also of Śiva, Sūrya, Soma, and Guha. || 43 ||
O Mohinī, there are also separate sacred fords (tīrthas) belonging to Pārvatī and Agni; O highly fortunate lady, a man who bathes in them with a concentrated mind [attains great merit].
Having given gifts to the Brahmins, one attains the supreme goal;
bathing at Puṣkara is difficult to obtain, and performing penance at Puṣkara is difficult to obtain. (45)
At Puṣkara, a gift is difficult to obtain; at Puṣkara, a residence is difficult to find.
Yet, whatever man is present even at a distance of a hundred yojanas at the time of the ritual bath, [he attains the fruit]. || 46 ||
One who meditates upon Puṣkara with devotion shall obtain the fruit of bathing there;
Maṅkaṇaka and others, perfected through austerity, serve Puṣkara with joy. (47)
O daughter of Vidhi, wherever one may go by good fortune, one shall attain the desired success; even he who has merely uttered the name "Puṣkara" [shall achieve this].
That man who listens with devotion to the greatness of Puṣkara shall undoubtedly obtain the merit born from bathing at Puṣkara. (49)
He too, having obtained the fruit of the bath, rejoices in heaven like a god. || 50 ||
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Puṣkara," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī within the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 71 ||
Thus ends the glorification of Puṣkara;
now begins the glorification of Gautama’s Hermitage.
This is the seventy-second chapter.
Mohinī said:
"O Lord, the majesty of Puṣkara, which destroys all sins, has been heard;
now, O Master, proclaim the majesty of Gautama’s hermitage."
Vasu said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the supreme hermitage of Gautama, having gone to which a man with devotion never again undergoes torments. || 2 ||
The holy hermitage of Gautama, frequented by hosts of celestial sages, which pacifies all sins and brings an end to all calamities. || 3 ||
He who serves for twelve years, endowed with a spirit of devotion,
attains the abode of Śiva, having gone to which he does not grieve.
Where the son of Māyādevī established himself in fierce asceticism,
there flows the Godāvarī, a Gaṅgā that destroys all sins.
O son of Vidhi, as that sage performed penance, there occurred for twelve years a terrible drought that caused the destruction of all living beings.
During that terrible famine, all the sages, emaciated by hunger,
came from various countries to the auspicious hermitage of Gautama.
They made this request to Gautama as he was practicing austerities:
"O sir, give us food, so that our lives may remain within our bodies. || 8 ||
Thus addressed by those sages, the sage Gautama,
moved by compassion for them, spoke to those who were confident through the power of their asceticism.
Gautama said:
"Stay all of you, O sages, near my hermitage;
I shall provide food for you as long as the famine persists."
Having thus inspired confidence in all the sages, Gautama, by the power of his asceticism, meditated with a tranquil mind upon Gaṅgā, the accomplisher of all aims.
As soon as she was remembered, that goddess emerged there from the surface of the earth; and seeing Gaṅgā flooding the surface of the earth, the sage—
Having sown the śāli rice in the ground in the morning, he reaped it when it was ripe at midday;
then, with that very rice, he fed those sages.
Then those sages, being pleased and having attained satisfaction after eating the food, joyfully took up residence there in Gautama’s hermitage.
In this manner, O blessed lady, every day he, filled with a spirit of devotion, provided hospitality for them with rice that had reached full ripeness. || 15 ||
Then, as that lord of sages fed the twice-born daily,
the famine passed away at the end of its twelve-year duration.
Then, when a time of abundance had arrived, all those sages, having informed that best of sages, returned once more to their own respective countries. || 17 ||
Possessing such power, that sage Gautama performed penance for a very long time there, O Mohinī, with his senses fully restrained.
Then, pleased by that austerity, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Ambikā, appeared together with his attendants and said, "Choose a boon."
Then that best of sages, having beheld the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, the three-eyed Tryambaka, prostrated himself upon the ground before him and paid his respects.
Then, rising up suddenly with palms joined in reverence, he stood before him and said: "Grant me perpetual devotion at your feet."
O Śaṅkara, seeing you stationed right here upon this mountain near my hermitage— this alone is the boon I desire.
Thus addressed, the Lord of Pārvatī, the bestower of the desires of his devotees,
granted him his own presence there and immediately made him joyful.
In that very form, Tryambaka dwelt there; from that time forward, he has been celebrated by the name Giri-tryambaka.
But those men who, endowed with devotion, reach the Godāvarī and the Gaṅgā and perform their ablutions, O blessed lady, they shall be liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
Those who, having bathed in the waters of the Godāvarī, worship Tryambaka residing on the mountain with ritual offerings, they shall become Maheśvaras in person.
The greatness of Tryambaka has been described by me in brief;
even your father, O dear one, is not capable of describing it in detail.
From there, as far as the Godāvarī itself becomes visible, there are indeed many holy hermitages situated in that place. || 28 ||
Having bathed in them according to the prescribed rite and having satiated the ancestors and deities, a person shall obtain his desired objects; of this there is no doubt. (29)
O blessed lady, the holy river Godāvarī, manifesting in some places and hidden in others, thereafter flooded the entire earth.
Wherever the Great Goddess has become manifest through the devotion of men,
there is a great and meritorious sacred site (tīrtha) that removes sins merely by bathing.
Then, having reached Pañcavaṭī, that goddess of firm vows arrived at the place of supreme radiance, bestowing the ultimate goal upon the worlds.
O daughter of Vidhi, that man who, firm in his vows, bathes at Godāvarī and Pañcavaṭī, shall attain his desired objects.
When Rāma arrived at Pañcavaṭī during the Tretā Yuga, he dwelt there with his wife and younger brother, performing most meritorious deeds.
Thus, O auspicious lady, all this concerning the hermitage of Gautama has been narrated;
it is meritorious for those who hear or read it, destroying sins and granting all desires. (35)

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Gautama’s Austerities," within the "Glorification of the Hermitage of Gautama" in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, in the "Great Narrative" of the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 72 ||
Thus ends the majesty of Gautama’s hermitage; now begins the majesty of Tryambaka. This is the seventy-third chapter.
Mohinī said:
"O Guru, you have narrated the meritorious account of Gautama, as well as the greatness of Tryambaka arising from Godāpañcavaṭī. (1)
Now I desire to hear how Mahādeva performed the tāṇḍava dance there in the city of Puṇḍarīka.
"O Mahīdeva, speak thus for me, [something] more meritorious than my merit.
Vasu said:
"Mahādeva is subject to his devotees and is indeed a grantor of boons instantly. (3)
He becomes manifest to his devotees and acts according to their will;
once, the lordly sage named Jaimini, a disciple of Vyāsa, [appeared]. || 4 ||
Wandering among sacred fords together with his disciples, beginning with Agniveśa, he arrived at the city of Puṇḍarīka, which was like the very city of the King of the Gods (Indra) itself. || 5 ||
It was adorned on all sides with glorious trees bearing flowers of every season, and beautified by reservoirs of white lotuses providing cool shade.
It was filled with most delightful lotus-pools teeming with birds of various ages and species,
and it was frequented by women who were like apsarases and by men who possessed the splendor of vidyādharas.
With its gleaming white mansions, it shines like a celestial chariot;
seeing the splendor of that city, the sage was filled with great joy.
And he set his mind upon bathing there in that lake,
which was endowed with trees of lush shade and fragrant with various flowers.
Having rested for a moment on its bank, which was rich with the shade of trees, the sage bathed and performed his daily rites, including the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Having fashioned an earthen linga,
he worshipped it according to the prescribed rites with various offerings, including water for the feet and the guest-offering, remaining unperturbed.
Having worshipped with perfumes, incense, lamps, various kinds of food offerings, and fragrant flowers, the sage remained standing there. || 12 ||
At that moment, the Blessed One became pleased and appeared in person within that very earthen linga, which was emitting the luster of various jewels.
Then Jaimini, having beheld the Lord Umāpati in person, fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff; rising again, he stood with palms joined in reverence.
Jaimini said: He spoke to the all-pervading Hari, who occupies half the body of Hara and removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge:
"O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose. (15)
Since you, who are to be meditated upon by Brahmā and others, have now come directly within the range of my vision,
the Lord of the Mountain, being pleased, has extended his own hand to him.
Placing the *agadatta* upon his head, he said, "Tell me, son, what do you desire?
Having heard those words of Śambhu, Jaimini replied.
I beheld the Lord Sāmba, together with Vighneśa and Kumāra;
thereafter, Śaṅkara, accompanied by Sāmba and his son, came into my sight.
Once more, with a serene soul, he said, "Speak, my son, what do you desire?
Then Jaimini, beholding the compassion of the Teacher of the World, [spoke].
Smiling, he said, "I behold you who have entered into the *tāṇḍava* dance.
Then the Blessed Lord, the husband of Ambikā, desired to perform that very act.
He remembered all his attendants, who were skilled in various sports; and as soon as they were remembered, they all appeared, led by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin.

Filled with curiosity, they gathered together and conversed; having offered salutations to Vighneśa, Kumāra, and Ambā, they stood with restrained speech and joined palms, awaiting the command of the God of gods.
Then Hara, at the command of Hara (Śiva), assumed a wondrous form and appeared ready to dance, adorned with various garments and ornaments;
his armpits were entwined by the swaying creepers of serpents, his face was slightly upturned, the crescent moon graced his forehead, and his upper arms served as raised banners.
His body was smeared with ashes that surpassed the brilliance of the moon’s rays; his form was moistened by the celestial river Ganges flowing from his mass of matted hair;

his forehead-eye blazed like a fire that heated the cool-rayed moon; and he uttered roars of defiance at the deer-king (Śiva) who was sustained by the trickling nectar [of the crescent moon]. || 24 ||

It resounded with the *phuṅ* cries of serpents dragged by the beaks of the sons of Kumāra; it echoed with the trumpeting of the lotus-born Brahmā as he was brought back to life by the flowing nectar; it was filled with the *cuṅkṛta* roars of the mouse, the vehicle of Gaṇeśa, who was terrified by the serpent; and it was made to bellow by the great bull who was struck with fear by the roar of the king of beasts. || 25 ||
Frequently causing the surface of the earth to tremble with the falling of his lotus feet, the bristles on the rows of hair on his body thrilled with joy at the excellent music;
his lotus feet illuminated by the jewels in the crowns of the lords of gods and asuras, and his face gazed upon by Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya, and the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī). || 26 ||
His name correctly proclaimed by the multitude of devotees whose joy was fully increased, the Lord shone forth, illuminating the quarters with his commenced tāṇḍava dance. || 27 ||
Then Jaimini, immersed in an ocean of bliss upon seeing the dance of the Great Lord, praised him with a hymn composed of a quarter-verse from the Veda, being fully concentrated in mind.
O Goddess who dwells in Kāmpilya, salutations to you, the mother of the universe, whose lotus feet are bowed to by Viriñci, Viṣṇu, and Giriśa.
Obeisance to you, O Gaṇapati, Lord of the Vedas, who are worshipped by Vighneśa, Vidhi, Mārtaṇḍa, Candra, Indra, and Upendra. 30.
I bow to Kumāra, whose forehead is honored by the soft lotus-like hands of Umā, who wears golden earrings and a garland of lotuses. 31.
Who among men is worthy to praise Śiva, who is difficult even for Brahmā and others to behold?
Yet, through your vision, my praise has become as real as rain from a cloud.
Homage to Śiva accompanied by Ambā; homage to Śarva, the source of bliss;
homage to the dancer Rudra, the Lord of the Assembly. || 33 ||
Salutations to the Lord of beings, who split the worlds with his feet, shattered the walls of the cosmic egg with his crown, and caused the horizons of the quarters to whirl with his arms. || 34 ||
Salutations to the Lord of Beasts, who wears a pair of tinkling anklets, who is radiant in his garment of tiger-skin, and who has the king of serpents as his girdle. || 35 ||
Salutation to Kālakāla, to Soma, to the Yogi, to the wielder of the trident, to the one adorned with bones, to the Pure One, to the Lord of the worlds. || 36 ||
Salutations to you, the vessel of the entire world, the eye of all the inhabitants of heaven, the lord of the lineages, and the lord of the sacred fields. || 37 ||
Salutations to you, Śaṅkara; salutations again and again to you, Maṅgala. Salutations to you, the lord of riches; salutations to you, the lord of foods.
Salutations to you, the sovereign of the self, and to you, the most bountiful giver.

Salutations to the one who is exceedingly pleasing with his eightfold limbs, who grants the desired objects to those whose devotion is afflicted, who destroys the sacrificial offerings [of enemies], who is perfectly contented, and who is the Lord of the nourished. || 39 ||
Homage to the lord of the five elements, homage to the lord of time; homage to the lord of the self and to the lord of the quarters. || 40 ||

Salutations indeed to the creator of the universe, the great lord, the sustainer of the universe, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the destroyer of the universe, the one whose eye is fire, and who possesses the form of the universe. || 41 ||
O Īśāna, obeisance to you; O Tatpuruṣa, obeisance to you; always obeisance to you, the Terrible One; O Vāmadeva, let there be obeisance to you; and indeed obeisance to Sadyojāta. || 42 ||
Salutations to Bhava, the ornament of prosperity for his devotees and the bestower of the destruction of fear; salutations to Bharga, to Rudra, the bountiful giver.
Salutations to you, the thousandfold mother, accompanied by Ambā, possessing a thousand rays, with a thousand arms, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful bestower. || 44 ||

Salutations to you, who have beautiful cheeks, who are like the moon, who have a lovely forehead and beautiful eyebrows, who possess a magnificent body, who are most gracious, and who are the bountiful giver. || 45 ||
Homage always to you, the unconquered one, the bountiful giver, who endures all and brings about the simultaneous severance of both existence and the afflictions that cause it.
I bow to the Lord of the assembly, the wonderful protector of all worlds, who is a mass of bliss, beautiful in his dance, and marvelous. 47.

I bow to the Lord, the imperishable and supreme Master, who has beautiful calves, who wears exquisite linen garments, who is capable of protecting against Rākṣasas and Bhūtas, and who is beloved by the Lord of Yakṣas.

I bow to the dark-brown Person, who has one half of his face and one half of his body bare, who wears a garland of bones and lotus petals, and who possesses the characteristics of both male and female.
I bow to that Lord, the master of all that moves and stands, who enables one to cross the great ocean of saṃsāra with a single prostration. || 50 ||
I bow to the sustainer of the worlds, the Lord, the bestower of all prosperity, the leader of the Maruts, the unconquered conqueror. (51)
I bow to you, the leader who brings about the end [of rebirth] and the sustainer of the Mandākinī, who maintains these three worlds while establishing me within them. 52.
I bow to that Lord, the omniscient, the all-pervading, the all-encompassing sage, from whom the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born together with the Yajus-formulas.
I salute you, O Sudṛśa, who abandons past, future, and present [actions], and who perceives all things through all [senses]. || 54 ||
I bow to Hara, the controller of the gods, who draws away pride from me;
by whose command Nārāyaṇa remains pervading the entire universe.
I bow to that Mahādeva, by whose command the Blessed Creator fashioned this world at the beginning of the kalpa, just as it was before.
I am that Lord, that God, whose linga the hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, worship day and night together with their wives.
I bow to that Rudra, by worshipping whom in the past even once, the gods, with Pūṣan as their leader, attained each their own sovereignty. || 58 ||
I bow to that Lord Īśāna, whom peaceful ascetics, ever-perceiving him as Śiva within the lotus of their hearts, worship. (59)
Therefore, we constantly offer salutation to him, the one who is lovely as a lotus, whose chest is the garment for Umā’s breasts—that auspicious form of yours, O Rudra. (60)
Salutations to you, O Rudra, for your being; salutations to you, O Rudra, for your play;
salutations to you, O Rudra, for your peace; and salutations to you, O Rudra, for your wrath. || 61 ||

O Destroyer of Tripura, salutations to you for your two feet, which are established upon the Vedas as horses and chariots, and salutations also to your two arms, which are equipped with the arrow and the bow.
Salutations to you, O Śaṅkara, who are worshipped by Vāsuki, who are the scatterer [of enemies], who are the great one in the form of Mount Meru; salutations be to you, the wielder of the bow.
Salutations be to you, the axe; salutations to the trident of incomparable luster;
salutations to you, whose self is Hayagrīva; and also salutations to the arrow. || 64 ||
O Hara, I offer my salutations to those other weapons of yours which carry away the necklaces of the wives of the enemies of the gods, as well as to this quiver.
Salutations to you, the non-terrible one (Aghora), whose arms were struck by the lotuses in the playful sport of the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī); salutations to you who are worthy of fame.
Protect me, O Nīlalohita—the ignorant, the undecayed, the untrained, the one who has no other resort, the protectorless, the wretched, the afflicted, and the poor. 67.
O Lord, protect me—wretched-faced, of evil deeds, wicked, and in a miserable state;
for the attainment of prosperity, I find no one other than You to look upon me with favor. 68.
O Śambhu, O Compassionate One, become our protector as we are being consumed by the fire called worldly existence, with its flames of passion, hatred, and pride. (69)
O Puruṣa, praised by many, take away my wife, my dwelling, my clothes, and my shelter; protect me from the food of others. 70.
O Lord of Gods, we endure the insults inflicted upon us by wicked worldly men; grant us abundant gifts from Your servants, and bestow much wealth upon us. (71)
O Lord, while we noble families, free from effort yet full of pride, look on,
bestow upon us that desirable field, long life, and wealth.
O storehouse of compassion, you alone know the great shame we feel regarding this request; therefore, quickly bestow this upon us, your worshippers.
My wife, mother, father, and others hate me, who am immeasurably emaciated;
grant me great knowledge along with all-sustaining wealth. (74)
O Merudhanvan, bestow strength upon our bodies for all actions whose results are unseen, as well as for those whose results are seen, against those who are powerless.
O Lord of Gods, destroy the heartache and the paleness of my heart, which has obtained thousands of undesired things and is constantly separated from what is desired. (76)
Whatever diseases or piśācas, or men or gods, or any deities here afflict me, do you, O Great One, subdue them all! 77.
"You alone are our protector; no other whatsoever exists.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, O Brahmaṇaspati, accept us and protect us. (78)
O Lord of Umā, you alone are our mother; you are our father; you are our grandfather.
You are our life-force, you are our intellect, you are our prosperity, and you are indeed our brother and our friend.
Since you alone, O Lord of Gods, are the agent of every action, therefore forgive all that evil deed which has been committed by me. (80)
In terms of sovereignty there is none equal to you, and in terms of insignificance there is none equal to me; therefore, O God, Great God, you belong to us and we belong to you. (81)
I praise you with a song of homage— you who possess a beautiful smile, whose limbs are white as ash, whose form is like the rising sun, and whose face is serene and gentle.
This alone is our boon: that we may behold you, O Lord of Umā, as the presiding master of the assembly, dancing and looking upon us, for a hundred autumns.
O Blessed One, through your grace, may we live for a hundred autumns, free from disease, highly fortunate, wise, and deeply learned. (84)
Together with our wives and kinsmen, drinking the nectar of your *tāṇḍava* dance at will, may we rejoice in the Lord for a hundred autumns. || 85 ||
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, having drunk our fill of the honey-filled lotus of your feet, may we rejoice for a hundred autumns. 86.
O Mahādeva, whether we be insects, nāgas, or piśācas, or whatever else we may be in birth after birth, may we remain your servants for a hundred autumns. (87)
O Lord, O God, O Mahādeva, may we hear with our two ears the sound of dancing, instrumental music, and singing in your assembly for a hundred autumns. || 88 ||
We shall indeed proclaim your divine names for a hundred autumns—names that bring about the destruction of saṃsāra by mere remembrance. (89)
O Dhūrjaṭi, by the mere act of aiming your arrow, you burnt down the three cities;
may we remain unconquered by mental and physical ailments for a hundred autumns.
When indeed shall I behold that youthful lord of the people, the seer, who possesses the luster of beautiful gold and the broad chest of a fair-skinned maiden? 91.

When shall I serve the Lord of the Pramathas, who is surrounded by his attendants, whose face is joyful, who is fond of fine garments, who is accompanied by Ambā, who is resplendent, and who possesses the brilliance of pure light? (92)
Will the Lord, whose neck is blue and who is crimson-hued, indeed accept me—who am full of many faults, devoid of even a trace of merit, and evil-minded? (93)
When indeed will the Lord—whose neck is thick and unbending—look upon me, who am afflicted by the fire of the Kāla-śūla, terrified, and distressed in mind? (94)
O singers, come here if you desire passion and the like; O men, sing for him as he approaches that friend of the Giver of Wealth. (95)
"May it be well with you, O friend tongue! Speak this most exalted hymn of the Lord of Umā, the giver of knowledge, like the drum of the victorious."
"O Creator, you are tranquil; you do not know this entire world.
Since Gaurī is not thirsty, drink [from] this [stream] which satisfies Śambhu in its entirety. (97)
Fragrant, pleasant to the touch, granting desires, and adorned with the moon, she firmly embraced my mind as a woman embraces a beloved lover. 98.

To the one with great rays, the one with great arms, the one with a great body, the one with great garments, the one with a great crown, the Great Lord—I utter this great and excellent hymn of praise. || 99 ||
In whatever manner possible, with compositions that are slightly clear and beautiful, I reverently worship Maheśa—the unassailable, fierce, and enduring one—with these hymns of praise. 100.
Salutation to Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, the Lord of the three worlds, the one clad in the directions;
let there be salutation to the foremost Hara, and again salutation to the lowest and to the primordial one. 101.

Homage to you who are the transformation and the transformer; homage be to Bhava, the source of worldly existence, O you of manifold forms at the end of many births, from whom the procreation of the universe has issued forth. 102.

Salutations to that Supreme One, whose golden throne is covered with various jewels from the broad crowns of the lords of the gods, who has ashes as his body-unguent, and than whom there is nothing else higher or lower. (103)

Salutations to you, whose beautiful *tāṇḍava* dance causes the thicket of his matted locks—disturbed by the battle between the king of serpents and the lord of herbs—to become a deep cavern, wherein all this universe moves about. 104.

I bow from afar to the Lord whose lotus feet are worshipped by the eyes of Murāri, whose hands are reddened by the lac-dye from Umā’s feet, who is borne by the bull, whose throat is dark blue, whose teeth are golden, and whose complexion is pure. 105.

I bow to the infinite, unmanifest, inconceivable, and singular one; to him who withdraws all things, whose garment is the sky and whose body is the firmament; to the unborn, the ancient, the sacrificial post, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great. (106)

Failing to perceive the unborn Self dwelling within, the deluded wander in mountain caves, wondering: "Was it behind? Was it above? Was it to the north? To the south? In front? Or was it below? || 107 ||

I bow to this Lord, the moon-crested Śiva, who is great bliss and free from sorrow and suffering; he is the Supreme Self who dwells within the lotus of the heart, and from whom all the intermediate and cardinal directions proceed.

Beholding me bewildered by the great delusion called worldly existence, which arises from the ignorance of passion and other afflictions, protect me; O Moon-crested One, I hear that you are the best of physicians among physicians. 109.
I am an ocean of suffering, devoid of even a trace of happiness, untouched by merit and burdened with many sins;
I am in the very grasp of death. Protect me, who am terrified, from behind, from before, from below, and from above! 110.

O Lord, King of Mountains, by your very gaze—which is exceedingly cooling from beholding our beautiful faces and filled with compassion—we shall cross over our misfortunes; we cannot do so by means of a boat upon the waters. 111.
Protect me, who am sinking in the midst of the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, crying out with unabated passion and lacking self-control;
O Maheśa, favored by the Great Lord, protect me with your most powerful grace, as one protects a gift with a skillful right hand. 112.

O enemy of Yama, remembering my previously accumulated sins, I am terrified even of the harsh face of Yama; grant me whatever lifespan I desire, whether it be a short life on earth or the state of having passed away.

When will the wielder of the Pināka bow, who possesses many forms and is fierce, embrace me with his firm limbs—limbs that are fragrant, as fair as beautiful ashes, infinitely long, soft, and non-terrible? (114)
When will the God of gods, who is golden-hued and possesses a golden vision, protect me as I cry out, fallen into the ocean of existence like a terrified frog at the edge of a pond? 115.

When indeed shall I behold the auspicious one, who possesses a beautiful smile, who is adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, whose two eyes are like the sprouts of Gaurī’s sidelong glances, and who, radiant as the sun, stands beyond the darkness? 116.

Come, O you seekers of liberation from beginningless time, who constantly meditate upon Śiva within the lotus of your hearts for the sake of emancipation, having ascertained the true meaning through the realization of Vedānta. || 117 ||
"Come, you shall rule as sovereigns; worship at will the Lord of the House (Gaheśa) and the Lord of the Mountain (Giriśa).
Thus, having been worshipped in the past, Hiraṇyagarbha became the sole lord of all that has come into being. (118)
May those of virtuous deeds bow down to this Śrīkaṇṭha, the sole path for you, whose glory is vast;
he who is glorious, whose feet are worshipped by the Lord of Śrī, and who is the noble sustainer of all fortunes and riches. (119)
Even those men who desire excellent sons should worship this youthful Giriśa, for from him arose Hiraṇyagarbha, the self-existent creator of the world, in the beginning. 120.
Enough with these many words; everything desired is accomplished by taking refuge in him.
For, having formerly taken refuge in him, the pot-born Agastya became young again, whereas Palita remained old neither by day nor by night.
Abandoning everything else, O bees that are my eyes, always take refuge in this auspicious one; for he is fragrant, gentle, and brings welfare, and he is indeed sweet and full of honey.
You shall become one devoid of equal measure, having utterly conquered all men and gods;
therefore, O Vāṇī, pay homage to this Great Lord and praise him—the youthful Gartasat who has been heard [of]. 123.
Whatever desired object you contemplate in your mind, all that shall certainly come to pass for you.
O Rudra, we shall never again engage in a life of suffering regarding sense-objects; instead, we shall strive for your favor.
O Compassionate One, having endured all that improper conduct which was previously performed by us through the application of ignorance, favor us as a father favors his sons. || 125 ||

Seeing me bitten by the fierce fangs of passion, hatred, madness, greed, and the like—the enraged serpent known as saṃsāra—may the compassionate god Pinākin, the protector, protect me without fail. 126.
Having spoken thus, those who at the conclusion of their meditation bow to you, O Rudra, they go [to liberation], though they are like those bitten by the serpent of rebirth;
through the blue-necked one, the thread of the Self, I go to the reality, saluting with the sacred syllable Om. || 127 ||

O Lord of the helpless, touch with Your hand—Your healing medicine—the ones afflicted by the terrifying fever of worldly existence, who are the abode of all diseases and sins, and whose vision of the end of time is not near; O Hero, O Vasu, O Destroyer of Time, touch them for their great prosperity. 128.
May we conquer by means of this all that is desired: the eightfold division of the earth, the land of heaven, and the realm of the sky, including whatever resides therein—
this very lord of all gods and dānavas, the master of the assembly.
May he grant us that wealth, vast and appearing golden-hued. || 129 ||
Homage to you, Bhava; homage to Hara, whose essence is illumined by prosperity;
homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is joined with the fear of overcoming worldly existence;
homage to Śiva, the protector of the universe, the eternal, the playful one.
His friend is never slain, nor is he ever defeated. || 130 ||
Salutation, salutation to the Lord of the gods; salutation, salutation to the Lord of the progenitors;
salutation, salutation to the Lord of the lords of the earth; salutation, salutation to the Lord of Ambikā, the Lord of Umā. || 131 ||

I perpetually bow to Vināyaka, whose head is struck by the sound of the prostrating [worshipper], whose crown is touched by the crowns [of other gods], the destroyer of the suffering of those who seek refuge, the poet among poets, possessed of most excellent fame. 132.
In battle, the gods, and in sacrifice, the Brahmins—both find their refuge in Skanda; I bow to him.
*Subrahmaṇya*, *Oṃ Subrahmaṇya*, *Oṃ Subrahmaṇya*. 133.

Salutations to Śivā, the Mother of the World, the beloved of Śiva, whose form is auspicious; she who was born as the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, the young woman with four braided locks, beautiful in appearance. (134)

I bow to Gaurī, who is golden-hued, whose feet are adorned with jeweled anklets, whose face is serene, who holds a parrot and a lotus in her hands, whose eyes are wide, who is skilled in speech, and who utters sacred words. 135.
I bow to this immeasurable Umā, the daughter of Menā, who possesses immeasurable splendor; she, embracing her dear friend, makes both her breasts appear white with laughter. 136.

I bow to Umā, who is beloved, whose bodily luster resembles that of her husband, who shines resplendent, and who is attended by the lord of the gods who has bowed down; she who, as the Goddess, beholds all the worlds at the side of Giriśa. (137)

I bow to that Gaurī, whose breasts are high and full, who has the moon as her crest-jewel, and whose bodily ointments have faded; she who, as the Goddess, impels the splendor of the Goddess Rādhā for the sake of the liberation of suffering beings. 138.
I bow to this daughter of Menā, whose delight is the protection of the distressed, who bestows honor and joy;
she who is the leader of all sciences, auspicious words, and of truthful speech that brings prosperity. (139)

O Śivā, who removes both the heat and the fear of saṃsāra, grant us an excellent and unimpeded intellect, which finds its sole enjoyment in the food and ornaments [of devotion], so that by it we may cross over all misfortunes. 140.
O Śivā, how can there be equality with you? Where could the creation of the universe be bestowed [upon another]? This Lord Śiva is but sport;
Hari is his servant, and Indirā, Śacī, Sarasvatī, or even the fortunate Vasu are but his attendants.
Vasu said: Having thus praised the Lord with this hymn, that great sage,
his eyes filled with tears of affection, bowed down to the Lord of the assembly.
Drinking again and again the auspicious nectar of the Lord’s *tāṇḍava* dance,
he attained all his desires and, in the end, achieved the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (*gāṇapatya*).

The best of the twice-born who recites with devotion this hymn uttered by Jaimini in this world is embraced by desired eloquence, perfection, intelligence, splendor, and fortune, just as wives embrace their husband. 144.

But that lord of the earth who, desiring to fight, recites this with reverence—he too, likewise, will see his enemies swiftly approach the presence of the Destroyer of Women, bearing fear in their hearts. (145)

Whosoever among the three social classes recites this constantly at any time with devotion to Īśa, shall, at the end of the body, stand by the side of Śiva as the stainless one and attain divine equality.
Those desiring intelligence obtain it by reciting this; likewise, those desiring prosperity obtain prosperity;
men desiring grain obtain grain, and men desiring sons obtain sons. || 147 ||
He who constantly retains in memory even a single quarter-verse, or half a quarter-verse, or a full verse, or even half a verse, goes to the world of Śiva. || 148 ||
O auspicious lady, that place where Śiva performed the Tāṇḍava dance is a holy site more meritorious than the most meritorious; by bathing there, one is liberated.
O best of men, he who performs a śrāddha for his ancestors there shall lead his forefathers to heaven; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (150)
One should give a cow, gold, land, a bed, clothing, a sunshade, drink, and food to a twice-born; all of that becomes inexhaustible there. || 151 ||
Whoever should hear or cause others to hear this meritorious narrative originating from Puṇḍarīkapura shall also become dear to Rudra. || 152 ||

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Hymn to Vedapāda," within the *Tryambakeśvara-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, in the latter section of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya-purāṇa*. || 73 ||
Thus ends the majesty of the Tryambakeśvara Jyotirliṅga. Now begins the majesty of Gokarṇa;
this is the seventy-fourth chapter.
Mohinī said:
"O Guru, the narrative of Puṇḍarīkapura has been told by you and heard by me; now, please instruct me regarding the greatness of the holy site of Gokarṇa."
Vasu said:
Listen, O Mohinī, I shall describe the holy place that bestows merit upon men, known as Gokarṇa, the field of Hara, which destroys all sins. || 2 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, on the shore of the western ocean there is a place extending for one and a half yojanas, which grants liberation even by its mere sight.
O Goddess, when the earth was gradually excavated by the sons of Sagara,
the ocean increased its waters and flooded the world.
It was thirty yojanas in extent, containing sacred fords, fields, and forests;
then all those who dwelt there—the gods, asuras, and humans—[departed].
Having completely abandoned that place, they settled upon the Sahya and other mountains;
from there, they went to the supreme secret pilgrimage site known as Gokarṇa, situated by the ocean.
Reflecting on this, the best of sages set their minds upon its extraction;
then, having consulted together, they all took up their positions in the valley of the mountain.
O Goddess, desiring to see Paraśurāma at Mahendra, who was established there in motionless form, the best of sages went forth with the longing to redeem Gokarṇa.
