Having ascended that mountain, they beheld his hermitage,
which was filled with peaceful and non-cruel creatures and was pleasant in all seasons.
That penance grove was dense with trees bearing fruit and flowers, providing pleasant shade, unsurpassed in its beauty, and filled with a fragrant, soothing breeze.
Having reached that hermitage resounding with the chanting of the Vedas,
they entered it with joyful hearts, proceeding according to their seniority.
They beheld that ascetic, peaceful and seated comfortably in the Brahmāsana posture upon a soft black antelope skin, surrounded by his disciples.
Having burnt the three worlds like the fire of cosmic destruction, he remained established in his asceticism;
they approached that best of the Bhrigus and paid him homage with humility.
Then, seeing that the sages had arrived, the scion of Bhrigu’s lineage duly honored them with respectful offerings of water for the hands and feet and other rites.
When they were seated and hospitably entertained, the descendant of Bhṛgu said to them:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones; for what purpose have you come here? (15)
"Trust me fully and speak; there is something that must be done by me.
Thereupon, the best of sages spoke of the purpose for which they had come to Rāma.
"Come to us, O best of the Bhṛgus, for we are sages dwelling at Gokarṇa who have been banished from that sacred ford by those who are digging up the earth with the oceans. (17)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, by your own power, you ought today to grant us this most excellent field after having drawn back the waters of the ocean.
Having heard those words of theirs, he laid down his weapons and reflected;
then, having reflected, the Blessed One considered the righteous and excellent means of protection.
Grasping his own bow and arrows, he set out together with them;
having descended from Mount Mahendra, he proceeded toward the south-western direction.
Having set out quickly, he crossed his own mountain and reached the shore of the ocean together with the inhabitants of Gokarṇa. || 21 ||
Having rested there for a moment, that best of speakers addressed Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: ||| 22 ||
"I am Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, who has arrived with the sages on a mission; O Pracetas, grant me an audience, for there is urgent business for you. (23)
Thus summoned by Rāma, the lord of aquatic creatures, out of self-conceit,
did not come into Rāma's presence even after hearing those words of his.
When he still did not come despite being summoned by him again and again,
Bhārgava, becoming violently incensed, took up his bow.
Aiming an arrow at him, he joined it with the Bhārgava weapon, whose deity is Agni, for the purpose of drying up the lord of rivers.
O blessed lady, when that weapon was joined by the high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu, the ocean became agitated, teeming with its hosts of aquatic creatures.
Tormented by the missiles and overwhelmed with fear of Rāma, Varuṇa returned in his own form and grasped the feet of Rāma. || 28 ||
Then, having withdrawn that weapon, Gokarṇa quickly said to Varuṇa:
"O Lord, let Gokarṇa be seen; indeed, draw back the water."
Then, by Rāma’s command, he too brought water from Gokarṇa;
and Rāma, having worshipped that Śaṅkara named Gokarṇa, [honored him].
Having reached Mount Mahendra once more, those twice-born ones remained right there,
where all the sages of celebrated vows had performed their austerities.
Through the power of that field, they attained supreme Nirvana, free from rebirth, together with hosts of spirits out of joy.
And Śaṅkara dwells there eternally with the Goddess and all the gods; by the mere sight of that Maheśvara Gokarṇa, sins are destroyed.
They depart immediately upon being separated, like dry leaves in a strong wind;
thus, a delight in frequenting that field never arises in men. (34)
But those creatures, whether stationary or moving, who die there by force, O Goddess, go immediately to the eternal heaven. (35)
Even by remembering it, a human being is liberated from all sins;
that sacred field named Gokarṇa is the abode of all holy fords (tīrthas).
Whatever fruit mortals obtain by bathing in all sacred fields and constantly worshipping Sadāśiva, all of that is gained there simply by beholding him.
Those who dwell there, indeed free from desire, anger, and other such passions, attain perfection in a very short time. || 38 ||
Those who dwell there—devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, peaceful, self-restrained, and celibate—they shall indeed attain their desired perfection. (39)

When that fruit exists, acts such as giving gifts, fire-offerings, recitation of mantras, and the worship of ancestors, gods, and brahmins become ten million times more effective than when performed elsewhere.
Thus, O blessed lady, has been narrated this majesty arising from the Gokarṇa field, which destroys all sins for those who read or even hear it. || 41 ||

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gokarṇa," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 74 ||
Thus ends the *Gokarṇamāhātmya*.
Now begins the *Lakṣmaṇācalamāhātmya*,
being the seventy-fifth chapter.
Mohinī said:
"O Vasiṣṭha, I have heard the majesty of Gokarṇa, which destroys all sins;
you should now likewise speak of the majesty of Lakṣmaṇa."
Vasu said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the majesty of Lakṣmaṇa;
by beholding that deity, a human being is liberated from all sins. (2)
In the descent of the fourfold manifestation, that god who is himself Saṅkarṣaṇa, the self-ruling one with a thousand faces, [pervades] this entire circle of the earth.
Even Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, Rāma, who is directly worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, did not perceive the mustard seed placed upon his single head. || 4 ||
O auspicious lady, Pradyumna is Bharata, Śatrughna is indeed Aniruddha,
and Lakṣmaṇa, O highly fortunate one, is Saṅkarṣaṇa himself, who is Śiva.
Formerly entreated by Brahmā and others, the Lord himself, the husband of Ramā,
was born in four ways from King Digpatha under the names of Rāma and his other brothers.
Then, O Goddess, after some time, Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages,
arrived for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice and requested Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then King Daśaratha, fearing the curse of the sage, gave those two sons, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who were dearer to him than his own life.
Having gone to the sacrifice of that lord of sages, Gādhipati, they protected it;
indeed, having slain Tāṭakā along with Subāhu, they cast them far away.
He gratified Viśvāmitra with the Mānava weapon against Mārīca,
and thereafter, having obtained the collection of weapons from that most excellent of sages who was pleased with him.
He said: "For some time he was honored by him along with his younger brother, and thereafter he was led by Viśvāmitra to the city of Videha."
Then King Janaka, having honored Viśvāmitra most respectfully, asked: "To which lord of a kṣatriya lineage do these two boys belong?"
Then that best of sages introduced to King Daśaratha those two sons, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Videha, being delighted upon seeing Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
mentally chose them as husbands for his two daughters named Sītā and Ūrmilā.
But that sage, knowing the three periods of time, understood what was in his mind and, rejoicing, said to Janaka: "Show him that bow. (15)
Having heard those words of Viśvāmitra, the king quickly [recollected] that which had been entrusted as a deposit to the Great Lord at Sītā’s svayaṃvara.
Having summoned three hundred servants, Rāma respectfully showed him that bow of Caṇḍīśa, lifting it up in an instant with his left hand.
Having suddenly drawn the strung bow, he broke it like a stalk of sugarcane by a lordly elephant;
thereupon, the King of Mithilā was exceedingly pleased and gave his two daughters to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having worshipped them thoroughly according to the prescribed rites, he offered them to those two,
knowing that they were other than the two excellent sages, for the sake of King Daśaratha.
Then, having summoned him along with those two, he caused him to give away his two sisters-in-law; thereafter, he [departed] together with his four sons who had taken wives.
Having been honored by the King of Videha, that descendant of Raghu, having subdued the pride of Bhṛgu’s son on the way, departed for Ayodhyā at the sage’s command. (21)
Accompanied by his father and brothers, the illustrious one rejoiced for many years;
yet, enlightened by Vasiṣṭha and other sages, he realized his own true majesty.
Then King Daśaratha, imitating human nature, recognized that his own son Rāma had realized the state known as Brahman, having known all that is to be known.
Eager and joyful, he was prepared to consecrate Rāma as the heir apparent, when Queen Kaikeyī— the king’s youngest wife and most beloved— learned of it.
Having forcibly restrained her son, that [proposal] became pleasing to him; then Rāma, with his father's permission, went there for the sake of her joy.
Accompanied by his wife and Saumitri, he, wearing the garb of a sage, dwelt for some time on that auspicious Citrakūṭa mountain.
Having heard that from his maternal grandfather's house, he came there and learned of his father's death; crying out "Alas, Rāma! as his father lay dead.
Having reproached Kaikeyī, he set out to bring Rāma back;
then, having given him his own sandals and having turned Bharata back, [he departed].
Rāma, the scion of the Raghus, went to the hermitages of Atri, Agastya, and Sutīkṣṇa, and spent twelve years among them.
Accompanied by his wife and younger brother, the illustrious one then went to Pañcavaṭī; there, at Janasthāna, he encountered Triśiras, Khara, and Dūṣaṇa.
He then destroyed those who had been incited by the deformed Śūrpaṇakhā,
as well as those who arrived with fourteen thousand rākṣasas.
He brought Yama’s abode by means of iron arrows with variegated feathers;
hearing of which, the king of the Rākṣasas [pursued] Mārīca as a golden deer.
Having shown them [the way] and sent them away, he abducted Sītā, struck down Jaṭāyu who was blocking his path, and brought her to Laṅkā. || 33 ||
Having arrived and searched everywhere for the abducted Sītā, they saw Jaṭāyus lying dead; having cremated him and slain Kabandha, [they proceeded].
Then, having felt compassion for Śabarī, they went to Ṛṣyamūka;
subsequently, at the word of Hanumān, the friend of their lord of monkeys, [they proceeded].
Having slain his enemy Vālin, he made Sugrīva the king;
then, commanded by him, those monkeys assembled from all directions.
Led by Hanumān, while searching for Sītā, they reached the southern ocean and, following the words of Sampāti, became certain that she was in Laṅkā. || 37 ||
Then the monkey Hanumān alone, having reached the city of Laṅkā on the further shore of the ocean, beheld his beloved, the virtuous Rāmā.
Having given her the jewel from Rāma’s finger, having inspired confidence in her, and having announced their welfare, he then received the crest-jewel from her.
Having destroyed the Aśoka grove, having slain Akṣa along with his army, and having rescued Indrajit from his bonds and even conversed with Rāvaṇa; || 40 ||
Having burned the entire city of Laṅkā and having seen Maithilī once again, he received permission, crossed the ocean, and reported this to Rāma.
Having heard that Sītā had gone to the dwelling of the Rākṣasa, Rāma also arrived at the abode of the sea-monsters together with the army of monkeys.
With the consent of Sāgara, he constructed a bridge across the great ocean using mountain peaks; having reached the opposite shore, he encamped his army there.
Then that Rāvaṇa, although exhorted by his younger brother, did not approve of the giving away of Maithilī to her husband.
Then, struck by him with his foot, Vibhīṣaṇa sought refuge with Rāma; Rāma, for his part, marched upon Laṅkā. || 45 ||
Then the ministers, counselors, sons, and servants,
having been incited for battle, were brought to destruction by those two lords of monkeys in the conflict.
Lakṣmaṇa struck down the conqueror of Śakra with sharpened arrows,
and Rāma likewise slew Kumbhakarṇa and Rāvaṇa as well.
Having caused Vibhīṣaṇa to perform that task and having purified his beloved in the fire, Rāma bestowed upon him the lordship over the hosts of Rākṣasas.
Having fulfilled his vows, he went to the city of Laṅkā at the end of the kalpa by means of the Puṣpaka chariot, accompanied by Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having brought Bharata from Nandigrāma, he entered Ayodhyā;
then, together with his brothers and the family priest, he bowed down before all his mothers.
After Vasiṣṭha had made his request, they consecrated Rāma in the kingdom;
then the blessed Rāma, too, ruled over his subjects as if they were his own biological sons.
Terrified by public censure, the knower of dharma abandoned Sītā;
she, for her part, having reached the hermitage of Vālmīki, dwelt there in happiness. (52)
And there she gave birth to two sons, renowned by the names Kuśa and Lava; Vālmīki, for his part, performed for them all the prescribed rites as they were due.
Having composed the Rāmāyaṇa, that noble-minded one taught it to those two; as they sang it at the sacrificial sessions of the sages, they attained great renown. (54)
When Rāma had arrived at the sacrifice and the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha) had commenced, he,
with a serene mind, listened there to that account of their own life as sung by the two of them.
There in that assembly, the mother of the world, having introduced those two sons to Rāma, summoned the sage together with Sītā.
He entered again through the opening of the earth; that was a marvel.
Then followed the supreme celibacy (brahmacarya) and the sacrifice itself as the thirteenth.
Having performed [austerities] for a thousand years, that best of the Raghus remained upon the earth;
then, in the course of time, Durvāsas arrived before the descendant of Raghu.
O blessed lady, sent by Brahmā for the purpose of going to Vaikuṇṭha, he went into a secluded place and said to Rāma, "No one at all should go here."
"Let him who comes here go to his death," Rāma promised;
then that joy of the Raghus, having summoned Lakṣmaṇa, spoke to him.
"Stay here at the gate; once he has entered, let him be slain.
"So be it," he replied, and having accepted Rāma's command, he carried out his order.
He did not grant entry to anyone in the presence of Rāma;
thus Rāma remained in solitude, established in the consciousness of Time.
Then, having learned of this, Durvāsas approached the gate; seeing that he had arrived, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, prostrated before him.
"Wait for a moment," he said; "Rāghava is occupied with his mantra.
Having heard those words, Durvāsas, who understood the requirements of time, [remained]. (64)
Enraged, he said to the son of Sumitrā: "Give me entrance;
otherwise, I shall instantly reduce you to ashes—consider this well! (65)
Having heard the words of Durvāsas, Lakṣmaṇa was seized with agitation;
fearing the sage, he entered the inner quarters to inform his elder brother.
But having seen Lakṣmaṇa, Kāla rose up after performing his ritual consultation; saying "Fulfill your vow," he departed, dismissed by Rāma.
Then, having departed from there, the Blessed Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
being pleased, gratified that sage Durvāsas and fed him.
Having fed him, bowed to him, and dismissed him, he said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Brother Lakṣmaṇa, a crisis has arisen on account of dharma."
Since you have fallen into my power to be slain, destiny is indeed more powerful;
therefore, O hero, being released by me, go now wherever you desire.
Then, having bowed down to that Rāma who was established in truth and righteousness,
he took refuge in the southern direction and performed austerities upon the mountain.
Then the blessed Rāma, at the request of Brahmā, again entered his own abode undisturbed, together with Sāketa and Kośala.
Those who, having meditated upon Rāma, plunged into the Sarayū at Gopratāra, entered the abode of Rāma, which possesses divine limbs and is difficult even for yogis to attain. (73)
But Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga, after following Rāma for some time, entered his own imperishable abode.
Having established his presence on that mountain every day, the son of Sumitrā then entrusted the wheel with its own duty to that supreme sacred field.
Those men who behold Lakṣmaṇa on Lakṣmaṇācala with devotion have accomplished their life's purpose; of this there is no doubt, for they go to the abode of Hari.
In that place, they praise the gift of gold, cows, land, and horses;
everything given there is inexhaustible, as are all oblations offered, recitations performed, and deeds accomplished.
What is the use of saying more here? His vision is difficult to obtain;
O Goddess, if he is seen within the command of Agastya, there is liberation without a doubt.
Whoever causes this life-story of mine, together with the narrative of Lakṣmaṇa, to be heard, or whoever listens to it, both of them shall become beloved of Rāma. (79)

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Lakṣmaṇācala Accompanied by the Deeds of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 75 ||
Thus ends the majesty of Lakṣmaṇagiri; now begins the majesty of Setu. This is the seventy-sixth chapter.
Mohinī said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born! That you have caused me to hear the Rāmāyaṇa—which destroys all sins and increases the merit of men—is truly wonderful. (1)
"Now I wish to hear the supreme majesty of the Setu.
Vasu said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme majesty of the Setu. (2)
O Goddess, upon seeing which a person is liberated from the ocean of existence;
the sight of the Setu is meritorious, where the omnipresent Lord Rāmeśvara resides. || 3 ||
By merely beholding Rāmeśvara, a man of restrained mind who worships him bestows immortality upon mortals. (4)
One attains all prosperities; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Furthermore, another Tīrtha called Cakratīrtha exists here, which destroys sins.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, and fire-offerings performed there attain infinite merit; indeed, that man who reaches Tālatīrtha and bathes there [attains the same].
Having obtained an excellent birth, he rejoices like a god upon the earth; thereafter, having reached that auspicious holy site which destroys all sins, || 7 ||
Having bathed there and shaken off his sins, that man is glorified in heaven;
thereafter, having reached Sītākuṇḍa and performed his ablutions properly, he attains the same.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one shall obtain all desires;
and having reached the auspicious Tīrtha and bathed there, one shall be liberated from sins.
By bathing in the Amṛtavāpī alone, a human being shall attain immortality;
by bathing in the Brahmakuṇḍa, a man shall reach the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed at Lakṣmaṇatīrtha, a man indeed attains the state of yoga;
having bathed at Jaṭātīrtha, a man becomes free from disease on this earth. || 11 ||
Having bathed at Hanumatkuṇḍaka, one becomes invincible by enemies;
having immersed oneself in Agastyatīrtha, one shall possess sons and wealth.
A mortal who bathes in Rāmakuṇḍa shall attain the same world as Rāma;
by bathing in Lakṣmītīrtha, one becomes endowed with fortune and beauty.
Having bathed at Agnitīrtha, a man is liberated from all sins;
by bathing at Śivatīrtha, however, one attains the world of Śiva.
A man who has bathed at Śaṅkhatīrtha shall not go to an evil state;
having bathed in the Yamunā and other sacred fords, a man shall go to heaven. || 15 ||
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, one obtains the fruit of all holy places;
having bathed at Sādhyāmṛta, a man goes to the same world as the Sādhyas.
By bathing at all the sacred fords, a man obtains his desired objects;
however, one who has bathed according to the prescribed rites at Dhanuṣkoṭi shall be liberated from bondage.
A mortal immersed in the Kṣīrakuṇḍa shall obtain various enjoyments;
having bathed at Kapitīrtha, a man shall not enter a degraded womb.
One who bathes in the Gāyatrī and the Sarasvatī shall be released from sin;
by bathing at the Ṛṇamocana-tīrtha and other such sites, one shall be liberated from debt.
Thus, O auspicious lady, this majesty of the Setu-tīrthas has been recounted;
it destroys all sins for those who read or even hear it.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Setu," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 76 ||
Now begins the majesty of the Narmadā Tīrtha.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter.
Mohinī said:
O best of the twice-born, I have heard the supreme majesty of Setu;
now I desire to hear the compendium of the holy sites along the Narmadā. || 1 ||
Vasu said:
Listen, O Mohinī; I shall describe the collection of four hundred most excellent sacred sites (tīrthas) situated on both banks of the Narmadā. || 2 ||
On the eleventh shore to the south, the twenty-third is proclaimed as the confluence of the Revā and the ocean, the thirty-fifth. || 3 ||
Around the Oṃkāra-tīrtha, extending two krośas in every direction from Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, there reside three and a half crores [of deities]. || 4 ||
One crore of sacred fords (tīrthas) is situated at the confluence of the Kapilā, and one hundred thousand tīrthas are established in the Aśoka grove. || 5 ||
A hundred [times] at Aṅgāragartā, ten thousand at Kubjā, a thousand at Vāyusaṅga, and a hundred [times] at Sarasvatī. || 6 ||
They know that at Śuklatīrtha there are two hundred, at Viṣṇutīrthaka one thousand, at Māhiṣmatī one thousand, and at Śūlabheda ten thousand.
In Devagrāma there are one thousand [deities], and seven hundred are situated in Ulūka;
at the confluence of the Maṇinadī, there are one hundred and eight holy fords (tīrthas). || 8 ||
There are that many [shrines] at Vaidyanātha and just as many at Ghaṭeśvara;
and one hundred and fifty thousand holy sites (tīrthas) are situated at the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
There are eighty-eight thousand [yojanas] up to Vyāsa and one hundred islands; however, at the confluence of the Karañjā, ten thousand and eight [yojanas] remain.
Likewise, there are one hundred and eight holy places at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī;
sixty-eight at Dhūtapāpa; and eighty-five million at Kokila.
O Queen, there are one thousand at Romakeśa, one thousand at Dvādaśārka, two hundred thousand at Lakṣāṣṭaka, and two thousand at Śuklatīrtha.
They know that at all confluences there are one hundred and eight; at the confluence of the Kāverī, O Nanda, five hundred sacred sites (tīrthas) are situated.
In the field of Bhṛgu, ten million holy sites (tīrthas) are established,
and in Bhārabhūti, one hundred and eight holy sites are situated.
At Akrūreśa it is one hundred and fifty; at Vimaleśa it is ten thousand; and that [at the next] is eighty-seven million—such is the enumeration of the sacred sites (tīrtha) along the Narmadā.
There are ten for Āditya, nine for Kapila, eight for Vidhu, and likewise eight crores known as Nandins, O lady of auspicious countenance. (16)
O Mohinī, there are seven [tirthas] known as Nāga, Agni, Siddha, Āvarta, Saptasaṃkhyāni, Kedāra, Indri, Yavārī, Īśa, and Nandi; indeed, these are the five [groups]. 17.
Yameśas, Vaidyanāthas, Vāmanas, Aṅgārakeśvaras, Sārasvatas, Munīśas, Dārukeśas, and Gautamas; || 18 ||
Indeed, four are proclaimed as the Vimaleśvaras, three as the Sahasrayajña-Bhīṣmeśas, and there are also the Svarṇatīrthas.
[He visited] Dhautapāpa, Karañjeśa, Ṛṇamukti, Guhāhvaya, Daśāśvamedha, Nandākhya, Manmatheśa, and Bhārgava. || 20 ||
The one known as Parāśarāyoni, the one who delights his father named Vyāsa, the one called Gopeśa and Māruteśa, and the white one called Jaṅgaleśa. || 21 ||
Akṣareśa, Pippaleśa, Māṇḍavyadīpakeśvara, Uttaresha, Aśokeśa, Yodhaneśa, and Rauhiṇa; || 22 ||
O auspicious one, two Lukeśas are each mentioned;
O auspicious one, there are one hundred and nineteen holy sites (tīrthas) for each individually.
In these clusters, there are two hundred and fourteen holy sites;
of these, the Śaiva holy sites are one hundred and twenty-two, and the Vaiṣṇava ones are twenty-two.
There are all the Brahma-tirthas, as well as twenty-eight Śākta ones;
among them, O fair-faced one, seven belong to the Mothers and three to Brāhmī.
Two are Vaiṣṇavī, two are Bhadrā, Raudrī is established in the remaining ones, and one Tīrtha of Kṣetrapāla has been described, O fair-faced one. (26)
O deluder, the intermediate secret and manifest sacred sites— three and a half crores in number— have been described here by Vāyu.
In heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, as well as in Revā—all these exist;
and wherever among these, O highly fortunate lady, a human being [dwells]... || 28 ||
One who performs the bath with a purified soul shall attain the supreme goal;
[the path consists of] bathing, giving, recitation, burnt offerings, study of the Vedas, and worship. (29)
Everything performed on the bank of the Narmadā becomes inexhaustible; O virtuous lady, the water of the Sarasvatī lasts for three days, while that of the Yamunā lasts for seven days.
"The merit of the Gaṅgā comes from a single immersion, but that of the Narmadā comes from the mere sight of her;
thus, O Goddess, has this compendium of the holy sites of the Narmadā been told. (31)
Even for mortals who merely remember it, this collection of Narmadā tīrthas bestows peace from great sins; so too shall it for the mortal who hears it. (32)
Or, O auspicious lady, he who causes it to be heard or recites it is also liberated from sins, as is the one in whose house this majesty arising from the Narmadā is written down. (33)
When it is worshipped there, there exists no fear of pestilence, nor fear born of fire; there is no fear from kings, thieves, or enemies, nor any fear of disease.
That house is constantly filled with prosperity, wealth, and grain, and is rendered most auspicious by the marriages and other ceremonies of sons, grandsons, and others. || 35 ||

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Narmadā Tīrtha," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 77 ||
Thus ends the majesty of the Narmadā Tīrtha.
Now begins the majesty of Avantī.
This is the seventy-eighth chapter.
Mohinī said: "O Brahmin, this most wonderful majesty arising from the Narmadā, which destroys the sins of men, has been heard by me as it was narrated by you. (1)
Now, O illustrious lord, tell me about the origin of Avanti and the majesty of Mahākāla, who is worshipped by the gods.
Vasu said:
Listen, O blessed lady, for I shall duly proclaim the greatness of Avanti, which bestows merit upon men and destroys all sins, as it has been celebrated.
The Mahākālavana is meritorious, an unsurpassed place for asceticism,
where the god Mahākāla has always remained engaged in penance.
O Goddess, there is no other sacred field on earth superior to Mahākālavana; having gone there, O Goddess, a man rivals even the gods.
O fair-eyed one, at that sacred ford named Kapālamocana,
even a man who has slain a Brahmin is purified by bathing there with devotion.
Likewise, by worshipping the deity named Kalakaleśa, a person attains victory in disputes and constant success in their undertakings. || 7 ||
There is another sacred bathing place here called Apsaraḥkuṇḍa; a man who bathes there shall become fortunate and possessed of enjoyments, appearing like Kandarpa himself.
Likewise, one who has bathed in the pool named Mahiṣa shall conquer his enemies in battle; and one who has bathed in the Rudra-saras lake is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having reached Kuṇḍaveśvara and having worshipped according to the prescribed rites, one obtains profit in business and becomes beloved of Śiva. || 10 ||
Having bathed at the sacred ford called Vidyādhara, a man is purified;
and by worshipping Mārkaṇḍeśvara, he shall become long-lived and wealthy. || 11 ||
Having worshipped the goddess Śītalā who resides in Kālavana, a man will never again experience the fear of eruptive boils. || 12 ||
Having reached Svargadvāra, a man who bathes and worships Sadāśiva does not go to an evil state; he is glorified in the heavenly world. || 13 ||
Having reached Rājasthala and then bathed in the Sāmudrika lake, a man obtains the supreme fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 14 ||
Likewise, a man who, observing the prescribed rules, bathes in the step-well of Śaṅkara,
shall obtain his desired enjoyments in this world and, at the end, go to the city of Rudra.
Having worshipped Śaṅkarāditya, a man becomes invincible;
and having bathed in the Nīlagaṅgā, a man [should worship] the goddess Gandhavatī.
Having worshipped with a spirit of devotion, one is liberated from all sins;
by bathing at Daśāśvamedhika, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Then, a mortal who, having approached the sovereign goddess Ekānaṃśā, worships her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, shall obtain all his desires. || 18 ||
Having worshipped Hara-siddhi, a man shall become the master of all accomplishments;
and having duly worshipped the fourteen [deities] beginning with Piśācaka, a mortal [attains the same].
One obtains all desires; there is no need for hesitation in this matter—having bathed in the Rudra-sarovara, one should worship Hanumatkeśvara.
The man who is endowed with faith shall obtain all prosperity;
by worshipping Vālmīkeśvara, he shall become a treasury of all branches of knowledge.
The man who worships with faith the Śukreśvara and other Liṅgas shall be enriched with all enjoyments and freed from all diseases. || 22 ||
Having worshipped the five Īśānas, a man shall partake in all spiritual perfections;
by circumambulating Kuśasthalādya, one obtains the desired fruit.
By worshipping Akrūreśa, one obtains fearlessness even from cruel beings;
and by bathing in the Mandākinī, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. || 24 ||
By worshipping Aṅkapāda, a man shall become an attendant of Śiva;
and by fully honoring Candrāditya, he shall obtain various kinds of enjoyments. || 25 ||
By worshipping Karabheśvara, one shall obtain the comfort of vehicles;
by properly worshipping Vighneśa, who is fond of sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), one shall become happy. || 26 ||
Having worshipped Kusumeśa and all the others, a man enjoys every kind of enjoyment; likewise, having bathed in the Yajñavāpī and worshipped Mārkaṇḍeśa.
O virtuous lady, having bathed at Somavatī and worshipped Someśvara, a man shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices and dwell in heaven for one yuga.
O deluder, having bathed in this calculation of torments, one obtains the desired objects both here and in the hereafter, and one never again beholds torment. || 29 ||
Having worshipped Narakeśa, one shall attain the state of the heavenly world;
thereafter, having worshipped Kedāreśa, or likewise Rāmeśvara.
By worshipping Keśavārka, a man obtains his desired fruit from Narāditya, the Lord of Good Fortune, and becomes dear to Keśava.
Then, having bathed at Śaktibheda, one is liberated from even the most terrible distress;
and having bathed in the Svarṇakṣura-Brahmavāpī and worshipped Abhayeśvara.
And at Agastyeśa, O son of Vidhi, there shall be an abode of prosperity for that man who duly worships the Liṅgas beginning with Oṃkāreśa. || 33 ||
By the grace of Maheśa, he shall obtain all his desires;
O Goddess, in Mahākālavana, there is no known number of liṅgas.
By worshipping a *liṅga* situated anywhere at all, one becomes dear to Śiva;
likewise [are] Kanakaśṛṅgā, Kuśasthalī, and Avantikā. (35)
Likewise, Queen Padmāvatī, Kumudvatī, and Ujjayinī—though distinct and bearing different names in each kalpa—are [all] known as Viśālā and Amarāvatī. || 36 ||
Indeed, having bathed in the Śiprā, whoever worships Maheśa shall obtain all desires through the grace of the two deities. || 37 ||
Having bathed in Gomatīkuṇḍa, a man attains the path to heaven;
and having bathed in Vāmanakuṇḍa, he praises [the Lord] with the Thousand Names.
He who, having bathed in the Vīreśa lake, worships Śrīdhara, the lord of all gods—who is Hari himself manifest on earth—and Kālabhairava, [attains the highest state]. (39)
Having enjoyed all prosperity, he who, having obtained the Lord of the Family, worships him with ritual offerings, shall attain the world of Śiva.
Having enjoyed various desires, one who worships Lord Mādhava at the lake of Devaprayāga shall attain the state of heaven in the end.
Having attained devotion to Mādhava and having bathed in the holy ford of Kakarāja with a restrained mind, he shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
One who is liberated from all diseases shall become wealthy and an enjoyer of pleasures;
indeed, during the journey of the inner chamber, one should worship Vighneśa, Bhairava, and Umā.
Any man who worships the Rudras, Ādityas, Suras, or others with faith, using whatever offerings he has obtained, shall become a partaker of the heavenly world.
O beautiful lady, there are many other sacred fords (tīrthas) such as Rudrasaras; by worshipping Śaṅkara at those places, a man shall become happy. || 45 ||

O knower of the rules, a man who bathes in the eight holy sites (aṣṭatīrthī) shall obtain the fruit of a pilgrimage performed with all its constituent parts; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth. (46)
All this greatness of Avanti, which destroys sin, has been told to you; by hearing it, a man is liberated from all evils.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Avantikā," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the latter portion of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 78 ||
Thus ends the *Avantīmāhātmya*.
Now begins the *Mathurāmāhātmya*,
being the seventy-ninth chapter.
Mohinī said:
"O Vāsudeva, the greatness of Avantī, which removes the sins of men, has indeed been heard by me;
now I desire to hear the greatness arising from Mathurā. (1)
Vasu said:
Listen, O Mohinī, I shall describe the auspicious majesty of Mathurā, where the Lord was born at the request of the Lotus-born Brahmā. || 2 ||
Manifesting himself there, the All-pervading Lord arrived at Nanda’s cowherd settlement;
staying there, he performed all manner of sports together with the cowherds.
And having slain the night-stalkers such as Pūtanā sent by Kaṃsa, he sported with the cowherd girls in all twelve forests.
I shall now declare to you those holy places that exist in the forests and those that are in Mathurā; listen, O Mohinī, at this moment.
The first is named Madhuvana, where the best of men, having bathed and offered libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, O Goddess, there is the second excellent forest called Tālavana, where a man who bathes with devotion becomes one who has accomplished his purpose. || 7 ||
The third is named Kumuda; having bathed there, O fair-eyed one, one obtains one's desired objects and rejoices both in this world and the next.
Next, the fourth is proclaimed as Kāmyavana, which is endowed with many sacred fords; having gone there, one becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu.
O auspicious lady, that stainless pool there, which is the most excellent of all holy fords (tīrthas), grants a man who bathes therein the station of Viṣṇu.
The fifth forest is named Bahula, which destroys all sins;
indeed, a person who bathes there shall obtain all their desires. || 11 ||
There is a sixth [tīrtha] named Bhadra-vana; having bathed there, a person, by the grace of Lord Kṛṣṇa, beholds all auspicious things. || 12 ||
O Goddess, at the seventh forest, Khādiravana, a person attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu merely by bathing there.
And the eighth is Mahāvana, which is always beloved by Hari;
having seen it with devotion, a person is glorified in the world of Śakra. || 14 ||
The ninth forest is Lohajaṅgha, where a man who bathes obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the grace of Mahāviṣṇu. || 15 ||
The Bilva forest is the tenth; O slender-waisted one, having bathed there, one goes by one's own will to the world of Śiva or the world of Viṣṇu.
The eleventh is Bhāṇḍīra, which is exceedingly dear to the yogins;
a man who bathes there with devotion is liberated from all sins.
Vṛndāvana is indeed the twelfth, which destroys all sins; O virtuous lady, there is no other forest on the surface of the earth equal to it.
Having bathed there and performed the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors, a person is liberated from the three debts and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 19 ||
The region of Mathurā extends twenty yojanas in circumference;
wherever one bathes there, one shall attain devotion to Viṣṇu.
In the midst of that is the city named Mathurā, the most excellent of all excellences,
by the mere sight of which one attains devotion to Mādhava.
O Queen of Men, at that jewel among holy fords known as Viśrānti, a person who bathes with devotion attains the station of Viṣṇu.
Near Viśrānti, on the right, is the supreme Tīrtha called Vimukta;
a person who bathes there with devotion certainly attains liberation. || 23 ||
O Queen of Men, further to the south of that is Rāmatīrtha,
where a man who bathes shall certainly be liberated from the bonds of ignorance.
Therefore, the liberation from saṃsāra is found at that supreme tīrtha on the southern bank;
having bathed there, a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
To the south of that is the holy site named Prayāga, which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
by bathing there, O Goddess, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (26)
Then there is the Kanakhala tirtha, where a man who has bathed, O virtuous lady, attains heaven and rejoices in the Nandana and other celestial groves at the end of his body's life.
To the south of that is the Tinduka Tīrtha, wherein the best of men, having bathed and obtained the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice, rejoices in heaven like a god. || 28 ||
After that, one should bathe at the Paṭusvāmin Tīrtha, which is dear to the Sun; having bathed there and beheld the Sun, one goes to heaven after having enjoyed worldly pleasures.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, to the south is the unsurpassed Dhruvatīrtha,
where one who has bathed beholds Dhruva and attains the station of Viṣṇu.
To the south of Dhruvatīrtha is the holy site frequented by the Seven Sages;
having bathed there and beheld the sages, one rejoices in the world of the ṛṣis.
To the south of Ṛṣitīrtha is the unsurpassed Mokṣatīrtha,
where indeed by merely bathing, one is liberated from all sins.
To its south is the Bodhinī Tīrtha; having bathed there and offered funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors, a human being leads them to the abode of the gods.
To its south is indeed Koṭitīrtha, where by bathing a human being,
liberated from all sins, shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
On the northern side of Viśrānti, there is a sacred site called Asikuṇḍaka; O Goddess, a man who bathes there attains the station of Viṣṇu.
To the north of Asikuṇḍa, O beautiful-eyed one, is Navatīrtha,
where a mortal, by bathing, is glorified in the heavenly world.
To the north of that is the sacred ford named Saṃyamana;
by bathing and giving gifts there, one does not behold the world of Yama. || 37 ||
North of that is another supreme sacred site known as Dhārāyatana;
having bathed there, a person rejoices together with his ancestors.
North of that is the Nāgatīrtha, where, O Mohinī, by bathing one obtains freedom from fear of serpents and is glorified in the heavenly world. || 39 ||
North of that is the holy site called Ghaṇṭābharaṇaka; by bathing there, one's sins are destroyed and one attains the state of the world of Brahmā.
To the north of this is the supreme holy site called Soma; having bathed there, the best of men, freed from sin, attains the world of Soma.
Having bathed in the Prācīsarasvatī, to the north of that auspicious place, a man indeed becomes a master of speech merely by bathing there. || 42 ||
North of that is Cakratīrtha, where a man who bathes,
having conquered the hosts of his enemies, rejoices in heaven for seven yugas.
To the north of that is situated the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha, O blessed lady, where by bathing one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Having worshipped there the Lord Śiva known as Gokarṇa according to the prescribed rites, a person attains all desires and is glorified in the world of Śiva at the end. || 45 ||
To the north of that is the holy site named Vighnarāja;
by bathing there, one indeed obtains the fruit of all undertakings without obstacle.
To the north of that is the sacred ford named Ananta; a man who bathes there obtains the fruit of the twenty-four Mathurā tīrthas.
O illustrious lady, in Mathurā the Lord Hari himself resides in the form of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), bestowing liberation upon the people of Mathurā.
One is the form of Vārāha, another is called Nārāyaṇa, the third is named Vāmana, and the fourth is Haladhāriṇī. || 49 ||

Having seen the one who bears the fourfold manifestation and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, a person attains liberation; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. || 50 ||
Having seen Raṅgeśa, Bhūteśa, Mahāvidyā, and Bhairava, and having worshipped them according to the prescribed rites, one obtains the fruit of a pilgrimage.
By bathing in the well of Catuḥsāmudrika, at the shrine of the Lord of Ganas (Gaṇeśa) known as Kubjā, and likewise in the Gaṅgā called Kṛṣṇā, one is liberated from sin.
O fair-faced one, the god Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, resides in the sovereignty over the entire district known as Mathurā.
O blessed lady, for one who has not seen Keśava in the meritorious region of Mathurā,
their birth is in vain and they shall wander in the ocean of worldly existence.
O lady of auspicious countenance, there are many other sacred fords (tīrthas) there; having bathed in them and offered something as a gift to one staying there, [one attains merit]. || 55 ||
A person does not go to an evil state; this truth has been spoken by me to you.
Furthermore, whoever causes the greatness of Mathurā to be heard or who hears it themselves, having attained devotion to Hari, shall obtain all their desires. (56)

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Mathurā," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the latter section of the *Bṛhad-upākhyāna* of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*. || 79 ||
Thus ends the *Mathurāmāhātmya*.
Now begins the *Vṛndāvanamāhātmya*,
the eightieth chapter.
Mohinī said:
O giver of honor, I have heard the greatness of Mathurā and also of the forests; now please reveal some of the secrets of Vṛndāvana as well. || 1 ||
O Brahmin, Vṛndāvana is the very form of the earth’s fame residing in solitude;
I have a desire to hear about it, so describe it to me in detail.
Vasu said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to my secret concerning Vṛndāraṇya, which I have not revealed to anyone, having received it from my supreme guru. (3)
O blessed lady, this secret of the Lord of the Gopīs was told by the high-souled Nārada to his guru, and it was told by Vṛndā to Nārada.
I shall now fully declare to you that cause for the liberation of the world;
once, Nārada, the beloved of the Blessed One, was wandering through the worlds.
O Goddess, having reached Vṛndāraṇya, he stayed on the bank of Puṣpasaras,
situated in the northwestern part of the Māthura maṇḍala.
Vṛndāvana is a fourth part [of the forest], the secret abode of the Lord of the Gopīs,
where Mount Govardhana is situated near the place of the friends.
O virtuous lady, that penance grove of Vṛndā is near Nandigrāma by the Yamunā;
on the delightful bank of the Yamunā lies the most beautiful Vṛndāvana.
O fortunate one, even there is the highly meritorious Kausuma lake;
and on the beautiful bank of the Vṛndā is a hermitage that brings supreme happiness.
At midday, Hari always rests there for a moment with his friends beneath the shade of a tree with glossy foliage.
Having sipped the cool water of the Puṣpasaras lake and performed his midday rites, Nārada stood there upon the shore of the lake.
There, in the beautiful hermitage of Vṛndāvana, O Mohinī, the cowherd girls and cowherds come and go in groups while Nārada looks on.
Then, having stayed there for one watch (yāma) in this manner, Nārada entered that wonderful hermitage when half a watch of the day still remained.
There the goddess Vṛndā resided, wholly devoted to devotion for Kṛṣṇa, offering hospitality with fruits and other gifts to those who arrived.
O blessed lady, having seen that female ascetic, Nārada, who is honored by the virtuous,
bowed with his body humbled and sat down upon the ground.
Then, at the conclusion of her meditative yoga, she opened her eyes and offered a seat to the guest, Nārada.
Then Nārada, having been honored there by Vṛndā, dwelt with her out of respect, desiring to know the secret of that Lord of the Gopīs.
Having accepted the hospitality offered by her and perceiving that Vṛndā’s inner heart was perfectly serene, the son of Vidhi (Brahmā) made his heart's desire known to her.
But she, O beautiful woman, having understood that desire through the power of meditation,
summoned her friend Mādhavī there and spoke these words.
O Mādhavī, accomplish this which is dear to the high-souled Nārada, so that my hermitage may attain great sanctity.
For one who does not provide what is pleasing to a guest who has come to his own hermitage, that hermitage is fruitless, resembling the den of a king of jackals. (21)
Then, by the command of her presiding deity Vṛndā, Queen Mādhavī took Nārada to the excellent bank of the lake.
O auspicious lady, at his command, Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, was then directed by him to bathe there in the northwestern quarter.
While the best of sages, Nārada, was immersed in that water meditating on his union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the lake itself began to submerge him.
O blessed lady, having accomplished what she desired, he went into the presence of Vṛndā;
then Nārada, having submerged himself there, emerged once more.
Then, looking all around, that woman of pure smiles beheld her own self in a wonderful female form, and she [perceived] Nārada.
Standing in the north-eastern direction, beckoning with gestures of her hand,
he beheld a beautiful woman adorned with the finest ornaments.
Then, summoned by her, Nāradī arrived at her presence; she was reassured, set at ease, and led to another location. (28)
Having brought her to that palace, which was inlaid with jeweled walls and crowded with women, he returned; she too was well-honored by them.
Then, O Goddess, having been consoled by her group of friends beginning with Viśākhā and led into the interior by one of them, she beheld the Lord of the Gopīs.
When that female messenger had returned, Nāradī, summoned by her beloved, prostrated before the Lord and, bowed down with modesty, approached his presence. || 31 ||
Embraced and delighted by the connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, she was eventually dismissed;
in due course, she reached that very lake of flowers once again. || 32 ||
Then, having been bathed there by Mādhavī at the southwest corner, Nārada attained the state of a male and was filled with wonder. || 33 ||
Then, by the command of Vṛndā, he remained there to the southeast of the lake, undertaking solitary penance, eager for a vision of her.
While the high-souled Nārada was thus performing austerities,
he sustained himself with fruits sent by Vṛndā for his livelihood.
Once, while wandering there within another hermitage, Nārada heard an auspicious sound uttered by a certain woman.
Having heard that, Nārada, who possessed the vision of the supreme self, was filled with curiosity; entering the forest and searching, he did not see that place.
Then, filled with wonder, he respectfully questioned Vṛndā;
she, in turn, related to him the entire account of Kubjā from the beginning.
A hunchbacked woman dwelling in a house on another floor was the most excellent of women for the Lord;
she herself served her own master in private according to his desire. || 39 ||
O best of sages, no one knows that [truth] except for me; therefore, I shall speak of it in brief, which you, desiring to see it, have practiced as penance.
Wakened by his mother in the morning, he bathed, ate, and, accompanied by his followers,
entered the forest of Vṛndāvana to graze the cows.
Playing with his cowherd friends and driving the cows,
he approached my hermitage here accompanied by two or three dear companions.
Satisfied by me with all his desires through the food provided in Vatsabhavana— such as fruits, roots, and other edibles— he slept with his beloved.
There, served by his dear friend Rādhā, the Beloved of Vraja sports for one and a half watches of the night in various separate groves.
There, having gone to his bed, he was fanned by Rādhā and the others while asleep;
at the end of one and a half watches, he himself awoke and honored those beloved women.
Surrounded by cowherds and cows, he goes to the cow-pen at evening, filled with great joy; having reached the place of his friends, he gathers his beloved friend Rādhikā.
Every day, that large-eyed man would go to his own home with her;
thus, while making this constant coming and going, he arrived daily at the bower.
"O child, it is seen by me alone, and not even by Brahmā, Bhava, and the other gods;
yet, O child, the power of the secret signal with the hunchbacked woman was not perceived even by me. (48)
Through your pleasing and affectionate words, I know that you shall tell me what is most secret; by the merit of offering this cosmetic ointment, I have attained the highest place of appointment.
Always intent on serving Him, she dwells with each and every one of them in manifold ways;
indeed, millions upon millions of couples reside there in this manner.
Resembling Kubjā and Kṛṣṇa, and intent on various sports,
they were born from the first couple and speak even as stationary beings.
Devoid of coming and going, eternally ever-new,
it is inaccessible to the third and has attained oneness with the second.
O Brahmin, form is characterized by diversity, yet it is unified in creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
I alone know this, and you too shall understand it after hearing what has been heard. (53)
"A mantra that reaches six ears is burnt," so it has been said;
having heard this, the sage Nārada also acted accordingly, for such [instruction] is difficult to obtain, according to the words of Vṛndā.
Reflecting upon both, the sage attained that supreme state right there; this is the secret concerning the subject matter of teacher and disciple, O knower of rites. (55)
"O auspicious one, no other person knows this Dharma; it is known by us two alone, for the speaker and the listener are one and the same."
"Therefore, there is only that one reality; there is no diversity here at all.
Thus has the secret of the Lord of Gopikās been told to you, O highly fortunate one. (57)
I shall also relate the life of Prakāśa; listen attentively, O daughter of Vidhi, wherein the truth was demonstrated to your father.
This is indeed that meritorious Brahma-kuṇḍa in the forest of Vṛndāvana;
the person who bathes there while meditating upon the form of Mūla-Veṣa [attains the highest goal].
One who dwells thus eternally perceives some degree of majesty,
wherein Govinda was meditated upon by Śakra, who had realized the truth.
O blessed lady, by bathing there at Govindakuṇḍa, one may also obtain that [fruit] which was attained by Him who sports in the forest groves, appearing in both single and manifold forms.
The rāsa dance was commenced by the cowherd women in that very same manner,
wherein the cowherds, Nanda and the others, beheld the divine glory of the Lord.
And that sacred ford named Tattvaprakāśa was revealed in the waters of the Śrī Yamunā, where the subduing of Kāliya by the cowherds took place.
And that merit-bestowing holy site (tīrtha), which removes the sins of men, is fully described; there, women, children, the elderly, and the young were rescued from the forest fire.
The cowherds [went to] that meritorious holy place (tīrtha), which removes sins through bathing, where Keśī, who was in the form of a horse, was slain by Kṛṣṇa as if in mere play. || 65 ||
Having bathed there, a person indeed attains the abode of Viṣṇu;
for it was there that the wicked bull was slain by him, and he became pure.
The famous Ariṣṭakuṇḍa grants liberation merely by bathing in it;
[therein dwell] Dhenuka, Agha, Baka, Vatsa, Vyoma, and the Asura Lamba.
Having bathed in those holy fords where [demons] were slain by Kṛṣṇa during his divine sports, a devoted man, having satiated the ancestors and the deities, [attains merit]. || 68 ||
Through the grace of Gopāla, one obtains all desired objects—whether asleep, eating, wandering, hearing, seeing, or anything extraordinary. (69)
And that field, where [merit] has been performed, bestows the attainment of heaven through bathing;
it is so even when heard, reflected upon, seen, bowed to, embraced, praised, or sought after. (70)
O auspicious lady, that sacred ford (tīrtha) where meritorious men attain their goal is the place where Śrī Rādhā performed most rigorous austerities, O blessed one.
That great and meritorious Śrīkuṇḍa is excellent for bathing, giving gifts, chanting, and other rites;
likewise are Vatsatīrtha, Candrasaras, and the lake of the Apsarases.
There is the Rudra-kuṇḍa, the Kāma-kuṇḍa, the supreme abode of Hari, enriched by the Viśālā and Alakanandā rivers, and the enchanting Nīpa grove.
The Vimala-dharmakuṇḍa, the Bhojanasthala, the Balasthāna, and the Bṛhatsānu are the meeting places of Hari. || 74 ||
Nandigrāma, the pool of Kiśorī, the Kokila forest, the ocean of milk where He reclines upon Śeṣa, and the imperishable banyan tree as the place of His divine play. || 75 ||
Rāmakuṇḍa, Cīracaurya, O auspicious one, Bhāṇḍīrabilvaka, the merit-bestowing lake called Māna, Pulina, and Bhaktabhojana. || 76 ||
O auspicious lady, this place named Vṛndāvana extends for five yojanas in every direction, containing Akrūra, Tārkṣya, Govinda, and Bahulāraṇyaka.
It is supremely meritorious, frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds, and bestows liberation merely by being seen;
even the gods long for its sight, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (78)
Even through ascetic penance, they are not capable of beholding the inner pastimes;
yet he who, having abandoned all attachments everywhere, takes refuge in Vṛndāvana— [is truly blessed]. (79)
O beautiful one, O beloved, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain in the three worlds for him who utters even the name "Vṛndāvana. (80)
He too constantly possesses devotion for the Delight of Nanda in that holy Vṛndāvana, where men, women, and monkeys [dwell]. (81)
O enchantress, worms, insects, moths, and the like; birds, trees, mountains, and wild animals—these all constantly utter the names "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa."
I consider the sight of Vṛndāvana to be unattainable even in a dream for those men who are overcome by the illusory power of Kṛṣṇa and whose minds are defiled by lust. 83.
O auspicious lady, those virtuous men by whom Vṛndāvana has been seen have made their birth fruitful; they are the objects of Hari’s grace.
But what is the use of much speaking? O daughter of Vidhi, Vṛndāvana—the meritorious and auspicious place—must be resorted to by those who desire liberation. (85)
Vṛndāvana is always visible, accessible, countable, and meditable;
there is nothing equal to it in this world for increasing one's fame upon the earth. (86)
In that ancient kalpa, there was a twice-born named Govardhana who,
being detached from all worldly existence, performed supreme austerity.
Having gone there, O Goddess, the Lord of Gods, the imperishable Blessed Viṣṇu, reached his own playground in order to grant a boon to the twice-born.
Having seen that Lord of the gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, whose chest is adorned with the radiant Kaustubha gem, and who wears earrings shaped like sea-monsters; 89.
Wearing a beautiful crown and fine bracelets, adorned with tinkling anklets, his body draped with a forest garland, and his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa sign.
Clad in yellow silk garments, with a luster like a fresh rain-cloud, he possessed a beautiful navel, a handsome neck, lovely cheeks, and a shapely nose. || 91 ||
With beautiful teeth, a lovely smile, and well-proportioned knees, thighs, and waist; an ocean of compassion, joyful, with a most serene lotus-face. || 92 ||
Having seen him, he rose up suddenly and prostrated himself on the ground like a staff;
when commanded, "Choose a boon," Govardhana spoke to Hari: (93)
"Having stepped upon my back with your feet, remain there; this is my boon.
Having heard that, he who is subject to his devotees reflected again and again.
Having stepped upon his back, he stood there, and then the twice-born one spoke again:
"O Lord, O Master of the Universe, I cannot bear you upon my own back. (95)
Therefore, remain steadfast in this very way so that he may be brought down;
from that time forward, the Soul of the Universe abandoned the brahmin Govardhana.
Sometimes, assuming the form of a mountain, he goes to the forest of yogis; in the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, the Blessed One recognized Govardhana as a brahmin.
Having attained a state of likeness with himself, he fed the mountain-like twice-born one together with Nanda and the others, satisfying him with a heap of food and a milch cow.
Perceiving him to be overcome by thirst, he caused him to drink from fresh clouds;
by that deed, he became a friend of Vāsudeva.
O Goddess, that man who worships her with devotion through ritual offerings and circumambulates her shall not be born again.
Mount Govardhana became holy by virtue of being the abode of Hari;
having seen it, one has had enough of seeing any other meritorious mountain.
O fortunate one, tell me yourself: where else on the surface of the earth is there a delightful sandy bank of the Yamunā, graced by the playful sports of Kṛṣṇa? (102)
Therefore, with every effort, one should abandon forests, rivers, and mountains— though they are very meritorious and bestow merit upon men— and always resort to Vṛndāvana.
Where there is the holy Yamunā river and the sacred Govardhana mountain, what forest on earth can be found more meritorious than Vṛndāvana? (104)
For those terrified by the impurities of the Kali age and whose minds are attached to sense objects, there is nothing else in the three worlds to be served that is superior to Vṛndāvana. (105)

In which [place] Hari always wanders with the cowherds, cows, and gopīs—He who wears a crest of peacock feathers, possesses the form of the best of dancers, has ear-ornaments of *karṇikāra* flowers, whose voice is like the song of the female swan of the flute, whose body is encircled by the Vaijayantī garland, and who, having taken from the body of Nanda the swan-like collection of jewels known as Yaśodā—[there He dwells]. (106)
Girīśa, known as Ardhanārīśvara, joined by the daughter of the mountain, performs meditation day and night in secret, his heart overflowing with devotion; likewise,
the lotus-born Brahmā holds Gāyatrī, the woman, within the hollow of his heart.
Indra indeed gazes upon that Śacī with his thousand eyes.
The Lord of the Earless protects his own beloved in secret; being a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, he fears hearing the sound of the flute—what need is there to speak of other people?
Having encountered cutting, drying, burning, and piercing, she continues to devotedly relish the nectar born from the lips of the Lord of the Gopīs. 108.

What can I possibly describe now of the destiny of those cowherd women, by whose company the son of Nanda followed into Vṛndāvana and took delight in forest bowers auspicious with the moonlight whitened by the rays of the moon during the nights?
The dust of whose feet is directly unattainable even for Śrī, Śiva, Brahmā, and others.
In that forest of the multitude of worms and living beings, even the grass-eating deer and birds that have reached it become worthy of worship by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Lakṣmī;
having attained that non-dual state and become one with Brahman, he who is devoted to it sports, affectionate with love and submerged in the waves of the ocean of bliss.
Wherein even cruel beings, born from the same womb as living creatures, cast aside their enmity at will and take refuge in that very happiness as if they were friends—
is that not like a person who, having obtained a lord, departs after completely abandoning him?
Elsewhere, one may be happy in some other place, but [truly] one is happy within the casket of Kṛṣṇa’s Māyā.
Resorting to that Vṛndāvana forest, which is the very embodiment of the merit of the entire earth,
my heart dwells eternally, having cast this world beneath it; for the Lord of the Gopīs, his mind perpetually melting with love, abides at every step.
He takes no account of whether one is lowly or exalted; he simply uplifts those who are devoted.
Remembering and seeing the cowherds, cowherd-maidens, birds, deer, mountains, trees, cattle, earth, and dust, he— who is bound by the rope of love for people who bow before him—
exercises supreme servitude toward his devotee; what else could there be greater than the Lord of Vraja?
O son of the Creator, consider the God who is to be served; as for me, I do not know him at all.
O son of Vidhi, this greatness arising from the Vṛndā forest has been declared to you in brief; nothing remains to be told.
This alone should always be heard, recited, remembered, and meditated upon by men who are afraid of saṃsāra and ever free from sin. (115)
O son of Vidhi, that pure man who hears the majesty of the Vṛndā forest, or even recites it, is undoubtedly Viṣṇu himself. || 116 ||

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Śrī Vṛndāvana," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the latter portion of the Bṛhad-upākhyāna of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 80 ||
Now begins the eighty-first chapter.
Vasu said:
"O Goddess, regarding this supreme majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha) which has been proclaimed,"
"O highly fortunate lady, having performed your pilgrimage through the circle of sacred fords (tīrthamaṇḍala), obtain [the fruit]. || 1 ||
O Queen, having taken leave of Brahmā, your father, I shall go to Vṛndāvana and wander there with the deer.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, having spoken thus to Mohinī, Vasu, her family priest, honored and repeatedly worshipped by her, departed for the world of Brahmā. || 3 ||
Having gone there, he bowed down to the Creator Brahmā, the ordainer of the worlds, and reported to him in its entirety the conduct of Mohinī.
O twice-born ones, having heard those words of the Brahmin Vasu, Brahmā was pleased and said to him: "My child, you have indeed performed a meritorious deed."
O Brahmin, that deluding daughter of mine who was appointed for the sake of the gods' mission has, having failed to accomplish her task, been cursed by you and has gone to her destruction.
Furthermore, my child, by my command she has now been restored to life by you;
therefore, who else is more successful than you? (7)
"O twice-born one, I am pleased by this excellent account of Mohinī that you have related to me; tell me what boon I shall grant you."
Thus addressed by that Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, the twice-born one bowed down and chose as his boon residence in the Vṛndā forest.
O lords of sages, having heard that, the Creator of the worlds, whose four faces were smiling and who removes the distress of those who seek refuge, said, "So be it."
Then, having bowed to the Creator, Vasu, with a joyful mind and composed in spirit,
went to Vṛndāvana and performed austerities.
O twice-born ones, as that Vasu performed his penance, five thousand groups of years passed by; then Hari himself was pleased.
Accompanied by two or three dear friends who were cowherds, he approached the best of the twice-born and said:
"Tell me, O Brahmin, what do you choose? I am pleased with your asceticism."
Then Vasu, rising up and touching the earth with his eight limbs, said:
"O Lord, I desire to dwell forever in Vṛndāvana."
Then, O best of the twice-born, Viṣṇu granted him that desired boon;
having been saluted by him once more, he indeed vanished from sight. || 15 ||
From that time forward, that twice-born remained able to assume any form at will,
constantly meditating upon the Lord who delights in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Once, while staying on the banks of the Yamunā reflecting upon him,
he saw Nārada, the son of Brahmā, arrive at Vṛndāvana.
Having seen him and paid homage to his supreme teacher, he questioned him about various dharmas that increase devotion to the Blessed One.
Thus thoroughly questioned by him, Nārada, who possessed insight into the supreme self,
recounted to him the entire future life-story of Hari.
Once, O brāhmaṇa, I went to see the God who dwells on Kailāsa, in order to ask about the future and the secret of Vṛndāvana.
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, Maheśa— who was surrounded by the Siddhas and whose own city pervaded the entire sphere of the Brahmāṇḍa— [he spoke].
I asked for my desired blessing, and Hara, smiling, said to me:
"O son of Brahmā, regarding that future conduct of Hari which you have asked about."
I shall tell you that which was previously heard from the mouth of Surabhi:
once, Surabhi was seen by me in the midst of Goloka.
Then the milch-cow, the mother of cows, being well-pleased and affectionate in heart, and associated with her own continuum, will be questioned regarding the future.
O celestial sage, he told me the future deeds of Hari: "The god Kṛṣṇa now dwells happily together with Rādhā. (25)
O Maheśāna, O Śiva, that one who brings happiness to the cowherds and cowherdesses in this Goloka once appeared in the earthly world, within the district of Mathurā.
Manifesting herself, Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, will perform wonderful pastimes in the forest of Vṛndāvana with Śrīdāmā, the beloved of Hari. 27.
Then, being enraged, she will curse her friend who is standing at the door of Viraja’s house; and he too, O fortunate one, will curse Rādhā in return.
"Go to the world of men because of a mutual curse; thereafter, Hari shall also descend to the earth at the request of Brahmā. (29)
To remove the burden of the earth, Vāsudeva, the delighter of the Yādavas, will take birth in the house of Vasudeva.
Out of fear of the demon Kaṃsa, Hari will later go to Nanda’s Vraja; having gone there, he will encounter Pūtanā, the slayer of infants.
He will deprive the Dānava Cakravāta of his life and will slay the massive-bodied Vatsāsura, the oppressor of the gods.
Having subdued the serpent Kāliya, he will uproot Yamī; having slain the unbearable Dhenuka, he will likewise slay Baka and the demon Aghāsura.
He shall slay Dāva, Pradāva, and likewise Pralamba,
as well as Brahmā, Indra, Varuṇa, and the two sons of Kubera when they are heedless.
Having rendered them free from pride, the Lord, dwelling in Vraja after slaying Śaṅkhacūḍa, Keśin, and Vyoman, will kill the demon Vṛṣa.
There he will sport with the cowherd girls for eleven years; thereafter, having reached Mathurā and having slain the washerman, || 36 ||
Then, having straightened the hunchbacked woman, broken the bow, slain the excellent elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, and killed the wrestlers headed by Cāṇūra; || 37 ||
After that, Kṛṣṇa will release his parents who were bound, slay the lord of the Yavanas, and then kill his maternal uncle Kaṃsa.
Out of fear of Jarāsandha, Kṛṣṇa dwells in Dvārakā with Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Satyā, and likewise Jāmbavatī.
Having slain Bhauma, the powerful one will marry Kaikeyī, Lakṣmaṇā, Mitravindā, Kālindikā, and sixteen thousand other wives.
Having slain Pauṇḍraka, Śiśupāla, Dantavakra, and Vidūratha, as well as Śālva, he will cause Dvivida and Balvala to be killed.
Together with Vajranābha and Sunābha, along with the inhabitants of the six cities,
he will then slay the Daitya Triśarīra, who is exceedingly powerful due to his boon.
Making both the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas the mutual cause for his action, he, eager to remove the burden of the earth, will slay them, O Śibi.
Having caused the Yadus to destroy one another by means of their own kinsmen, Hari will again return to his own abode along with his followers.
"O Śambhu, this future life-story of Hari has been told to you; go, and you shall see all of that when Hari is upon the surface of the earth. (45)
Having heard those words of Surabhi, the son of the Creator was greatly pleased and returned to his own abode; this has also been told by me to you. (46)
"And you shall, in due time, behold the deeds of the Lord of Gokula.
Having heard these words of Śūlin, Vasu’s hair stood on end with joy.
Singing and intoxicated, I delight the omnipresent Lord with my lute; thus have I described to you, O best of the twice-born, what will come to pass for this afflicted world. (48)
"Just as Gautama is, so am I also devoted to his welfare.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to that Vasiṣṭha, the twice-born, Nārada [departed].
Playing his lute and thinking of the joy of the Yadus,
Vasu went to Vraja with a very joyful heart upon hearing those words.
O brahmins, he dwelt there at all times, eager to behold the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Vasu’s Conduct," in the dialogue between Vasu and Mohinī, within the latter portion of the Great Narrative (Bṛhad-upākhyāna) of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. || 81 ||
Now begins the eighty-second chapter.
The sages said:
O virtuous Sūta, you have narrated the nectar-like life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
We have heard [this], and by your grace we have achieved our purpose. || 1 ||
Once Vasu had departed for the world of Brahmā, what did Mohinī, the delighter of Vidhi, do thereafter? You should explain that to us.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to the auspicious account of Mohinī’s deeds, how she subsequently performed the service of visiting sacred fords after Vasu.
Instructed thus by Vasu, that deluding daughter of Brahmā went,
according to his direction, to the bank of the celestial river for the purpose of a pilgrimage.
Having gone there and bathed in the Gaṅgā and other rivers, she joyfully performed the rites prescribed by the Creator according to the rules, accompanied by Brāhmaṇas.
She proceeded, performing the service of that sacred ford according to the specific rite described by her priest Vasu.
Then, at those sacred fords, they worship the gods beginning with Viṣṇu and present various kinds of gifts to the Brahmins.
Having duly offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for her husband at Gayā,
and having worshipped Viśveśvara at Kāśī, she arrived at Puruṣottama.
Having partaken of the food offering (naivedya) of the Lord of the Universe at that sacred field, she, with her body purified, subsequently reached Lakṣmaṇācala. || 9 ||
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, and having gone to the Setu and worshipped Rāmeśvara, he paid homage to Bhārgava on Mount Mahendra.
Having gone to Gokarṇa, that sacred field of Śiva, and having worshipped that Lord,
O Brahmins, he proceeded to Prabhāsa together with those best of the twice-born.
Having bathed, offered libations to the gods and others, and performed his pilgrimage rites,
she beheld Hari in Dvārakā and then proceeded to Kurukṣetra.
Having duly arranged for the journey there as well, the queen of men arrived at Gaṅgādvāra and bathed there according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having seen Kāmodā and having paid her homage with joy,
she reached the hermitage of Badarī, where the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa resided.
Then, after worshipping Kāmākṣī, she went in haste to see Siddhanātha; having paid her respects to him, she subsequently arrived at Ayodhyā. || 15 ||
Having bathed in the Sarayū according to the prescribed rites and having worshipped the Lord of Sītā, he then set out for Amarakaṇṭaka, embarking upon his mid-journey.
Having worshipped Maheśa there and having bathed in the Narmadā against the current, he beheld Oṃkāra Īśāna and proceeded to Māhiṣmatī.
Then, having worshipped Tryambakeśa, she arrived at Tripuṣkara; there, at Puṣkara, she gave many gifts according to the prescribed rites.
Having performed an internal pilgrimage for twenty yojanas, she reached Mathurā, the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
After circumambulating the city, she beheld the Caturvyūha; having bathed in the twenty sacred bathing places (tīrthas) and completed her circumambulation, she then stood there.
With a heart moistened by devotion, he gave ten thousand cows, adorned with ornaments, to the people of Mathurā after having fed them excellent food.
Having paid homage and dismissed them, she approached the Kālindī;
then that goddess entered the river Kālindī, the destroyer of sins.
Even now she has not departed, remaining instead as a guest of Yama until the end of the day—
until sunrise for those following the Smṛti rules, and until the dawn of the Aruṇa for those following the Śruti.
O Brahmins, having reached the night of the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) which is devoid of the piercing of the moon (mohinī-vedha), a man who fasts thereby defiles his vows dedicated to Viṣṇu.
O twice-born ones, having worshipped Viṣṇu on the twelfth day, one goes to Vaikuṇṭha without a doubt;
for the goddess Ekādaśī is born from Viṣṇu, while the twelfth day is born from Brahmā and is delusive.
That Mohinī was created by the Creator in rivalry with Viṣṇu’s wife;
meanwhile, the royal sage Rukmāṅgada was solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
But she was not able to prevent him from that Ekādaśī vow;
for when the king had gone to the world of Viṣṇu along with his wife and his son, [she could do nothing].
"O best of Brahmins, I have thus related to you this account of Mohinī, who remained at the end of Yama's realm, vying for the eleventh perfection."
For what purpose it was created by the Creator and how it is established here—this answer from Nārada has indeed been told to you, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (29)
In this [Purāṇa], the correct devotion to Hari is established for men step by step;
the Nāradīya Purāṇa, moreover, is endowed with ten characteristics.
The man who hears this with devotion shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu;
it is the supreme cause of the four goals of life: dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

O best of the twice-born, this eternal seed of all the Purāṇas— both that which pertains to worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and that which pertains to renunciation (nivṛtti)— is contained within this Purāṇa.
The wise son of Parāśara has related in full this Nārada Purāṇa, which is rich in extraordinary accounts.
Vyāsa proclaimed that this Nārada-saṃhitā should not be given to just anyone; having excluded his own disciples such as Paila and others, he entrusted it to me alone. || 34 ||
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, who is Vedavyāsa,
who expounded this Purāṇa-saṃhitā to the wise Nārada.
The highly fortunate sages, Sanaka and the others, shone forth when the Blessed One, in the form of a swan, [revealed] that eternal Brahman.
Therefore, let the Blessed One Nārada, who possesses direct vision of the supreme self, teach this very expansion of consciousness to these [disciples]. (37)
He indeed revealed this secret to the sage Vedavyāsa; for this secret, which is difficult to obtain on earth, has been made manifest by me. || 38 ||
Bestowing the four aims of life upon men who always hear or recite it, may the Brahmin become a treasury of the Vedas, and the Kshatriya conquer the earth. (39)
A Vaiśya shall become enriched with wealth, and a Śūdra shall be liberated from suffering;
this compendium of twenty-five thousand verses has thus been proclaimed.
Indeed, when this [work] consisting of five chapters composed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana is heard, there is the shattering of all doubts.
For men who are devoted with desire and those who are free from desire, there is liberation upon reaching the holy pilgrimage sites of Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, and Gayā.
O brahmins, [they went to] Mathurā, Dvārakā, the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
Kurukṣetra, the Narmadā, and the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
Eating sacrificial food, sleeping on the ground, free from attachment and having conquered his senses, one who has recited this Saṃhitā is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. 44.
Just as the Ganges is among rivers, so is Ekādaśī among vows;
just as Vṛndāvana is among forests, so is Kurukṣetra among sacred fields. || 45 ||
O Brahmins, as Kāśī is among cities and Mathurā is among sacred fords, so is Puṣkara among lakes; likewise is this [Purāṇa] among the Purāṇas. || 46 ||
Worshippers of Gaṇeśa, Sauras, Vaiṣṇavas, Śāktas, and Śāmbhavas—all are indeed qualified for this, whether they possess desires or are free from them. || 47 ||
Whatever desire a man or a woman contemplates with devotion, whether they listen to this or cause it to be heard, they will certainly attain that very thing. || 48 ||
One afflicted by disease is liberated from disease; one afflicted by fear becomes fearless; and one desiring victory shall conquer his enemies through the study of the Nāradīya.
Salutation to that Soul of All, who at the beginning of creation protects the universe with *rajas*, sustains it in the middle with *sattva*, and swallows it at the end with *tamas*.
Salutation to that one whose nature is Brahman, by whom the ṛṣis, Manus, Siddhas, world-protectors, lords of creatures, and those beginning with Brahmā were created. || 51 ||
That from which words turn back and where the mind cannot enter—that one should know to be the form of the Self, for the Self is consciousness without form. 52.
I bow to Him who is beyond qualities and beyond darkness, by whose truth this world unfolds in its manifold forms as reality. (53)
I bow to that stainless one, the all-pervading Lord who is without birth in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, and who shines in manifold forms as the single-syllabled reality.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings has arisen from the Stainless One; that in which it abides and into which it dissolves is Truth, Knowledge, and Non-duality. 55.
The Śaivas call him Śiva; those who know the Sāṅkhya call him Pradhāna; the Yogins call him Puruṣa, O Brahmins; and the people who are Mīmāṃsakas call him Karma. || 56 ||

I bow to that which is the all-pervading Lord for the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the power of consciousness for those who contemplate power, and the non-dual Brahman for others— the locus of diverse forms and actions.
Devotion to the Blessed One brings about the very form of the Blessed One for men;
having obtained that, who would desire any other gain, except for a beast? (58)
O twice-born ones, for those wandering beings who are turned away from the Blessed One, there is no liberation from the forest of worldly existence without the company of the virtuous. (59)
For the virtuous, who are well-behaved and bring benefit to the whole world,
and the Brahmins who are compassionate toward the wretched— those who have taken refuge in them are indeed delivered.
You are most blessed in the world, O sages esteemed by the virtuous,
since you repeatedly proclaim the ever-fresh glory of Vāsudeva.
I am blessed and I am graced by you all, who have caused me to remember Hari himself—the cause of all causes—who is the auspiciousness of the world. (62)

Oṃ! Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Hearing and Other Acts Pertaining to This Purāṇa," in the latter part of the Great Narrative (Bṛhad-upākhyāna) within the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Mahāpurāṇa. || 82 ||
This Nāradīya Mahāpurāṇa is completed.
